ticisme,and carried out by brutal iglorance, and

—if the term 28 not 'misapplied -to those who
could- .associate ,themeelves with a body of. rrif-

CroWels of unemployed men, women, and children
throng the streets and thoroughfares, with haggard
looks-sad sunken eves, which betoLen hearts fast
sett* down into•deepair. It is .a fearful picture
to contemplate,---mill,s closed, shediiille, and store,
housesiempty ; a:population of twotcillions of peo-
ple suddenly converted into paupers, with little.oe.

theijaws of starvation. Week•Sby -week this has"

be :•ernoontered. ',Speculation has- been rife at

mains of a rich man, Whose preperty is left to be
the .prey of greedy lawyr.rs and famishing barristers;
Something is done to alleviate the hunger of the
poor, starving workmen, but whatisit-f The Lord
Mayor of London senU us a few thousands, and.
the A.lan-:.!liester Central Relief Committee a few,
hondreds,vreekly to feed hosts of unemployed-4
drop in the ocean of misery, still a welexne drop-7:
a fewtweakhy millowners :nun their machinery a few.
days per week, just to .enable them to stop their
cottage rugs, and help themselves to the labour of
their starving hands. Engineers, . overlookera,
, maehinists,:aud skilled hands are to be-seen break-
ing ,stones, delving ponds,- cleaning ,reservoirs,

—mills and cotton are profitless,, that the -skilled

We art, I trust, &ring our duty-so far as lie in
our Dower to arrest the present :sufferings. At
Padiham and Haberham the condition of the :pooris
deplorable, atd requires every aid to .alleviateit.
The employers I am sorry to say, are quite indifferent
to the cries of their people—old'gratiges are rennin-
bered, feuds revived, past struggles recovuted,,and
feelings which ought to be buried are often resusi-
cated before the relief committee. lam IntX.o and
more convinced every day that sooner than apply to
their employers for relief, thousands of indeperkdent
minded men will enter the workhouse.
The relict committee of Padiliam presided over by
an executive of employers is described' by the poor
as a perfect Inquisition. Before relief is given the
applicant must hring a schedule filled up by his em-
ployer or employers for the last twelve months. His
earnings, savings, debts, &c., are minutely chronicled
under a severe cross-examination. He is censured,
bullied, and harassed, with scores of irrevelan ques-
tions, to refuse one of
,which is followed by dismissal.
Is this rational treatment of the poor? There is
only one coure open to the working classes of Lan-
cashire to remedy this, and that is to establish a
working man's Relief Committee in every town to
counteract this ruffianly treatment. We have es-
tablished one in Padibam, and appeal to all working
men to help us by their weekly pence. Those who
are in work will not feel the sacrifice, and I trust the
time is not far distant when we ourselves shall be in
condition to repay it to our fellow workmen.—l am,
JOSEPH PEACOCK, Hon. Secretary
to the Padiltam Operative Relief Committee.

kindness in °poling your columns to our wants,

END—lnformation has been received by Mr. Hum-
phreys, coroner for the eastern division of the county,
from Mr. Pemble, one of his summoning officers, of
the discovery of tha body of a newly-born female child,
which was found under the following circumstances,
and which, it appears, has come to its death by some
violence :—On Saturday afternoon a man was passing
along the side of a lock at Shadwell, connecting the
Regent's-canal with the Thames, when he saw a bundle
floating on the surface of the water. He took it out,
and found that it had been tied up with apiece of cord.
He untied the cord; upon having done which he dis-
covered the contents to consist of the body of a dead
infant female child, which was wrapped up in pieces of
old linen, and there was a piece of tape or twine round
its throat. The unfortunate infant appeared to have
been a few days old, and to have been some tin 0 in tho

DEVELIATE ATTEMPT AT SUICIDE 13Y A GUARDSMAN.
—A. singular and desperate case of suicide was at-
tempted by a private of the Coldstream Guards,
named Sayers, in Sale-street, Paddington; on Satur-
day night, under the au.hjoined circumstances. At
half-past eleven o'clock on Saturday night police-con-
stable 175 D was attracted to a scene of uproar and
excitement near a public-house in the above street,
and found the soldier struggling in a semi-unconscious
state, in the arms of two civilians, who stated that
they had been in his company in the course of the
evening, and that he had just wilfully swallowed some
oxalic acid while under the influence of liquor. The
constable removed the wretched man with assistance
to St. Mary's Hospital, near at hand, and his case
being made known, four or five medical gentlemen of
the hospital immediately attended on him and admini-
stered several emetics, which seemed to produce the
desired results, and he was at once put to bed. In his
conscious state he pulled out of his p9cket a piece of
paper labelled poison,' which he said contained oxalic
acid, that he purchased with his last penny at the
chemist's shop of Mr. Watts, Edgware. road, avowedly
for the purpose of removing stains from his tunic, and
instead of applying it in that way he took it by means
el eating it up in its dry state. He is progressing
favourably, Anil Lopes are entertained of his recovery.

WITHDRA.WAL OF THE BUDGET.

BEIILIN, Sept. 20.

In the sitting of the Chamber of Deputies to-day
Count von Bismark-Sehonhausen read the following
communication from Government :

-" The Chamber baying rejected the charges for
reorganising the army included by government in
the 'budget for 1862, ;the ,government must presume .
hat the:house would adopt a • similar•course with
regard to the new items in
.the budget for 1863.
The government, on its part, maintaining the views
already _expressed by its organs upon the occasion
of the discussion of the budget of 1862, the results
of a present debate upon the budget of 1863 would
not only be unfavourable to the chances of any
further settlement of the question, but would, on
the contrary, greatly enhance its difficulties. Look-
ing at:the spirit of the discussions which have hitherto
taken place,' it seems impossible to arrive at an.
understanding without the introduction of a fresh.
budget.. On the proposition of the ministry, his
Majesty has therefore 'authorised me "to withdraw
tho budget for' 1863. By this act, however, the
principle of the budget being early submitted to •
the house is not conceded. But the government is
of opinion that its present duty is not to raise still
higher the obstacles to an understanding. Next
session we shall lay before the house the budget ,
for' 1863, with a bill supporting as a vital condition
the rborganisation of the army, and we shall at the •
same time 'submit to the Chamber the buiget for
1864." •

many. The resolution was pussed with but one
dissentient voice.

articles.text:
ADDRESS OF GA.RIBALDI. TO TUE
ENGLISLI _NATION:

TO THE ENGLISH NATION.

It is while under the double pressure of bodily and
mental pain that man can most truly and most acutely
appreciate good and evil, and, leaving the authors of
his misery to eternal shame, devote unlimited affection
and gratitude to his benefactors. And that to you, 0
people of England,.
inmost I owe a heavy debt f
my u. You
ebotfor benefits be-
stowed, I feel in the recesc
were my friends in prosperity, and now you continue
the precious boon in the days of my adversity. May
God reward you! And my gratitude is the more
intense, 0 worthy people, inasmaeh as, rising as
it must do beyond the mere level of indivi-
dual feeling, it becomes sublime in the gene-
ral sentiment towards those nations whose pro-
grecs TM represent. Yes you are deserving of
the gratitude of the 'World, because you offer an asylum
for misfortune; from whatever part it may come; and
you identify yourselves with misery, pity it, and relieve
it. The French or Neapolitan exile finds in your bosom
shelter from his tyrant;
,he finds sympathy; ho is
helped, because an exile, because unhappy. The
Haynaus—the hardened instruments of siutoerats—find
no rest in your nerd land, and fly terrified before the
bitter scorn of your generous sons. And, in truth,
without your noble bearing, what would Europe bee?
Tsranny seizes its exiles in those other lands where
v!etne is unnatural, where liberty is a lie; but they
are still safe on the sacred soil of Albion.. I, like so
many others, seeing the cause of justice trampled under
foot in so many parts of the world, despaired of human
progress. But, turning to you, my mind is calmed—
calmed by the contemplation of your fearless progress
towards that end to Which the human race seems called
by Providence. Proceed on your way, 0 calm, uncon-
quered nation and be less tardy. in calling your sister
peoples into the same path of. .nman progress. Ca_u
the French nation to co-operate with you. -rem two
are worthy to march bana_in_hawl in the vangnar.d. or,:e
social progress! Yes, call bet! 111 all you:. meeatese
let concord between the two great sisters be your cry.
Yes, call her! Call to her always, and in every manner
—with your voice, and with the voice of her great exiles;
___of Victor Hugo, the high priest of human brotherhoo&
Tell her that conquest is, in this age, an anomaly the
,
emanation of an unsound mind. Why should we covet
the land of others, when all men ,should be as bite-,
tbren ? Yes, call her !: And she, forgetting that.,
sho is temporarily, under the dernimion of the Genius,
of Evil—if not to-day, to-rnotrow ;if not to-morrow, _
later—will reply as she ought to your generous and re-
generating appeal. Call, and at once, the bold sons of •
Helvetia, and clasp them firmly to your breast! The war- -
like children of the Alps—the vestals of the sacred fire of
liberty on the Continent of Europe—they will be with
you. What a host r Call the great American Re-
public, for she is, in truth, your daught(r, and is
struggling now for the abolition of that slavery which
you have already so nobly proclaimed. Help her to
escape from the terrible strife waged against her hy.
the traders in human flesh. Help her, and then place
her by your side at the grcat assembly of •nations—
that final work of the human intellect. Call to your
side all those people who would be free, and lose not
an hour. The initiative, which belongs to you to-day,
may to-morrow concern
.another. May God forbid
such a calamity !" Who ever more gallantly than Franco
in 'B9 assumed that responsibility ? At that solemn
moment she held up 'Reason' to the world, crushed
tyranny, and consecrated free brotherhood. Now, after'
nearly a century, she is reduced to combat the
liberty of nations, to protect tyranny:and over ths
altar of Reason to erect the symbol of that wicked and,
immoral monstrosity which is called the Papa..
Arise, then, Britannia, and at once! Arise with your '
undaunted brow, and point out to the peoples the path-
, they must tread! With a congress of the World to dc---
cide between nations, war would be an impossibility.-
No longer would there exist those standing armies-
which make liberty impossible. What weapons! What,
defences! What engines of attack and detei,ce: And
then the millions squandered in implements of de- .
struction would be employed in fomenting the in-
dustry and diminishing the misery of the human.
race. Begin, then, 0 people of England; and for
the love of God, initiate the vast human coeepeet, and
bestow this great gift on the present generation! Be-
sides Swi:zerland and Belgium, you would see other •
nations, urged on by the good sense of the people, ac-
cept your invitation, and hasten to enrol themselves
under your banner. Let London now be the seat of
this congress, which shall be in future agreed on by a
mutual compaet of arrangement and convenience. -
Once more, God bless you! May He repay you for
the benefits you have heaped so prodigally on me
With gratitude and affection, yours,
Varignano, Sept. 28.

AMERIC.d.

NEW Yons, Sept. 18.—The Federal forces which
surrendered at Harper's Perry consisted of the 12th New
York State Militia, 87th Ohio, Bth New York Cavalrit
111th New York Volunteers, 126th New York Volun-
tem, two companies of the sth New York Artillery,
and one Maryland Regiment. The battle at Harper's
Ferry commeneed on the 12th by a Confederate attack
on the Federals stationed on Maryland Heights.
The Federals sent reinforcements from Harper's Ferry
to Maryland Heights, and the engagement continued
daring the 12th and 13th. The Federals evacuated
Maryland Heights on the 13th, and crossed on a pontoon
bridge to Harper's Ferry, previously spiking the guns
on Maryland Heights. On the 14th the Confederates
assembled on London Heights and opened their batte-
ries from that point, and also from Maryland Heights.
Skirmishing continued during the 14th. During the
night of the 14th the Confederates planted additional
batteries on London Heights' and another battery on the
opposite side of the Potomac to the right of the Federal
position, thus enfilading the whole of the Federal in-
trenchments. The Confederates opened fire from these
batteries on the morning of the 15th, when a Federal
council of war was held, and a white flag displayed.
During the hoisting the white flag a shell struck Colo-
nel Miles, who commanded at Harper's Ferry, wound-
ing him mortally. The Federals surrendered to General
Jackson on the following terms :—` Officers and men to
have ready parole. ()liters to retain their side arms
and private property. All United States property to be
turned over to the Confederates.' The Confederates
paroled about 8,000 prisoners, and the New York Tri-
bune correspondent says they captured 10,000 stand
of arms, 40 cannons, and cartridges and stores. 1,500
Federal cavalry succeeded in escaping previously from
Harper's Ferry, and captured en route Confederate
General Longstreet's baggage -train. Rumours from
various sources state that the Confederates immediately
evacuated Harper's Ferry,and that the Federal General
Burnside has since Occupied it. The Federal General
Morgan, who is surrounded at Cumberland Gap, writes
that his troops are in good health and spirits, and that
his condition is in every respect better than that of the
enemy who surround him; It is stated that the reported
investment of Charleston by the Federal gunboats has
received some confirmation in, a letter received from the
Federal squadron, stating that Fort Sumter had been
fired upon with shot and shell, resulting in serious
damage. Fighting continues at Mumfordsville, Ken-
tucky, between the Confederates, under Bragg, and the
Federals, under Wilder, with a portion of Buell's army.
It was reported on the 16th that Buell himself
had arrived and joined in the engagement. The
Governor of Pennsylvania states that 72,000 have
responded to his call for the defence of the State,
and he expects the number will 'be increased to 100000.
These men are being furnished with equipments
and being moved to the State border as soon as possible.
Drafting is to comment.° in the State of New York on
the let of October. An explosion Occurred yesterday at
No. 8 Arsenal at 'Pittsburg. One hundred and seventy
boys and girl were employed; eighty were killed by the
explosion. The. medical Director General of General
M'Clellan's staff has telegraphed to New York for surgical
aid for the wounded in the late battles. The Federal
Commodore, John Percival, died yesterday at Boston.
The Associated Press, Washington, dispatches, dated
Sept. 17 (evening), says :—lntelligenee from near the
front of our army shows that, at noon yesterday, the retreat-
ing columns of the rebels under Gen. Longstreet were
overtaken by Gen. M'Clellan's advance division, when
they formed in line of battle on the range of the small hills
on the west bank of Antitam Creek, between Rohoea-
vile and Sharpsburg Ford on the Potomac. Late in the
afternoon more of our division came up, and shortly
after five o'clock attacked the enemy, the battle lasting
four hours, and the rebels, according to all advices,
getting the worst of it, being nearly surrounded, and
almost exhausted in provisions and ammunition. This
morning the battle was renewed, leading to the more than
probable inference that during last night' Jacks&l's, .or
some other diviiion; which left Harper's Ferry yesterday
morning, ostensibly for Martinsburg, has reinforced the
rebelarmy. The battle eontinaedduring the whole day.
No official news of this day's contest is at hand-to-
night, but the war department, nevertheless, has not an
unfavourable word at. a late, hour. No official news had
been received from the battle-field of yesterday and to-
day, owing to the interruption of the telegraphic com-
munication. A messenger ,who has arrived from the
army reports everything was progressing satisfactorily
when he left. That there could be.no doubt of a suc-
cessful result. The fight has raged some 12 hours, and
has undoubtedly been most desperate. Wounded
officers arrived here to-night from Western Maryland,
say when they left, at seven o'clock this, morning, a
battle commenced at Burkittsville about two miles from
Centreville.

THE FIGHTING IN WESTERN VIRGINIA.,
•
, A letter from Gailipolis, Ohio, dated' the 14th, briefly
describes the fighting which had been taking place in
Western n Virgiia :
_ _ _ _ _

On Wedneisday, a column of the enemy, about 500
strong, said to be under the command of General Loring,
the first notice of whom was his appearance in our rear,
between Fayette and Gauley, made ax attack on the
34th and 37th Ohio' under Colonel Siber, numbering
1,200 men, encamped at Fayette. A desperate battle
was fought, lasting till dark. Our forces cut their way
through, reaching Gauley during the night, having lost
100 killed and wounded. Meantime another column of
the enemy approached Gauley Bridge on the Levrisbur,
road, cutting off the 47th Ohio, two companies of the
9th Virginia, and one company of the 2nd Virginia
Cavalry, who were at Summerville. Nothing has since
been heard of them. Under these circumstances, Col.
Lightbum's front, flank, and rear being threatened by
an overwhelming force, he was compelled to evacuate
Gauley, which was successfully done on the 11th, after
destroying all the Government property he was unable
to bring away. He moved down the Kanawha in two
columns, one on each side of the river, reaching Camp
Platt on the afternoon of the -12th, skirmishing the
whole way here. He massed his troops on the north
bank of the Kanawha, but being hard pressed retreated
during the night, reaching Elk River just below
Charlestown. On the 12th he made another stand
on the lower bank of the Elk River, where a des-
perate fight ensued, lasting from morning till dark.
Our forces shelled and burned Charlestown, two
houses only being left. The result of the fight is
unknown. Nothing has been heard of Lightbum since
Saturday at six p.m. Up to that time our troops were
holding the ground and punishing the enemy severely.
It is understood that our forces destroyed all the salt
works. Lightburn brought 600 loaded waggons safely
to Elk River. The retreat to Elk River was conducted
in good order. Great anxiety is fe!t for the safety of
Lightburn's command, as well as Point Pleasant and
Gallipolis. The militia aro flocking here from this and
the adjacent counties. The enemy's force is represented
at 10,000.

OPERATIONS- IN TENNESSEE,

A dispatch from Nashville, Tennessee, dated the 11th,
is ai follows :—The whole of General Buell's army is
hastening to the support of this city, which is now
menaced by General Bragg, who follows our rear guard
at a respectful distance. The city is being fortified.
General Thomas will be placed in command, with orders
to defend the city at all hazards. Before this r.i.aches you
the fate of Nashville will doubtless have been decided.
An advance, composed of the Seventy-ninth Pennsylva-
nia, Twefity-fourth Illinois, First Wisconsin, and Seven-
teenth Kentucky, accompanied by two batteries, have
left here to tender their respects to 'General Kirby
Smith's rear. Fifteen thousand men, under General
Men, will leave to-night for the same destination.
Eight thousand men from the army of General Rosen-
cram, under command of General Jefferson C. Davis,
have arrived here to-day for the purpose of reinforcing
General Buell. Major Polk is in town to-day, a refugee
from Coluna\ia. Capitol Hill is being fortified. Gen.
Bragg will not catch us napping. The Secessionists are
'very bold, the Unionists trustful and undaunted.

LOCKED LT IN A RAILWAY Goons VAN.—About
midnight on the 27th ult. the attention of police ser-
geant Wines was attracted by cries proceeding from one
of the Taff Vale goods vans at the docks. lie went to
it, and found a man locked up in it. The sergeant im-
mediately handed the man over to the railway police.
Ile stated that ho got into the von at Dines and went
to sleep. When he awoke he discoveied that he was
()eked up in the van at Cardiff.
There was extraordinary excitement caused a few
.days since, in consequence of the report being circulated
that one of the domes of the International Exhibition had
fallen in, and a frightful loss of life had ensued. People
who had relatives and friends at the Exhibition rushed
off at once in consternation to ascertain the truth of the
report, and the greatest suspense and anxiety were
generally felt. It was one of the most abominable and
-malicious canards that the public (not the newspaper,
this time) have got up. It would not be, perhaps, im-
possible to traco the report to the idea that suggested it,
but the author or authors naturally were lost in the
mass that helped at last to spread the rumour.—auri

WEALTH OF GEN_EBAL GARIBALDI!

The --following report has been forwarded by Mr.
Partridge to the Garibaldi Italian Unity Committee
Spezzia Sept 20.
The reports received in England of General Gari-
baldi's health, and of the state of his wounds, were so
various, contradictory, and alarming; that. I was com-
missioned by some of the general's friends to visit him
professionally, and to ascertain from actual observation
lkis real condition.

, I arrived at Spezzia on the 16-th of September, and I
have since that time daily visited the General at Varig-
nano, in company with Dr. Prandina and *his other
medical attendants; and I have been constantly present
at the morning dressings of the wound. I have been
further permitted, through the courtesy of the surgesuzs,
to make a personal examination into th nature.and ex-
tent of the injury.
The accident may be described shortly as a transverse
compound fracture of the right internal' malleolus
(ankle bone), produced by a rifle shot, which, though it
opened the joint by a small aperture, did not eater it,
nor lodge itself in any other part of the limb. The
outer ankle bone remains uninjured, nor does the astra-
gains (the great pulley-like bone of the foot, which
sustains the leg), appear to have been injured; the
most careful examinations made immediately after the
accident, and since, have led to the conclusion that no
other bone except the tibi I (or greater bone of the leg)
was implicated in the injury. At first severe inflam-
mation s welling, and excessive pain followed upon
the infliction of the wound; but these were sub-
dued by cold appplications, cataplasms, leeches,
and rest, so that now the ankle and 51u-rounding
parts present nearly their natural size and form—
the foot being almost at a risht angle with the leg, .and
otherwise in excellent-condition, The wound, toe cir-
cumference of which (on its superficial aspect) is rather
larger than that of half a franc, looks well, and dis-
charges healthy matter, mingled with molecular frag-
ments of exfoliating bone, which are rarely larger than
grains of sand. The present unswollen state of the
ankle, and of theparts around t, permits of an examina-
tion; which has confirmed Vie assurance given by other
circumstances, that the bullet did not enter the joint,
nor effect a lodgment elsewhere. The injured par-talte
now free from inflammation, and unless moved are no
longer painful.. The wound is simply dressed with
charpie, spread with cerate, and covered with.a light
,pouliice ; the foot being maintained at rest and in posi-
tion by a suitable apparitus of small pads, pillows and
bandages. The wound of the left thigh, which Was ;light
and superficial, is now well. . - , .

The neral's manner is very patient aria tranquil-;
his health is fairly good, though he is mach emaciated;
his appetite is tolerable, his pulse is quiet, his tongue is
clean and moist, and, upon the whole, he sleeps: well.
He has within the last two-days been removed into a
larger, more airy, and quieter chamber than that which
he at first occupied. Every one about the general seems
attentive to his Wants and wishes, and his 'friends have
supplied him—and 4 hope will Continue to do se—with
those necessaries and comforts which his situation de-
mands. My opinion is, that, bearing in Mind his
habitually abstemious habits, if mental as well as bedily
repose are steadily enforced, if the injured limb be kept
at perfect rest, if the general health and strength be
sustained by suitable nourishments—and, if need be,' by
stimulants—by well-aired; well-kept, and quiet rooms;
and, lastly, by a continued supply of those comforts
necessary to his present condition,- the general will,
with time—certainly some months—and care, have a
good, useful foot, though the ankle joint may become
stiff, or, at the best, be only partially movable. I beg'
to express my entire concurrence 'in the treatment
pursued by the surgeons who attend General Garibaldi,
and who dress his wound with solicitous care and skill.

_
Upon one occasion I had the good fortune' to see
General Garibaldi in company with 'Professor Zanetti
of Florence, and I was gratified to find that my view of
past and Of- the prospective treatment, under certain
contingencies of this anxious case, coincided with those'
of that eminent surgeon. • - cannot cOnclucle this report
with expressing my grateful sense of the prompt
,aid
afforded me by.the authorities her in 'furtherance -of
the Objects of 'my visit ; and I would also especially
acknowledge the frank reception and kindness of General
Garibaldi's medical attendants, Drs. Ripari, Praudina,
Albanese, Bazile, and others with whom for the time
being I have had the pleasure of being thrown into
daily association. MCLIAILD PARTninoE, -P.n.s.,
Surgeon to King's College hospital; Professor of
, Anatomy in Kings College; London'; and Mem-
ber of .the Council of 'the Royal College of Sur-
geons
,of England. .

The question respecting whichno many doubtful ru-
mours have been _circulated sat length decided. A com-
munication from. the Prennt-i- has,been received by hr.
Longley, Archbishop of ork, at his palace, Bishops-
thorpe offering the vacant see for his acceptance. llis
grace Yost no time in intimating to Lo -d Palmerston his
willingness ta undertake the responsible duties attached
to the Prithaey. The antecedents of the new archbishop are
of a Very honourable chanicter ;
.and although he occu-
pied the see of York for two Years only, he is held in' the
highest estimation by the • clergy and citizens, and, his
removal will cause a
_general feeling of regret. 'His
grace, who wan born. in 17D4, was educated
at Westminster and Oxford, where he dis-
tinguished himself as a first - rate classical
scholar, filling. the position .in the University
of College Tutor, Censor, and Public Examiner.,
Ho was subsequently curate of Cowley, Oxon,.
in 1823, and rector of Wrot-Tytherley, Hants, from
'1827 to 1829. In the latter year he was elected head
master of Harrow School, the duties of which Past. he
rerformed until 1835, when he was appointed first
bishop of 'Ripon.
_ln 1856,' on the resignation of Dr..
Maltby, he was translated to the see of' Durham' from
which, in May, 1860, he was elevated to the Arc-
hbishopric of York, on the death of 'Dr. Musgrave. Dr..
Longley was most active in the discharge of his
episcopal functions as Bishop of Durham and exerted
himself nobly in. raising a pecuniary fund the benefit
of the sufferers by the calamitous accident in the Burra-'
don colliery, in 1860, while his -zeal and energy in his.
recent sphere of spiritual duty. resulted in the establish-
'ment of the York"Diocesaia Church Building and Endow-'
ment Aid Society, in the furtherance of which; mainly.
through his unwearied efforts,many thousands of pounds'
have been subscribed.

QUEEN VICTORIA AND THOMAS. CAMPDELL,.—The
following story narrates the most graceful compliment
and delicate return ever made by royalty ;—I was at
her Majesty's coronation, in Westminster Abbey,. said
Campbell, and she conducted
_herself so well, during
the long and fatiguing ceremony, that I shed tears many
times. On returning home, I resolved, out of pure
esteem and veneration to send her a copy, of all my
works. Accordingly, I lad them bound up, and went
personally with them to Sir Henry Wheatly, who when
he understood my errand, told me that her Majesty
made it a rule to decline presents of this kind, as it
placed her under obligations which were unpleasant to.
her. Say- to Her Majesty, Sir Henry,' I replied,_
that there is not a single thing the Queen can touch
with her, scepture in any of her dominions which I covet;
and I therefore entreat you, in your office, to .present
them with my devotion as a subject' But the next
day they were returned. I hesitated,' continued
Campbell, to open the parcel; but:on doing so, I fund
to my inexpressible joy, a note enclosed desiring my
autograph on them. Having complied with the wish, I.
again transmitted the Books to her Majesty.; and in
the course of a day or two, received in return this
elegant engraying,. with I or. Majesty's authograph, as
you see below,' He then directed particular attention
to the Royal signature which ,was. in her Majesty's
usual bold and beautiful handwriting
GIUCCIOLI AT BYRON'S GRAYE.—The lady went into
the Church alone. From the door, and before even there
was time to close it,. the attendant saw the visitor
prostrate herself upon the flags which cover the remains
of Byron. The door was closed and-she was left alone.
Alone with the dead poet—the dead. lover. , For this was
the Countesi Giucciolicalled then and now by a diffe-
rent name. She had been visiting with her husband in
England; and came a considerable way to have this:last
interview. She remained thus alone in the church,
while the servant and the attendant. waited outside, for
an hour and more. -What strange memories and wild
regrets must have passed through her mind during that
hour, which surely was not all absorded impious prayer
and mere devotion? What invitable, pardonable regret
for the youth which was one, and the love, such as it
was, which had left nothing behind but a melancholy,
lustreless memory. There is a dismal little story by Ei
poor, broken, ruined man of a right genius, who died in
Paris twelve months ago, of a French artist, at the inter-
ment of one he loved, who just before the grave was
closed flung himself passionately, on. the earth-covered
coffin and exclaimed in a wild burst of egotistic sorrow,
Oh my youth—it is my youth which is buried there!'
She who knelt upon Byron's grave may perhaps have
felt the same pang—have remembered days of passion
which at least had something of youth in it, and a bright
country, not like Nottinghamshire, and an admirer whom
such a woman could hardly fail to love. It was a mild
and melancholy day of autumn, and a soft sunlight must
have floated through the dingy old lattice windows and
may have fallen perhaps upon the very slab on which
the Italian woman knelt. Those' who walked and waited
outside had. little idea what a peculiar and. lamentable
claim the foreign ,visitor had to a place alone. in that
Church. She wds spared on her coming out all starings
of curiosity, and passed away as she had come, like a
shadow—like the brief days- when her llama was asso-
ciated with that of the poet. and her influence was felt
. . • ..• • -

articles.text:
TEE GREAT POISONING CISB:

On Saturday, the 27thr this case, whin ch occupied the
attention of the, judge at . the Central Criminal Court
for three days, was brought to a termination. We
must content ourselves with merely giving a summary
of the evidence. For the information of those of our
readers who may not have read the evidence given
before the magistrate at the preliminary examination,
we will commence with the leading circumstances of the
case. Mrs. Soames was residing at a house of her own
in Alfred-street, Bedford-square, and took lodgers, of
whom the prisoner was one. Two daughters, the one
married, the other unmarried, were living with the
deeeased, and it does not appear that Catherine Wilson
attempted to keep them out of their mother's room during
her short but fatal illness. They seem to have been willing
• enough that the prisoner should undertake tee nursing,
and to have believed her to be acting under the. doctor's-
orders ; nor does it appear- to:, have struck them
or another lodger as strange that she should lock
up the medicine bottle, after giving each dose, in
her room. Until the morning of Saturday, when ,
the deceased, having just before spoken of herself as
better, took some of the, mixture and immediately fell
into an agony which ended in death, there was nothing
which could suggest the idea of foul play to any one ig-
norant of medicine. Immediately afterthis the prisoner
volunteered a statement to Miss Emma Rose which
could not but weigh strongly against her. She called
me,' says this witness; 4 into her room, and said she
wanted to speak to me—she had a secret
.to tell me. I
asked, her what it was, and she said it was about Mrs.
Soamea's death. She said it was not a natural one, But
she had made away with herself. Shessaid she was
acquainted with some man who had borrowed money
of her and had disappointed her, and that she had
taken something to destroy herself. She said that she
had taken it in brandy and water in her
_presence. I in-
quired. of hei hove she MVO to ailawltekto db.aueh a
thing, and why she did not tell her family or the medi-
cal man, end the prisoner replied that- 44 was not her
basing* I then Said to the prisoner,e4 You are the,
villain)"

The main facts having been proved in evidence, the
addresa of the:counsel for the defence, and_ the reply of
the prosecution having been completed,
Mr. Justice Byles, the presiding judge,. proceeded to
sum up the evidence to the jury. He said he did not
-propose to go through the wholnof the evidence that
had been given, during a period of two long days, he
should only i:paother. them' with details if lie were to do
so; but he proposed to lay befere them what appeared to
be the principal points in that evidence that Were likely
to guide them to a decision. The first point of importance
in the case was the -evidence of -Mr. Barnes, the hall;
, brother of the decease-4 that on the day she-was.first
taken ill he gave her the Sum of £9, and that she took
it away with her ; and it was a very serious inquiry,
indeed, what had become of that money. He did not see
,anything in the evidence to contradict the suggestion
that the. deceased arrived at her own heuse, with this
money, in her pocket, and she was taken ill very shortly
afterwards, and. the money was never seen again. It
then appeared from the history of the case that early
the next morning she was taken very ill, and that she
stated that she had been attacked by sickness- the . ma-
meat after she Went to bed. The prisoner herself ap-
peared to have been the first person to raise the supposi-
tion that poison was the cause of this illness, and that
the deceased had taken it herself, but the evidence ap-
peared to be utterly inconsis:ent with such a supposition.
If the deceased Irld taken poison it was not likely that
she would have acted as -she did when she merely de-
scribed her mal tdy as a biliousattack, and did not appear
at all alarmed or to have the least idea that she was
going to die. Dr.'Whidborne was not called in, until
the Friday, and they had heard his evidence with regard
to. the' medicine that he had sent, and to the fact that the
deceased suffered great agony after taking th it ei•dieine,
and upon these facts they would form their own. eon-
j ecture wether the Medicine- itself.could. have caused. that
agony, and whether it was übt more probable that some-
-thing else had been mixed with it.-, With regard to.the
question of snicide, he asked the jury whether it was
probable if the prisoner, as she represented, had really
seen the de'eeased take the
.poison, she would. ha-ye
witnessed her dreadful agonies in the presence- of her
daughters and not have mentioned what had occasioned
them? They would remember that two witnesses, Mrs.
Matthews: and Mrs. Allen, spoke- to a statement
of a similar kind having, been made by the prisoner.
What, then, was the evident object.cf this extraordinary
story about the man who. was going, to Unmarried. to:the
deceased? It answered three purpOsee—to account for
the loss of the money, the suicide,. and also, suggested'
the possibility that poison might havebeen administered
to the deceased by some other person. He then ad-
verted .to the medical testimony.. It was- true
that to obtain possession of the sum of £9 was a v.ery
inadequate motive indeed. for the commission- of such a'
dreadful crime;' but they must recollect that there' was
no evidence to show that the prisoner was aware- that
the deceased had only received this- small amount: It
was probable, from the intimate terms that existedbe-
tween them that the deceased was. going on thisday to
receive some money front her brother,, Mr. Barnes ;; but
there was no evidence that she wasaware of the: exact
amount.. She very probably did. know that the last
time she went ihe'received £lO, and. she was very, likely
to have imagined that upon this occasion she would re-
ceive a larger sum than, £9. They would, also-remem-
ber-that-after the death of the- decetsed the prisoner
produced an I 0 II for £lO,. -which she represented
to have - lent the deceased ;, but it would. be for
them to consider whether i± was likely that she
should have - borrowed this sum. of the prisoner, or
whether the prisonar was in a. position to have lent it.
His Lordship then, called the attention of the...jury most
carefully to alithe other material, fa‘ts of the case, and
said. he regretted that it miglat be considered., that nearly
all the observations he had m..cle were tudavuurable to
the prisoner; but he was bound to perform his duty,
and he said no more in this respect than, he. considered
he wasjustiliekt in. do ng upon the evidence in. the case.
In conclueion,,he said that the jury stood, between the
prisoner and the public;, if they believed, the evidence,
there was undoubtedly sullicient to coairict her; but if
they had-any reasonable doubt upon the point she was
'entitled to the benefit of it. Let us trust (said his
Lordship) that you. may be guided. ta come to a right
conclusion..

The jury,. after consulting a short time in the box,
expressed a wish-to, retire. They were absent nearly
two hours. in deliberating upon their verdict. When
they returned intoo court the foreman uttered the fatal.
word, Guilty..
The prisoner beard the verdict pronounced without
exhibiting th,e Slightest appearance of emotion, and, the
blood did, not even, rise to her cheeks..

Ms.. Harker, the senior usher of the court, then outdo
the usual proclaraatiOn for silence wade sentence of
death, was passing upon the prisoner.
Mr..justice Bytes then, having first put on the, black
cap, addressed her in the tollowing terms:—Catherine
ater a lorg trial and a most patient and.anxieus
consideration of every circumstance in yew- case the
jury have come to the conclusion that you were wally
of this most atrocious crime. It is very seldom, that
think it any pare of my duty in a case of this or any
other description to express either coneurreace with or
dissent from the verdict of a jury; but, upon the pre-
sent occasion, I am bound to say that in my- opinion the
jury could net have arrived at any Other conclusion than
they hard done consistently with the facts that were laid
-before them. I never heard a case where it was BO
clearly proved that a murder was committed, and where
the. excruciating pain, and agony of the viotim were
watched with so much deliberation by the murderer,.
The greatest care was taken during the progress of the
trial that nothing should be improperly introduced into,
the ineuiryi 'and tint you should not be prejudiced
by anything that had happened before; but now that
the jury have delivered their verdict, and there can
-be no -longer any fear that their decision should be in
any way improperly influenced, I think it right that the
jury should know, and that the public should also know,
what sort of person it is that the avenging arm of the
law has at leitgth ourtaken. . I find, then, tint about
the year 1353-51 you were employecl in the capacity of
a servant or; housekeeper to a person named Mawer,
who lived at Beaton, in -Lincelushire, and that this per-
son'was in the habit of taking colchicum. He made his
will in the month of April, and by that will he left to
you the whole of. the little property he possessed. He
died in the month_ of October following. I will say no
more about this case except that it is. quite clear that ,
at this time you; were perfectly well acquainted with
the nature and
.effectt -colchieum. In the year 1856
I find that you were living with a young man named
Dixon, and that you came to London and went to
lodge with him at the house of the deceased. Dr.
Whidborne was called in to attend him. He was not
allewed upon the present trial to state any of the cir-
cumstances connected with the illness of this person;
but I may now state that it appears by his deposition
that Dixon was suddenly taken ill with violent vomit-
ing aid purging, that his- symptoms were exactly the
same as those exhibited by the unfortunate woman
Mrs. Soames, and that he died very speedily after-
wards, you yourself representing that he died of gallop-
ing consumption, but upon his body being opened his
lungs were found perfectly healthy. About the year
1859 I find that you were in the habit of visiting a Mrs.
Jackson, who also resided at Boston, and that you were
aware that she drew from-a bank in that town the sum
of Llal, and that this sum was in her possession. She
was taken ill with the same symptoms and died in four
days, and after her death the money was nowhere to be
found. -It appeared that upon this occasion you produced
a promissory note, apparently signed by two persons
residing at Boston, forthe amount thatwas missing; but it
was proved that both those signatures were forged. In
the month of October, 1860, [find that you were con-
nected with a Mrs. Atkinson, who resided in ,liirby

denee at Kennington, and it appears that you were aware
thatshe was in possession of a considerable sum ofmoney.
On the 19th of that month Mrs. Atkinson was taken,ill—
the same symptoms—retching, violent- purging,
vomiting, and great agony, and in four days she was
dead. If the jury had acquitted TQU upon the present
charge, you would have been immediately put upon
your trial for this murder. I have read the depositions
in the case most carefully and anxiously, and the result
upon my mind is that I have no more doubt that you
have committed that crime than if I had seen it com-
mitted with my own eyes. In 1861 I find that you
were living with a man named Taylor, and that he was
attacked in the same manner as the others to whom I
have alluded; but that, fortunately for him, remedies
were immediately resorted to, and he recovered. Again,
I find that only in the present year you were tried in
this court for an attempt to murder, by the administra-
tion of sulphuric acid, a woman in whose house you were
residing. You were acquitted upon that charge., but,
although this was the ease, there is too much reason to
believe that you were guilty" of this crime also, and I
am informed that the learned judge who tried you felt it
to be his duty to sum up the case,raost unfavourably to
you. These facts, I regret to say, render it extremely
probable that the startling statement made by Dr. Taylor
in the course of his evidence is correct, and that in the
midst of apparent prosperity and obedience to the law a
dreadful crime and vice is rife in this metropolis, the
destruction of life by secret peisoning. Your life is in
the hands of the Crown, and I think it right to inform
you that if I am consulted in reference to your ease I
shall not feel myself justified in interfering, and that I
cannot hold out to you the slightest hope-of any commu-
tation of your sentence.
The learned Judge then passed the Irwin' sentence of
death in the usual form.

During the whole of the trial the prisoner exhibited
the greatest coolness and self-possession, and she was
sot in the eligktest-degre.e affected at any-pottion of the
learned jUdge's address te her;-. and when he, had von-
eluded she walked firmly away from the bar.
A rather curious fact trauipirect after the jury flat
returned their verdict. They, took with them thOtiv6
letters that had been produeatin the course-of the 'case,
and upon a close examination of them it appeared that
thejurTdiscovered that they were both- writtennpon
the same description of paper and bore, the same water-

MAZZINL

The :following fetter was written by 3fazzini to Mr.
John 314 Adam, of Glasgow. It is dated about a week
before the affair of Aspromonte:

.'London, Augilat 22.

°Dear Friend,—.-It I, perfectly true, in. sprte of the
calumnies of the Timer, that for eighteen mouths I have
been endeavouring to persuade Garibaldi that we ought
to direct all our efforts towards Venice. Nowrhowever..
the die is cast. The absurd opposition of the Govern-
ment to every project concerning Venice, the insulting
obstinsey of Louis Napoleon, and the instincts of
the Italian people, have decided . the question, and

THE SAFE TRANSPORT OF PETROLEUIVE.—The removal
and storage of petroleum is a snbject which is now
creating much, controversy amongst the commercial
community in Liverpool, and has formed matter for
several discussions at the Dock Board, resulting in the
determination to erect warehouses on the margin of the
Great Float at Birkenhead, to be devoted exclusively to
the storage of. the oil. Mr. Cope, of Naylor-street,
Liverpool, has invented a cask 'for the use of petroleum
importers, by which they can store petroleum with othet
articles of merchandise, without any danger of explosion.
The danger of explosion in petroleum is not generally
understood to arise from the vapour of the oil coming in
contact with the atmospheric air, and as it is well-known
that combustion cannot be maintained without a supply
of oxygen' the inventor aseerts that it is impossible for
explosion to take place in his' casks as no atmospheric
air can penetrate them, as in the ease of the wooden
vessels. The casks of Mr. Cope are made of metal, and
can be stored very much deeper than the wooden ones
without fear of danger, and it is alleged that these casks
could be carried amongst the. general cargo of ri vessel
without any chance of ciplosion, and without injuring
the cargo by imparting to other goods its most objection-
able smell: So subtle is the gas which is given off from
petroleum that it penetrates through every portion of A
ship in which it is carried, and injures all other goods
carried in the vessel, so much so, indeed, that the im-

cask enable petroleum to be carried with a general
cargo, it will be of considerable value to a large branch

articles.title: SOLUTION OF THE NEGRO
articles.text:
SOLUTION OF THE NEGRO

DIFFICULTY.

The correspondent of the New York Timer writes from
Key West
That ceaseless, and as yet unended, cause of all our
national troubles and distress is now undergoing in our
midst some of the throes that the signs of the time in-
dicate as preceding final dissolution. Slavery is now
here on our island being brought to the test of the late
order Of the PrErcident, and the Quartermaster's depart-
ment are employing such negroes as are needed in that
department as labourers, nurses for the sick, and for all
or any purpose of labour. Those taken, who are claimed
by disloyal masters, are delighted with the change; and
others of the same class who are not thus em-
ployed are leaving their masters, and seeking labour
or employment on their own account. A custom
long in vogue here has prepared the negro for this, as
they have been allowed to hire their own time, and
make what they could, paying to their master a portion
of their earnings. This latter obligation the darkey
pr(poses to ignore for the future, and applications
have been mucle to the military commandant to have
punished such negroes as refuse to pay over their wages
or to work for their masters, which have been invariably
refused, on the ground that the soldiers of our army are
not to be used to compel the rendering of unrequited
labour, thus leaving the daveholder dependent on moral
suasion to sustain the old relationship. Haw far this
will be successful in keeping Sambo to the line of duty
which exacts all his labour for master's benefit, whilst
Sambo is merely receiving what will keep him in condi-
tion to continue the arrangement, is one phase of the
question now about to be solved. There are many
negroes employed here on our Government works and
otherwise who were purchased simply for the invest-
ment of capital by private individuals, adding negro after
negro out of the proceeds of such labour. This, although
done by men who are classed among good Christians,
is yet one of the harsh features of slavery, and stamps
the !operator -with; a haracter for unscrapulousness
even among slaveowners. ' The value of slave property
is materially affected by the existing state of things,
and an able negro man of middle age was a few
days since offered for sale at 200 dollars without
meeting a purchaser. This certainly bears with
much hardship upon certain families dependent upon
the wages and sale of their negroes for their own sup-
port 'and the education of their children. Yet it is
somewhat difficult to realise that all the wealth of the
Island does not still remain, with us, or that there is
any diminution of the power to do or accomplish. The
negro is no more unwilling to labour, when the proceeds
are expected to enter his own exchequer, than when he
knows they will go into master's. The State L( gisla-
ture of Florida passed an act in the winter of 1860 pro-
viding for the exile or enslavement of all free negroes
vtithin its borders. As there are many of that class of
labourers here, there was consequent perturbation
among them for a short time under the last of secession
rule, until the puny efforts to display the rebel flag be-
came hushed like the assassin's retreat, and the glorious
Stars and Stripes were given to the breeze by a force.
to maintain them. Then these people, reassured at
once, became quieted, and now remain, as they have
been for years, an orderly, industrious, law-abiding and
most useful class, many of whom are carpenters,. masons,
or seamstresses of respectable abilities.

27.411 T RAILWAY.

The- works of this great metropolitan improvement
may now be said to be complete, the small amount that
remains unfinished being, very minor details and decora-
tions. Col. -Yolland, thee government inspector of the
rail wary department of the-Board of Trade, has-finished
his inspection, and the company now only await the
receipt of his certificate to. open the railway to thehanb-
lie: The terminal station. in Farringdon-streetis a vary
commodious one. The platform, 'reached by a flight of
about a: dozen steps, is covered with a light iron and
glass roofing. The railway at this point is in an open:
cutting of nearly 100 feet in width. The Charles- street
bridge crosses the railway through the station. It is a
level bridge and possesses several very good_ points. It
is 40 feet in Width below the parapets, and has a: clear
span of 96 feet. Seven. wrought-iron girders-rest upon.
cross girders, which are- supported upon four circular
iron columns. . The spaces- between the seven longir
tudinal girders are filled inwith arched brickwork, upon,
which the roadway is laid. The parapets are formed of .
iron slabs, with panel moulding, which slide into their
places down grooves in cast iron standards secured-to the
girders. The bridge willhe painted bronze col Our, and
will have a very agreeable appearance from.the roadway.
The other bridges from,the station to the mouth of the•
tunnel are completed, and will be open for the traffic of.
vehicles next week. From the terminus in New
Farringdon-street to the commencement of the tunnel
under Coppice-row, the railway will be open, and mit, as
it is generally termed,. an undergoound one, and for
several hundred yards on the City side Of. IKing's-cross.
the railway will also run in an open cutting, as well as
for some short distance before entering the Great
Western Railway station. The branch, tunnel leading
to the eastern side of the Midland and Great Noethern
Railway at King's-cross has been for some time- com-
pleted, but a smaller branch is now - being made which
will enable the trains from the midland counties and
the north to run, right, through, to. London without
reversing at the junction. For the Continuation of this
short cut the contractors have again to 'overcome their
old enemy, the Fleet ditch, which will be carried., across
the crown of the tunnel in an iron. aqueduct. At the
King's-cross and other stations spring switches have been
laid similar to those laid by Mr. Brunel on the main line
of the Great Western Railway. These will admit of the
trains running through without requiring pointsmeri at
these parts. The construction of the telegraph,,.which is to
connect the various stations, and. by which. the signal-
men are to communicate from station to st,tion, is just
finished, and the signals have been partially tested.
The rails of the permanent way are steeled. by Dodd's
process, and. thejoints are fished and. bolted. with Low
Meer iron. In. securing the rails the expansion of the
metal has been duly provided, for by driving the bolts
through the rails with the point only at a, red heat, the
other portion being cold iron. The engine pit at the
station is provided with a tank, into whieh the water of
the condensed steam will be caught, andeonveyed away
to a reservoir to be again used in the engines, thus,
economising, the water and saving a proportionate outlay
for its supiily, the water rate charged by the New River
Company, forming a considerable item in the working
expenses,. The line is to.be.worked entirely by the Great
Western Railway Company,, to whose line it will ma-
doubteclly prove a most valuable feeder. The engines are
constructed upon the. plan o. Mr. Fowler, and consume
not only their own smoke but also their steam, so that
no inconvenience will be. felt by passengers in travelling
along the railway. These are now ready for action.
Twee of them have been at work. for some days past upon
the railway, making, themselves generally useful in
drawing laden trucks, and. bringing ills materials for
various parts of the line. Thoearriages are also finished.
These are of very large dimensions, and run upon eight
wheels. They will be lighted with gas. On the top of
each carriage is placed a small iron reservoir or gaso-
meter, which is filled at the station from the gas mains
in the same manner as.the tender is supplied with water..
Each gasholder will contain sufficient for several
journeys, and the light in the carriages will be very
agreeably diffused, and sufficiently light to enable
passengers to. read with ease. '

GATAZZI IN TIIALEE.—A riot has taken place in Tralee
on the occasion of a lecture being delivered by Gavazzi
on 'Garibaldi, and the present political state of Italy.'
The lecturer made some remarks on the Pope's Irish
Brigade, which roused the passions of nine of the Roman
eatholics who were present in the lecture-room. The
police, assisted by civilians, proceeded .to eject the dis-
turbers, during which time a great commotion ensued,
and eggs were smashed on the wall of the lecture-room.
The police having succeeded in ejecting the principal
rioters, Gavazzi proceeded with his discourse. At the
close of the lecture an immense mob attacked the hotel
in which the lecture was delivered, breaking almost
every pane of glass in the windows, and otherwise dam-
aging the premises. The audience were afraid to venture
out, as stones were flying in all directions. The police
from some of the country districts were immediately
summoned, as also the militia staff,. but the combined
force was totally unable to disperse the Mob, and merely
sufficed to keep them from entering the hotel. The
parish priest addressed the rioters, imploring them to
disperse, but without effect. The Riot Act was read,
still the crowd was increasing, and numerous parties
from the mob sallied out in all directions, and demolished
the windows of houses belonging to protestants. 'Several
persons-were struck with stones, but no material injury
inflicted.

THE REVENUE RETETRITS:

The Revenue Returns for the quarter and year end-
ing October 1 though not so satisfactory as could be
wished, are, considering the prevalent distress in Lan-
cashire and other parts of the country, not so bad as
was expected. The greatest relative decrease, both on
the quarter and year, as compared with the corre-
sponding quarter and year of 1861, is on the 'Excise.
This was to be expected, inasmuch as the consumption
of excisable articles, such as tea, sugar, &c., must
have been very largely diminished by the intensity
and universality of the distress in Lancashire. On
the quarter
,the•decrease is £617,000, and on the year
£1,194,000. From these figures it will be seen that
the deficit under the head of Excise dining
the quarter ending Tuesday, as compared with
the corresponding quarter last year, has been twice as
great as during the three quarters _ending in July last.
This one fact proclaims in language loud enough to be
heard throughout the country, how rapidly the Lan-
cashire distress is and extending itself.
The Customs show an increase on the quarter of
£219,000, and on the year of £375,000. The Stamps,
too, are• more productive than in the corresponding
quarter of last year by £167,00G, and, on the year, by
£398,775. The total results show a decrease on the
quarter of £249, and.on the year of £120,620. The
aggregate defalcation is certainly very slight, both on
the quarter and the year; but still the returns are not
satistactory,inasmuch as; with an increasing popula-
tion, and the constant additional development of our
national resources, there ought to be a steadily pro-
gressive augmentation of the income of the country.

articles.title: TITE MIDDLE LEVEL.
articles.text:
TITE MIDDLE LEVEL.

KING:s Lvxx,,Sept. 30.—The syphons which have
been in course of construction for some months past
for discharging the waters of the Middle Level drain
over the dam were tried for the first time on Monday
afternoon and evening, an so far with complete suc-
cess. The water had lately been rising within the dam
so as to again alarm some of the people of Marshland
Fen, and lead them to fear that the Middle Level must
be doomed in the ensuing, winter. The result of the
trial has done something to quiet these apprehensions.
Of the 15 syphons; each 3i ft. in diameter, 6 only have
as yet been laid down, and it was on these the experi-
ment was made. Mr. Ilawkshaw, C.E., Mr. Appold,
Mr. Harrison, C.E.,Mr..Linn, C.E. (resident engineer),
and other scientific men, were present to conduct and
test the operations. The air was exhausted from the
tubes by a -pump worked by a small steam engine
erected on the bank, wad the appearance of water in
the pump was the signal that all was right and tight.
The engine was stopped;and the valves at the outer
ends of the syphons opened,:and the water poured over
in continuous streams of the full capacity of the six
outlets, rushing into the outer side of the dam (which
now forms a creek from the Ouze) with the noise of a
tataract. *Of course the water only continued running
while the level outside was lower than that within the
dam, or from about half-tide to half-tide; but during
this interval the level of water within the dam was
reduced by 9 inches. This result exceeded -the most
Sanguine expectations of the engineers, and from it may
be drawn a satisfactory opinion as to the entire effi-
ciency. of the syphons when their number is increased
to fifteen, which it is hoped will be accomplished before
winter-fairly sets in.

articles.title: 1.11,61 SOUTH AND ITS CREDITORS.
articles.text:
1.11,61 SOUTH AND ITS CREDITORS.

(From the New York .Evening Post).
Mr. Z. C. Pearson, shipowner of Hull, is unatde to
poet his acceptances.' _ Mr. Pearson, who was appa-
rently a merchant in a good line of business when our
war broke out, went largely into the Southern trade,'
which seems to have a curious charm for John Bull.
He saw befere him the shadow of an immense fortune,
and, like the dog in the fable,, he dropped what he had
already secured, and plunged over head and ears into
the gulf of Southern trade, after the alluring shadow.
On.the first of this month he emerged, dripping, a
poorer, but, we trust, a wiser Bull. •
The liabilities of Mr. Pearson were stated, when the
steamer left, at four hundred thousand pounds sterling,
about two millions of dollars. The profits of the Southern
trade are great,-but they are hard to get. The Southern
merchant just inow demands a long credit; he likes
to owe, but he does net like to pay; he is apt to put
off the evil day, and has a gentlemanly aversion to
squaring accounts, which arises perhaps from the habit
of taking the labour of his slaves for nothing. He ex-
claims with the chivalrous Pistol, Base is the slave
that pays.'
Of all this Mr. Pearson might have got at least some
hint, if he had been prudent enough to make inquiry
in New York or Philaae Ala as to the commercial
character and standing ce the Southern gentlemen.'
But he chose to ask nebody's advice. He was not to
be cheated of his favourite gold mine; he was not to
be baulked of the fortune he saw within his grasp.
Ho would have his own way, like a genuine Bull ; and
he has now had it. .

It is ingeniously stated that while some of Mr.
Pearson's ships have been captured, from the cargoes
ofothers' which safely ran the blockade, he gained heavy
ts ,profi ; but 'his agents find diaculty in transmitting
the proceeds with safety and punctuality.' We fear
this will seem a-melancholy- joke to too many of our
own business men formerly in the Southern trade. The
'difficulty' which embarrasses Mr. Pearson is chronic at
the South. It is a difficulty which has embarrassed and
ruined a good many men besides Mr. Pearson. It has
ovendone more; it has caused the tarring and feather-
ing of northern collecting clerks; it has caused, on
several-occasions, "a mob of Southern gentlemen to rise
in chivalrous rage and chase out of , their neighbour-
hood the wretched Yankee abolitionists' who come
after filthy dollars. It has made the fortunes of some
Southern collecting agents, who, like the ingenious
Wigfall of Texas, stepped in generously to act as
middlemen between Northern creditor and Southern
debtor, and, repeating the old fable of the monkey and
the cats, first bullied the debtor and then cheated the
creditor, and thug managed to have justice done and
yet retain the specie in the South—a combination of
chivalrous-honour and tSouthern patriotism which
Davis made haste to imitate and by which the mer-
chants o this city are at this time some hundred
million dollars out of pocket. It will comfort Mr.
Pearson to know that he is not the only sufferer.

THE' FEAR OF TUE LORD IS THE BEGINNING OF
WISDOM.—Such terror of the unseen is so far above
mere sensual cowardice that it will annihilate that
cowardice; it is the initial recognition of a moral law
restraining desire, and checks the hard bold scrutiny of
imperfect thoughts into obligations which can never be
proved to have any sanctity in the absence of feeling.
'lt is good,' sing the old Eumenides in 2Eschylus, tint
fear should sit as the guardian of the soul, forcing it into
wisdom—good that men should carry a threatening sha-
dow in their hearts under the full sunshine, else how
should they learn to revere the right That guardian-
ship may become needless, but only when all outward
law has become needless—only when duty and love
have united in one stream and made a common force.—
Romola. _

THE TYPHOON AT CANTON. - The following is an
extract of a letter from Hongkong, dated August 10:-
6A typhoon of terrible violence passed over Canton and
Whampoa on the 27th ult., enough of it being felt here
to cause the detention of the Orissa. It is impossible to
describe the havoc to life and Property sustained in that
.part of the country, particularly in the towns of Canton
and Whampoa. Of the latter it may actually be said
that there is not a house left standing, but the whole
length and breadth of the 'country have suffered to a
degree unparalleled in its own history. The loss of life
at Canton is estimated at more than 40,000 persons, and
the Mandarins have paid already upwards of 16,000 dols.,
at a dollar a body, for the recovery of corpses from the
river. The boat population of Canton perished by the
thousand, and there was hardly any safety in the frail
tenements on shore. The river rose 12 feet above the
level of the highest spring tides. The mud docks at
Whampoa were without exception flooded, and the
vessels in them floated off the blocks, and were driven
by the force of the wind hard and fast into the mud, One
or two being hopelessly lost; the others, perhaps, may
be saved. Of the ves,sels'in Whampoa there were four
or five driven ashore, and there was hardly one of the
others that did not sustain some very serious damage.
The company bad tws steamers at Whampoa at the time
'—the China, then in the stone dock; and the Aden in
the Reach. Tbe China was within a few inches of
floating, the water having 'Come over the top of the
caisson : had she. actually floated, her destruction
would have been certain. The Aden was able to get
up her steam, and was kept from drifting by going
a-head 00 hard as possible. Great credit is due to the
officers of the China, and especially Mr. Blackmore, for
the manner in which that steamer was secured in dock;
for if she had been but ordinarily secured the chances
9f her floating Would have been much increased.'
