articles.title: BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 4, 1862.
articles.text:
THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 4, 1862.

/Wrii.6 DRAMATIC COLLEGE.

On Monday aL' irtre party, including Mr. Webster
Mr. 'Robert Bel,- lMr. Ohuld, Mr. -.Terwood, Mr
Churchill, the recipients of the bounty, and many
warm friends of the institution, proceeded to Maybury,
to assist at a ceremony which was affecting and grafi-
lying, and which ought to do much to assist the
charity. , Mrs. Shuter, a relict of a name which is an
old familiar sound to old playgoers; Mrs, Christian,
Mrs. Rivers, Mr. Campbell, an old melodramatic actor
for many years connected with Sadler's Wells in its
palmy days; Mr. Starmer, another well-known
veteran, Mr. Eugene Macarthy, and Mr. • Henry
Bedford, were escorted .by their friends, to the
pleasant retreat provided for their declining years,
and seen well settled in 'their comfortable
rooms by the kind-hearted warden and his assist-
ants. A. little banquet, to which they were invite*,
gave them an opportunity of expressing their thanks
for the timely and considerate charity bestowed upon
them; a charity that is given to them ungrudgingly,
as a right,.and which blesses both the giver and the
receiver. Without any feeling of dependence or
sycophancy, Mr. Macarthy and Mr. Campbell, both
honourably connected with the stage for more than
half a century, gave expression to their feelings in a
few heartfelt words, and the ladies were even more
eloquent in their thanks, though conventionally con-
demned to silence. What makes this charity pecu-
liarly gratefulto all true philanthropists is, that the
committee have liberally interpreted their charter, and
have permitted the pensioners to be solaced by the
presence of their wives and.-husbands. Out of, the
three ladies who on Monday took up their home on the
estate, two were accompanied bY their husbands, and
out of the four gentlemen, three wereraccompanied by
their wives.

The estate forms part of Woking Common,_ in
Surrey, and cOmprises five acres of freehold land,
given to the charity by the Necropolis Company. Mr.
Churchill, the active secretary of that company, has
been unceasing in his endeavours to benefit the college
from the first, and to him it is possible that the
dramatic profession chi,-fly owe this gift—the basis of
the whole charity. The building, planted on a slope,
withjan extensive wooded prospect, is of the Tudoresq ue
order; and the plan provides, we believe, about twelve
residences on each side of the central hall. An arcade
runs along the front of the housegt, and the columns of
the arches, here and there, are [carved in stone at the
expense of a few friends of the college. Each residence
is a model of comfort and completeness, the lower floor
being divided into three apartments with every- con-
venience for one pensioner, and "the upper floor
similarly' divided. The central hall, which will cost
£l,OOO, is now'being rapidly built, the subscriptions
towards it at present being £lOO, which Mr. Creswick
has promised to collect, another £lOO which Mr.
Augustus Harris has promised to collect, and another.
£lOO which Mr. Jerwood has promised to give. Where
there is so much liberality, the architect of the
college, Mr. Smith, is not to be 'outdone, and he has
given up half his fee, or £5O. Many other friends
have come forward most usefully. Mr. Burton, of
Oxford-street, has sent a complete warming appar-
atus; Mr. Daniells, of New Bond-street, has
given the majolica tiles for the central hall; Mr.
J. B. glickstone has promised £250 for a wing
or end house; Mr. Benjamin Webster has also
promised £250 for another end house; Mr. Graves,
of Pall-mall, has made the college a present of
some valuable theatrical engravings • Mrs. Rudell
promises some acceptable pictures; Messrs. Robinson
and Webster have given their legal services in all the
work of settling the charter án i deeds of gift'; and
Mr. Churchill promises £BO towards the central hall.
Many of these gentlemen and ladies, it must be
remembered, have already subscribed largely to the
charity, or aided it by invaluable services; and Mr.
Webeter, like Mr. Charles Kean and others, has built
one of the houses and fitted it up at his own cost.
Every credit is due to each and all of these gentlemen
—to Mr. Creswiclr, an energetic worker in the good
cause—to Mr. Anson, a secretary whose heart is-in his
labour, and to everyone in any way connected with
the undertaking. They look forward to the time when
the buildings will become not only a home for the aged,
but a 'school for the young, and extend its sphere of
usefulness. We trust that this time is not far distant,
and that the deserved publicity which we are always
willing to give the charity will help it on in its good
work.

articles.title: ESC.AP_E OF A BURGLAR I.ROM
articles.text:
ESC.AP_E OF A BURGLAR I.ROM

PRISON.

The Birmingham .Daily Post has the following:—
Should Mr. Ainsworth be in want of a hero for a
new novel of the downright blood and burglary cast,
we commend to the delicate manipulation of his har-
rowing pen the notorious thief and prison-breaker
Alexander.. From the tip of his quill such a scoundrel,
combining as he does a somewhat comely figure and
great physical strength, with a Certain amount of me-
chanical genius and a good deal of very delicate cun-
ning, would flow off the most virtuous of housebreakers,
the most fascinating of burglars' and the sweetest-
faced thief that ever drew breath. The ingenuity, of
the man is as great as his desperation, and his success
is almost equal to both. He ,is, in fact, at the top• of
his craft—the star' amongst burglars. Our readers
know something of his exploits. They know that he
had planned one of the most daring and extensive burg-
laries that ever took place in this town; that he came
specially from Manchester to superintend the execu-
tion of it by astute Birmingham thieves; that his
plans were carried out successfully, and that he made
a clear escape to Manchester. Followed _there by Bir-
mingham detectives, waylaid and overpowered by
numbers he fought for his liberty with a desperation
worthy of a better cause, ,and was not• captured until-
he was stunned with policemen's staves and handcuffs.
Brought to Birmingham, and committed for trial, lie
-managed to drop his shoelace. into the lcck-box of the
police-cell, to shoot back the bolt with' it,. and to make'
a clear escape out of the town. In the _course of two or
three days he was recaptured, and being a curiosity,
unusual care was taken of him until the assizes when
he was tried and sentenced. to penal servitude for
twenty years. No doubt the scoundrel, aware of his
boundless resources, laughed in his sleeve while the
judge passed sentence, and the public thouglst he was
safely disposed of at. last. Arrived at War wick Gaol,
he began to show symptom .of insanity, and feigned
so Well that the' doctors' judging that the blows be
had received at Manchester had affected his brain,
treated him accordingly. He grew gradually worse—
poor fellow about sixteen days ago was removed
to the County Lunatic Asylum, at Hatton. Here he was
still held to be-insane. For the success of his plan it would
not have done to be violent, so he afllieted himself with
that mild kind of insanity for which restraint is not
held to be a 'remedy. He was given to, gibbering and
apparent idiotcy, and was looked upon as a harmless
kind of imbecile. On Saturday evening, between.
seven and eight o'clock, according to Custom, he and
a real lunatic on the way to convalescence were con-
ducted by an attendant to their dormitories on the
third storey of the building. Before locking them in
the attendant left them-for a few minutes, turd on his
return discovered that the (gaol) bird had flown. The
real lunatic, on being asked what had become of his
companion, pointed to a ventilating trap in the ceiling,
and with mingled terror and satisfaction, informed the
astonished attendant that Mr. Alexander had gone tip
there to catch a rat. The attendant, who at that
moment undoubtedly smelt the rat,' called several of
his coadjutors, who, after a long search, succeeded in
finding out—not Alexander—but how he escaped. It
seems that the clever rascal on passing through the
trap, which he reached with the assistance of a broom
and the dormitory door, made his way to the venti-
lating shaft, and descended by that to the basement.
In this adventure the broomhandle would seem to
have been of some service to him, for he left the head
behind and took the stick, which if not of service
would have been an incumbrance to him in his descent
of the chimney. On gettingto the basement his egress
was barred by three locked doors. These, however—
to an old burglar who had possessed the finest imple-
ments ever seen at the Detective-office, and knew the
construction of a lock well enough to use them, and in
their absence to turn the first instrument that came to
hand to account—formed no impediment. The locks
were all picked in a few brief minutes, and Alexander
was once more free, and no deubt, a saneman. He has
not since been heard of. In case the poor fellow-should
have been really mad, and should be now, a wandering
homeless lunatic, we append his description, in the
hope that he may fall into the hands of some good Sama-
ritan who will return him to his bereaved friends. He
is a well-built man, between five feet seven and five
feet eight inches high. His head is large, his com-
plexion fair, his hair light brown or sandy, and his
eyes grey and deeply seated. From a peculiar twist in
his legs he is supposed to have been a tailor, and from
certain marks on his-head it may be inferred that De-
tective Sergeant Seal punished him severely at Man-
chester. When he escaped he had a moderato stock
of whiskers, but these may by this time have been
clean shaven or replaced by an enormous pair like those
found in his possession when he was apprehended for
the Bull Ring burglary.

GREAT INTERNATIONAL FRUIT SHOW.—The Corn
missioners of Customs have had under consideration an
application of the Royal Horticultural Society, stating
that a Great International Fruit Show will be held at
South Kensington on the Bth of October next, and re-
questing that packages of fruit arriving from the
colonies and from foreign countries for the Exhibition
may be passed without being opened or disturbed; The
board allow all such packages addressed to the Horti-
cultural Society to be forwarded without examination
under seals of office to the society's premises, at Ken-
sington' to the care of the officers of customs in charge
of tho International Exhibition,' subject to the same
regulations as were observed in regard to goods for the
International Exhibition.
Tun ASSASSINATION OF MR. BRADDELL.—The mur-
derer Hayes is reported to be still in the immediate
vicinity of his own residence, although reports have
been industriously circulated that he had gone off to
America. His continued success in baffling his pur-
suers is one of those extraordinary and mysterious facts
which in any country but Iteland would be thought
incredible. The police are still unceasing in their
efforts to trace him, but, with the aid of his sympa•
thetic friends, he continues to elude them. In addition
to the large extra reward offered by Mr. How-
ley, R.M., which, together with that offered by the
Government, made the whole amount nearly £7OO, it
is stated that Mr. Richard Hare offers a further sum of
£tOo for such private information, to be given to the
resident magistrate at Tipperary, ILS will lead to
Hayes's arrest. The Hon. Colonel Hare, of Devon-
port, the owner of the property over which Mr. Braddell
was agent, paid a visit to it last week, and instituted
inquiries, the result of which was that Moore, the
bailiff, who was with Mr. Braddell at the time of tho
murder, has been dismissed. - -

• WINTER AT SIERRA LEONE.—It was what they
called their winter! God_save the mark! It is within
nine degrees of the equator, and they have the sun ver-
tical both-on his way north, and when he comes' back
ag4in, during which process I should imagine they
might fry eggs in the sun; but when the Lion,' or the
King of Heat, as the ancient Egyptians called him, is
gone southwards past the equator, all the way to see
his friends at the tropic of Capricorn, as he then was,
they call it their winter. All I can say is, that we
were there shortly before Christmas for a week, and it
would be difficult for any one Who had not crossed the
line near the coast of Africa, to imagine anything hotter
and live. It was winter, however, and tornadoes Were
in season. Consequently the commodore ordered the
Vulcan to keep her- fires banked up all the time we
were at anchor in the river; and we had a tornado (as
the Spaniards have christened it), which is after all
nothing but a fearful thunder storm, and a whirlwind,
as its name implies. The collier whose cargo we were
transferring to our bunkers, was lashed alongside, and
the ship had two anchors down; but the whirlwind
swept the great heavy ship-round like a humming top,
and cast the collier adrift in less time than you can
tell it, and then it was as calm and lovely a night
again as you could wish to see.—United Service Maga-
zine.

ILLEGAL NETTING IN THE THAMES.-At Brentford,
on Saturday, the Thames Angling Preservation Society
charged Lewis Gibson' and George Dodd with taking
fish in the Thames at Richmond by using a net unlaw-
fully, according to the Act 20 and 21 Viet., regulating
the fishing in the River Thames, and the bye-laws of the
Thames Conservancy Commissioners. On the'l7th
September, between eight and nino, they 'were found by
three keepers in the employment of the society in a
boat on the river: One of the keepersolamed Howard,
searched the boat and found a dry net in it. Just before
that Milman' another of the keepers, Said to the third
keeper, Shove back,' saw him shoot a. net away from
the boat.' Howard shoved the boat back, and took hold
of the line attached to the net. Upon pulling it up a
heavy piece of chain was fastened to: one end, the other
end being made fast to a pole fixed' in the bank. There
was a great quantity of fish in the net. :The keeper
stated that the net would be legal if used in a proper
manner, with one end attached to a floating buoy and
the other to a boat. Thatis fteeting,': according to Act
of Parliament. The net was ordered to be destroyed,
and each of the defendants fined 40s. and costs, with one
mouth's imprisonment for default. Mr. H. Parnell,
secretary to the Society, informed the bench that Gibson
was the most notorious poacher on the river, and had
been convicted a great number of times in the full
penalty; and on the last occasion he paid the fine of V,
but left his man 'to work his month out.'

articles.title: SHOCKING AFFAIR AT EIRETIAIi:
articles.text:
SHOCKING AFFAIR AT EIRETIAIi:

A dreadful affair occurred at Kirkham, near Preston,
on Sunday night. It appears that a party of Irish
harvest men went to the Swan Inn, where they had
something to drink. About 11 o'clock they became
very noisy, and the landlord, Mr. Henry Rawcliffe,
expressed his desire to clear the house. Ile
asked the men to go, but they refused. He then
seized one of them, named Garrety, who seemed to be
the worst, and got him into the lobby, but was
unable to eject , him. Subsequently he went to
the door, and gave an alarm with a dog whistle.
This brought a policeman named Fletcher to his
assistance, who tried to get the men away, but
he could not do so. The officer then went
out and whistled, and Sergeant Lofthouse came
up, arid Garrety was apprehended. The other
Irishmen then turned out of the hourP. A man
•named James Cain, his wife, and Patrick Cain, their
nephew, tried, but ineffectually, to rescue Garrety,
who was taken to the lock-up. The three Caine then
ran away, but were pursued by the police. Whilst the
officers were thus engaged, they were informed that
Raweliffe, the landlord, had been killed. They then
went to the Swan, where they found Rawcliffe almost
dead, and attended by two surgeons. It appears that
after the officers had left, the door of the Swan Inn
was immediately closed, and Rawcliffe and his eldest
daughter, a girl fifteen years of age, went into an
upper room, with a view to see what was going on in
the street. At that time the crowd in front of the door
had gone away, and Rawcliffe was about leaving the
wi ,dow. His daughter had gone just before; but
she had not proceeded very far before she beard a
g eat crash, and, on looking round, observed her
father with his head near the window. She went up
to him, when, to her horror, she found that a poker
had been driven into his eye. It had been hurled at
him from the street. She did her utmost to extract the
poker,, but her efforts were ineffectual. She imme-
diately raised an alarm, and several neighbours came
in. Rawcliffe was found lying on a chair near the
window, bleeding profusely, and with the poker still
protruding from his right eye. A man named Smith
t, ied to pul out the poker, but for some time his efforts
p roved.unavailing. At length he placed the unfortunate
man's head between his knees, and even then it re-
quired all his force to extract the poker. Of course
Rawcliffe was quite insensible. Two medical men were
nt for; but Rawcliffe died an hour afterwards. The
poker had entered under the lower lid of the eye, and
had thence passed into the brain.
On Monday, Garrety and the three Caine were
braught before the Kirkham magistrates. Garrety
was committed for two months for assaulting the
police, and the others were remanded until Thursday.
On Monday, the inquestwas opened, and after some
formal evidence had been given, the inquiry was ad-
journed until Monday next. At present nothing defi-
nite is known as to who threw the poker.

A correspondent writes that after the bearing of the
case .tt the Police Court, the landlady of the Cains
volunteered a statement to the effect that on Sunday
night James Cain ran into her house and seized a
poker, swearing that he would have somebody's life,
or some one should have his, that night; and that he
took the poker out with him a few minutes before the
landlord was struck.

articles.title: WALKING MATCH A GAI_ZYST TIME.
articles.text:
A WALKING MATCH A GAI_ZYST TIME.

It will be remembered by persons interested in pe-
destrianism that James Miles attempted for the first
time to accomplish the- extraordinary feat of walking,
ftir heel and toe, 21 miles in three consecutive hours
for a bet of £5O a-side on Monday, ,August, 11th, when
he failed. Miles on that occasion became so used up'
that while walking the first lap of the 18th mile he
fell from sheer exhaustion. His backer, thinking the
failure arose solely from his not being in proper trim,
determined to let him have another chance. The pre-
sent match was therefore made the requisite articles
being entered into on Friday, die 29th of August, W.
Price laying the odds of £5O to £25 that Miles did not
succeed in accomplishing the above specified distance
within the allotted three hours. Miles had to make
the circuit of the course 84 times (less 70 yards).
Notwithstanding the unpropitious state of the
weather, the ground' was in splendid condition and at
three o'clock, .Miles, attended by young Smith, made
his appearance. The betting was 6 to 2on time, but
the backers of Miles did not feel much disposed to
whip it on' at the odds offered, as they said the day
was to all intents and purposes so much against their
man. The start had to be made by the report of a
pistol, and on the signal being given Miles dashed off
in magnificent style. • The first mile was accomplished
in 7 minutes 45 seconds, the second mile in 15 minutes
60 seconds; three miles were corrp.lsted in 23 minutes
69 seconds; four miles, 32 minutes 8 seconds; five
miles were told off by the young Brixton clipper in 40
minutes 13 seconds; six miles accomplished in. 48
minutes 38 seconds;' and the first seven miles were com-
pleted, and that with the most perfect ease to himself,
in 57 minutes. The first eight miles were done in 1
hour 5 minutes 33 seconds; nine miles were done in 1
hour 14 minutes 9 seconds;' ten miles were done in 1
hour 22 minutes 44 seconds; ten miles and-a-half (half
the distance) were accomplished in 1 hour 27 minutes;
eleven miles were completed in 1 hour 31 minutes 16
seconds' twelve miles were done in 1 hour 39 minutes
45. seconds ; thirteen miles in 1 hour 48 minutes 25
seconds; and the first fourteen miles were gallantly
wdked m 1 hour 57 minutes 11 seconds. The first
fifteen miles were accomplished in 2 hours 6 minutes
57 seconds; sixteen miles were completed in 2 hours 16
minutes 7 seconds; seventeen miles were splendidly
waned in 2 hours 24 minutes 33 seconds; eighteen miles,
2 hours 33 minutes 40 seconds; nineteen miles were
done in 2 hours 42 minutes 33 seconds. The excite-
ment which prevailed was of the most intense descrip-
tion, and Miles, as he rattled along, was hailed from all
parts of the ground with the utmost deafening applause.
Thera could be no doubt, and well it might, that the
pace and the long continuance of his exertions were
beetinning to tell on him, and that he was becoming
more and more terribly distressed. Still, the pluck he
exhibited at this trying and most critical time was de-
serving of the highest praise. Throughout the lest
mile and-a-half Miles struggled on with. the same un-
daunted pluck, the time when he had entered upon the
Bth and last lap being called out by the referee, so
that there should be no mistake. On came Miles in the
midst of the most deafening applause, but notwith-
standing the terrific exertions he had made; he had
faited., to resell the goal. when the referee had to an-
nounce to his friends those fatal words, Time's up,'
hut still,' so close was 'there' that he succeeded in
walking' the twenty-one miles in three hours and ten
seconds, thus only losing the match lay ten seconds.
Such a performance as this has not been witnessed for
years, and that, too, done in the midst of a pitiless rain.

THE GIfRAT GLOM, LEICESTER-SCLITARM—In a few
days this noted structure, which was sold a short time
ugo, wilt be entirely cleared away. A number of men
a t-e employed in its demolition, and the property, as it
i=t taken down, is disposed of and removed. It is stated
that there are about 400,000 stock bricks several tons
of lead, besides a • large amount of timber used in its
construction, and it is believed that the area will be
formed into an ornamental garden.
Tun POPULAR EMPEROR.—' But the Emperor is so
popular!' Those who are initiated into the secrets of
the popularity-manufacture laugh to hear this said. As
soon as the Emperor's visit to a given locality is ru-
,moured (and it is generally announced four, five, or six
months beforehand), no public improvement, no act of
public justice or benevolence, that can possibly be put
ails to be extracted from the local authorities. If there
is a street to be opened, a harbour to be improved, a pub-
lic promenade to be formed, an old soldier to be 'deco-
rated,' a widow to be pensioned, everything is saved up
for the Emperor's visit, that he may appear as the earthly
giver of all good. Do you wonder at his beingpopular ?
Is not the cat's-meat man popular among the cats? But
the genuine cat's-meat man trusts entirely to his well-
filled basket for his popularity. Not so the Third
Napoleon_ Whenever the Emperor is about to Pass by
a given line of railway, the officials of the company are
sure to see arrive, with free passes in their hands (which
the government have power to give without stint), some
seven or, eight hundred individuals in all manner of cos-
tumes, from knights of the Legion of Honour, who take
place en coupes, to mere navvies gravelling third-class.
They have; apparently, no connection with the Impe-
rial suite, or with the staff of police, in or out of uniform,
who necessarily go,down on the occasion ; but they travel
down a day or two before his Majesty's departure; they
travel Up again about the period of his return. Do not
suppose that they are gendarmes ; mouchards they may
be when requisite ; but their main office is a much
more cheerful one; they are • popularity makers. It is
they who fan the sometimes very dull embers of provin-
cial enthusiasm into" fiathe ; whenever the local supply is
deficient, from among their number can always be drawn
the old soldier, the bluff peasant, the intelligent artisan,
the hardworkinc, labourer, whose sayings and doings in
relation to the 'Emperor form, as it were, the feuilleton
of each Imperial progress.—Spectator,

THE GLASGOW MunnEn.---The exitement in Glasgow
on the subject of the Sandyford-place murder is 'still on
the increase. It has been remarked by a gentleman who
had some opportunity of estimating the prevailing
feeling, that not all the militaijr and police in Glasgow,
or even in Scotland, would, in the present temper of the
populace, be able to carry the sentence into effect.
Another informant „states that everywhere • people were
signing the petitions for a respite, in the public buildings,
in the sbops, and on the streets,

articles.title: COURAGEOUS YOUNG LADY.
articles.text:
A COURAGEOUS YOUNG LADY.

A desperate outrage was perpetrated on Sunday
night in
,Plymouth. - About, seven o'clock a young
lady, named Lucas, who belongs to one of the large
establishments in Bedford-street, was returning home.
While proceeding along- thei.‘ road leading from the
Roman Catholic Cathedral to the Church of St. Peter,
she was .stopped by some ruffian and robbed. The
fellow, when he approached, demanded her money,
and threatened that, if she screamed or-attempted to
make the least noise, he would lay her at his feet, at
the same time showing .her a stick with a large'knob
at the end of it. The young person was or course
greatly alarmed, as the night was very dark, and
the road exceedingly lone and he was afraid that
her assailant would really fulfil his threat, par-
ticularly as he at .first. attempted to place • some-
thing over her mouth. She, therefore,. gave him all
the money which she had in h,er possession, viz., ss.
The fellow then said, 'You have a watch, and I will
have that.' Miss Lucas replied, 'Only with my life,'
to which the highwayman answered, Well, then, I
will have it with your life,' and again threatened her
with violence if she resisted his demand. , The young
lady recollected that she had a ginger-baer bottle in her
pocket, and making a feint as if she was going to dis-
engage her watch, she took the bottle from her pocket
with her left hand,. passed it behind her into her right
band, and then, with a quick movement, succeeded in
.dealing the cowardly fellow a blow on the forehead.
.She-fancies that at the same moment he must have.
heard footsteps approaching; at all events he gave a
groan and let go hi. hold. She promptly took advantage
of his Confusion, and ran off as fast as possible. Upon
reaching home she found a stain of blood upoh her
hand, which proved that the blow she struck must have
inflicted a wound, and it is to be hoped that this will
partly lead to the villain's discovery. • . ,

LAMENTABLE SUICIDE OF A PEYSICIAN.—An inquest
was held at Mansfield, Vottinghamslaire, on the 29th,
on the body of Mr. Hatt, a physician of that town.
The deceased had been prevented from following his
professional duties for some time in consequence of
indisposition. On Friday morning last, about nine
o'clock, he went into the garden, shortly returning,
and in doing so called' in at the surgery. He then
returned to the house, remarking that he was afraid
he was going to have another attack of illness. He sat
down in a chair and died instantly. A
,post-mortem
examination was made on the body, when it was dis-
dovered that deceased had put an end to his existence
by taking 'oil of sweet almonds.' The jury retUrned
the following verdict: •‘ That the deceased 'poisoned
himself whilst in a. fit of temporary insanity.'
• THE CONVICT ROUPELL On the list of the Lorimers'
Company being taken at the City of London Registra-
tion, the name of William Roupell, described as of 16,
St. James's-square, and Roupell-park, Surrey, was ob-
jected to by the Conservatives on the ground that he
had teased to possess the requisite qualification, and
that two addresses were given. The reviSing barrister
said he apprehended that this was not an objection
which would justify him in striking out the name, Mr.
Ledger suggested that the only power the revising
barrister possessed of striking out a name was con-
tained in the 40th-section, and that was where there
was proved to be an insufficient qualification, or where
the person whose name was on the list was proved to
be dead. The revising barrister said he did not think
there was any fear of Mr. Roupell corning forward at
the next election and claiming to vote. The clerk of
the company said he would be off the list next year, as
he would then be unable to find him. The revising
barrister decided on retaining the name on the list,
therefore the objection was disallowed.

MURDER NEAR PRESTON.—OH Bunday evening a
party of Irish harvest-men had been drinking at the
Swan Inn, in the small town of Kirkham, about nine
miles from Preston, and had got primed in liquor. At
closing time the landlord, Mr. Henry Rawcliffe, requested
them to go away, but they would not do so, and it was
found necessary to call in a policeman. The men were
then removed. Whilst they were in the street Mr. Raw-
cliffe went to one of the room windows for the purpose of
seeing how the police-officer was going on with the men.
Ile was standing in front of the window when one of
the men observed him, and suddenly threw at him a
heavy poker' which struck his forehead, and penetrated
the skull to the depth of four inches. Mr. Raweliffe
died soon afterwards, and, what is still More sad to
relate, Mrs. Rawcliffe, when she became aware of the
circumstance, wasP so terribly shockel that she died in
about,an hour after her husband. Three of the men were
taken into custody, and were brought on Monday
before the Kirkham magistrates. 'They were remanded
until Thursday.

MURDER AND ATTEMPTED SUICIDE By A LUNATIC.
•-•,•A fearful occurrence took place on the 29th at a
place called Sundy's Gate, in the northern district of,
Drogheda, in Ireland. It appears that a man named
Dennis Deane, a gardener, had been for some time past
unsettled in his mind, and resided with hi & family, whir
considered that it was not necessary to put him under
any restraint until a few days ago, when a person was
employed to attend on him at his own house, and
watch his movements, in order to prevent him from
doing harm to himself or others. On Monday morning,
however, Deane managed to elude the vigilance of his
keeper, and slipped, away from the house. In a short
time ke was missed, but it was after he bad forced
open the door of a neighbouring woman, nained
Byrne, who at the time was in her bed, and,
it ist :stated, had just been pronounced con-
valescent from an attack of illness. He seized
some heavy instrument which he found in the
house, with which ho struck the unfortunate woman
repeat td Mows on the skull, and beat out her brains.
Re then proceeded to do violenc6 to himself by inflict-
ing wounds on his own head, and having run into the
street the alarm became general, and a large crowd of
perions gathered. A number of men rushed on the
lunatic, and captured him, when he was conveyed to
his house, anti bound hand and foot with ropes. Dr.
Ellis was soon on the spot, and having first visited the
woman Byrne, pronounced that death was inevitable,
as she was breathing her last. He next dressed the
Wounds on the head of Deane. A company of the
police force was shortly after in attendance. Had
Deane not been captured so promptly ashe was, there is
no knowing to what extent .his outrages might have
extended, for it appears that on his way to Mrs.
Byrne's house he met an unoffending little girl, and
struck her to the ground, inflicting a deep wound on
the head. Deane was for some length of time gar-
dener at the grounds attached to the School of the
Christian Brothers, and lived on the premises. He
was a man of good character, and is father of a family.
THE SHEEP Pox.--Dr. Kidd thus writes in the Mark-
lane Express :—‘l am desirous of mentioning a very ex-
traordinary discovery recently made in America. A
disease termed measles has raged like a plague amongst
the hundreds of thousands of sick and wounded of
the army of the Potomac—measles exactly as we see it
in children, but in a vast number of cases from a
secondary cause—so to term it, simple infection, the
disease once commenced going on spontaneously. This
disease has been distinctly traced, and by a Set of in-
ductive reasonings (from which it is impossible to
escape) proved to have arisen from clouds of micro-
scopic dust or sporules arising from large quantities of
rotten fermenting straw, that some wicked contractor
hn,a supplied to 1111 the soldier's bed-ticks. Wherever
the measles has raged, there the rotten straw has been;
where the measles has not been, the beds were of good
straw, inferior cotton, and feathers. Everybody knows
that many individuals are subject to measly skin• and
-high fever if: they go near hay-tossing in a field in
harvest. Persons have been taken with this disease
(" hay fever"), and others with most distressing hay.
asthma, in London' and they could not make it out till
they found they had been passing a corn-chandler's-
where new hay had been at the door. Ido not. believe
sheep can take "small-pox" at all, and
.certainly the
present disease, as it is described, is more of the nature
of some of the affections just referred to. I can quite
imagine the poor things bedded or lying at first on
straw; the new disease spreading then by infection, or
as yeast spreads (hence we call these diseases zymotic).
The hint may be useful, at any rate, to some of our
farmers who do not trouble themselves much with
zymotics or sporules. The sheep at present, too; seemed
to be killed by over-dosing.'

articles.title: TONIC SOL-FA ASSOCIATION.
articles.text:
TONIC SOL-FA ASSOCIATION.

A choral demonstration of this association was held
on Tuesday evening at Exeter Hall by a choir of 700
voices selected from the various metropolitan classes.
An audience respectable and appreciative crowded' the
hall in every part, and the entire performance went off
with an esprit and success which indicated careful pre-
paration and undoubted efficiency. The programme
,_,,ontained a judicious selection of vocal pieces, both
elementary and classical, but we must fairly state that
the former pieces were generally most successful. We
may particularly mention the part song for equal
voices, 'April Showers,' which was- enthusiastically
encored;'The Wanderer's Farewell,' Buttercups and
Daisies,' and The Old Cottage Clock,' which received
the largest share of applause. We must, how-
ever, award great praise to the performance of some of
the higher class of music, such as' the chorus from
Handel's 'L'Allegro,' 'Haste thee, nymph;' the
anthem, To Thee, 0 Lord,' by Haydn; the chorus
from HandePs 'Saul,' 'flow excellent,' and
The madrigal, 'ln going to,my'lonedome bed,'
received a hearty and well-deserved encore. The
pretty, musical effects of the part song, 'Brightly
beaming,' which were well brought out by
the entire choir, were highly appreciated and ap-
plauded. The heavier pieces of' sacred music
were overwhelmed by the thunder of the organ,
and we
.could not, therefore; judge so well of their
merits. The Xational Anthem, arranged by Mr.
Henry Leslie, concluded a performance which, con-
sidering the nature and tender age of the singers, re-
flects great credit upon it's promoters, and unmistak-
ably testifies to the advantage of their mode of musical
tuition. between the two parts of the concert one of
the concluders apologised for the necessary absence of
the founder of the association—Mr. Curwen ; and ex-
plained the objects of the society, as well as indicated
the progress that it had made. The conductors were
Messrs. Sarll and Evans, and Miss Elizabeth Stirling
presided •t the organ.

articles.title: III'ALTEI OI LONDO.Y.
articles.text:
III'ALTEI OI LONDO.Y.

The weekly return of births and deaths in London
published by authority of the Registrar-General, say s :
In the week that ended on Saturday the deaths of
1,140 persons (of whom 5-75 were males, and 565
females) were registered in London. If the deaths
from epidemic cholera in the thirty-ninth week of 1864
are withdrawn from the calculation, it will be found
that the average number of deaths in corresponding
weeks of ten years (1852-61) was 1,138, and if this re-
sult is corrected for increase of population, it becomes
1,251. The comparison shows that the deaths of last
week were less by 111 than they would have been if
the average rate of mortality had prevailed. Of the
1,140 persons who died, 651-were under 20 years of
age, 141 were 20 and under 40, 162 were 40 to 60,
154 were 60 to 80, and 30 were 80 years of age and
upwards.
359 persons died of zymotic diseases, including 2
by cholera, 72 by diarrhoel, 38 by measles, 84 by scar-
latina, 63 by typhus. Of 172 deaths assigned to
diseases of the respiratory organs, 72 were caused by
bronchitis, 71 by pneumonia, 9by asthma. Phthisis
was fatal in 121 cases.

The son of a clerk, aged 1 year, died at 5, Under-
wood.-street, Shoreditch, of cholera infant= (12
hours).' The son of a plasterer, aged 2 years, died at
41, Cumberland•street, Chelsea, of choleraic diarrbfea
(3 days).' A cab-driver, aged 25 years, died at the
Westminster Hospital from what appears to have been
glanders.
Last week the births of 899 boys and 843 girls, in
all 1,742 children, were registered in London. In the
ten corresponding weeks of the years 1852-61, the
average number (corrected) was 1865.

SINGULAR AND LAMENTABLE ACCIDENT AT CHARING-
CROSS THROUGH RAPID Dewixo.—Mr. Langharn, de-
puty•coroner for Westminster, held an inquiry at the
Charing-cross Hospital relative to the death of Mrs.
Anne Evans, aged 55, who was killed on Wednesday
by a cab opposite the Nelson column while returning
frota the Great Exhibition. It appeared from the
evidence that Mrs. Evans and her daughter, being at
the Exhibition on Wednesday, returned in the after-
noon by an omnibus to Charing-cross.. They alighted
opposite the column, but a'mistake being made in the
amount of the fare, deceased was called back by the
conductor. Just at that time a cab .carne round from
St. Martin's-lane at a very rapid 'pace, and, according
to two witnesses, struck deceased on the head and
shoulder, knocking her down violently. Two French
gentlemen called out to the -cabman, but he merely
looked at deceased lying on the ground, and drove on
the faster. Deceased was picked up, but in a few-mo-
ments became paralysed, and had to, be removed to
the hospital, where she died almost instantaneously.
The house surgeon said that the post-mortein examina-
tion disclosed extensive fracture of a -vessel of the
brain, but as it did not correspond with the external
injury he considered it -resulted from the emotion of
-terror at the prospat of being ridden over, and not
the actual collision. The jury returned a verdict of
'Death from apoplexy produced by excitement,'
and recommended that in future cabs should be-made
come round corners and off cab-stands at a more mode-
rat) pace than is custoruary.

THE STARVATION OF A FAMILY IN
WELLCLOSE-SQUARE.

The investigation into the circumstances of the
dreadful starvation of a family in Wellclose-square,
by which Mrs. Charlotte Crippin lost her life, as was
alleged, by the cruelty or neglect either of her hus-
band or the authorities of the 'Whitechapel Union,
was resumed on Wednesday morning.
It will be recollected that the deceased and her
family were removed from the union in question to a
house in Wellclose-square, where they were left for a
fortnight in a state of frightful suffering, and there
they were found literally dying from famine.
George.' Crippin stated that he was compelled by
the woilchouse people to act as ho had. done, under a
threat of three months' inaprisoninent, although he
mOe them aware that he had not a halfpenny to buy
them f00d....

Mr. Elves, relieving officer, was now recalled, and
said that Mrs. CripPin stated to the board ofsuardians
that her husband was starving her, and they forth-
with ordered him io be proceeded against, that was,
that he should be brought ,up before a magistrate.
Crippin, however; was never threatened-with anything
of the kind by witness, but said voluntarily that he
would take out his wife and family, as be had 'work
with .which he could support them. He said he would
furnish a home to take them to.

George Crippin (recDed) adhered to, his former
Statement, and said that Mr. Eaves distinctly said to
him, If you don't remove your family by four
o'clock on Monday, I shall certainly have you locked
up.' Witness was then ill and had no work. Wit-
ness contrived to borrow 55., and paid for the room in
Wellclose-Pquare, into which he removed his family.
Daniel Bradley said that he knew Crippin to be out
of work for the last twelve months. Witness hap-
pened to be near Wellclose-square when Mr. Eaves,
the relieving officer, came and took Crippin.aside; and
told him that if he did not take out his wife he should
be locked up for three or six months, Crippin told
Eaves that he had nothing to give them, and never
said that he had a room or furniture.

Mr. CI antrell, professor of gymnastics, said that one
of Crippin's sons was apprenticed to him, and that he
knew nothing against the character of Crippin. He
lent him £5 in May last, on account of the great dis-
tress into which his family had fallen. CriPpin was
constantly trying to borrow money from witness for
the support of his Lfamily. Crippin's son was with
witness since he was three years of age, and witness
woule not have to pay him enything. He would stop
, with witness till he was twentyyears of age, heing fed,
clothed, and taught. He performed at. Leicester-
square and elsewhere, and was very usefui indeed.
Witness lent the £5 to Crippin to induce him to leave
his son longer with him.
A. former landlady of Crippin said that be was very
kind to his wife awl family, and did everything in his
power for them.
The Coroner then read over the 'depositions, and said
that it was clear that the deceased and her family,
being in extreme starvation, presented herself at the
Union House, and to obtain admission represented her
husband as starving her. Without the most ordinary
inquiry as to whether he was -doing so from neglect or
through necessity, the board of guardians ordered Crippin
to be proceeded against. Mr. Eaves, the relieving officer,
went to Crippin and, under a threat of three months' im-
prisonment, compelled him to remove his family. They
were placed in a room, and there had to undergo such
dreadtul starvation that deceased died of the effects,
and they would have all perished had not their groans
attracted the attention of the neighbours. Mr. Eaves
certainly denied that he used any threat, but Crippin's
statement was the more probable. The workhouse au-
thorities seemed to him to be much to blame in the
matter in not having made proper inquiries into the
means of a man who, it turned out, was without_ any
employment, and was under treatment at an hospital
for rheumatic gout, and therefore could not possibly
support, his unfortunate family.
The jury returned the following special verdict
'That deceased expired from the ellects of inflammation
of the stomach, accelerated by the want of the common
necessaries of life; and the jury unanimously censure
the conduct of Mr. Eaves, the assistant relieving offiCer of
the Whitech,apel Union, in thematter, and consider that
he did not perform his duty; and the jury further de-
sire to recommend that in future the board of guardians
should make due inquiries
,as to bow inmates of the
union are likely to be taken care of outside the house,
before ordering their removal from it.'
The inquiry, which was very protracted, ti.en termi-
nated.

articles.title: ELIPORTANT RECISION UNDER THE NEW POACHING ACT.
articles.text:
ELIPORTANT RECISION UNDER THE
NEW POACHING ACT.

A man named Thomas Rowlson was charged at
Leicester, on Friday, with unlawfully having game in
his possession. Police-constable Smith said he met the
defendant, on the morning of the 20th, with a bag on
his - shoulder, in Bedford -street. Defendant had also
something bulky in his pocket. Witness searched him,
and found twelve rabbits in the bag, and a net and
pegs in defendant's pocket. Witness asked him where
he got the rabbits, and defendant replied, A good way
off,' and that he had had a hard night's work.' Police-
sergeant Neale gave corroborative evidence.—,The
Magistrate's Clerk (Mr. S. Stone) said, that as thiff was
the first case which. had come before the magistrates
tinder the new Poaching Act he thought it necessary
to cali their attention to the provisions of the statute.
The clause under which the information waS laid
might be divided into two parts—one relating to the
duty of the constable, and the other to the offence to
be proved before the magistrates. With respect
to the constable, his duty was to starch any per Son he
might meet upon the highway whom he had good
cause to suspect of coming from any land where he
should have been unlawfully in search of game, iknd of
having in his possession any game unlawfully obtained.
In this case it was clear that there were good grounds
of suspicion, and that the constable was justified in
searching the defendant, and detaining the rabbits so
found—rabbits being game for the purposes of the
Act. It was then the duty of the constable to lay an
information before the magistrates, and the offenoe to
be proved before them was that of the defendant
having obtained the game so found by unlawfully
going on land in search or pursuit of game. The
mere possession of the rabbits was not legal proof
of the defendant having unlawfully obtained them,
and the Act did not impose on him the obliga-
tion of accounting for their possession or of show-
ing how he obtained them. -The game might have
been lawfully obtained by purchase, or, as the de-
feskdant alleged in that case, by going on land, where
herhad a right to search'for game. It might have
also been received.from some person who had, without
the knowledge of the defendant, unlawfully obtained
it, or might have been taken_ on the highway. In none
of these cases would the offence be within the words of
the Act. A recent Act of Parliament required any
person found in possession of Zany deer to account for
his possession of the same, but there was no such
provision in the Act under which this information -"was
laid, and this difference confirmed him in his construc-
tion of it. Ile was consequently of opinion that it
was the duty of the prosecutor to prove the offence
charged by distinct affirmative -evidence, and as the
only proof before the _magistrates was that of mere
possession on the highway, be must advise the bench
to dismiss the case. The case was accordingly dismissed,
and the rabbits restored to the defendant. The case.
excited considerable interest, the magistrates in some of
tituaetty sessional divisions in the county having. re-
c'efttly convicted on mere evidence of possession.

MELANCHOL 5 EATH OF A•LADF.—An inquest was
held at Datch: 'near Windsor, on Saturday last, by
Mr. George A. Charsley, the deputy-coroner for Bucks,
on the body of Mrs. Margaret Watson, the wife. of a
gentleman residing near Tottenham. Colonel Thomas •
Sissmore said the deceased was his sister-in-law, and
they were both on a T6it to Mr. Fowler, of Soulley
house, Datchet, the father of the deceased. She had
exhibited a little excitement, but was under no restraint.
On Wednesday night, a little before eleven o'clock,
she retired to rest, and on the following morning at
eight o'clock the servant came to tell him that she
could not get into the bedroom of the deceased. .
Witness told the gardener to enter the room by a
ladder placed against the window. Deceased was not
there, but footsteps were afterwards,discovered below
the bedroom window, ilia there was a broken branch
of a tree which—convinced him that deceased had
escaped in that way. • After examining the grounds and
shrubbery, and obtaining no trace of her, witness sent
a man in a punt to search the water, in which she
was shortly afterwards discovered. Deceased was
about 58 years old. The two windows in her bedroom
were about 15 feet from- the ground, and very small.
Could assign no reason why she should commit suicide.
The jury after a long consultation returned a verdict
of Found drowned in the river Thames, without any
marks on her body, but by what means she came into
the river there was no evidence to show.'

SUDDEN DEATHS OF CHILDREN.—On Tuesday Dr.
Lankester, the coroner, held an inquest at the George
the Fourth, Spring-place, Kentish Town, on the body
of an infant named Graham, and another inquest at
the Three Tuns, Cross-street, Hatten-garden, on the
body of a child named Matthew Welch, aged three
years, both of whom expired suddenly under singular
circumstances. The evidence adduced cleared up the
mystery, however, in both cases, and the verdicts
recorded were that the deaths took place from natural
causes. In the latter case a serious charge of ill-
treatment of the deceased was made against the mother,
but totally unsubstantiated by the inquest.

STJAIMARY.

articles.title: FOREIGN.
articles.text:
FOREIGN.

Ocn foreign intelligence is chiefly American.
In Italy a princess of Savoy has been married
by proxy to the King of Portugal; while the
man who made her father King of Italy is in
a prison, wounded, and that an Italian prison,
for struggling to complete his work.

From the far east intelligence has come of
another great calamity in China, involving the
loss of more lives than have peiished in any
previous storm of the century.

By hail, and flood, and frost combined,
several hundreds of persons have been cut off,
and the growing crops destroyed in an impor-
tant district of Northern Africa, forming part
of the French Colony.
The French Court continues among the
Pyrenees, pondering over the position of
matters beyond the Alps. That iron hand on
the Italian neck grasps firmly, and there is not
much hope that the Imperial garrotter will
soon quit his hold.
The American papers describe a series of
terrible engagements in September. The mail
bring despatches to the 20th ult., when the
Confederates were pressed back, and out of Mary-
land, over the Potomac, by the Federals after
four or five days of hard fighting. The losses
are described by some of the Federal corres-
pondents as 10,000 to them in killed and woun-
ded; and one of these writers says that the
losses of the Confederates cannot be fewer than
those of their men. The Confederates re-crossed
the Potomac with all their spoil, stores, wag-
gons, and wounded. They touched no private
property without payment, and they inflicted
no personal injuries on dis-unionists or
unionists except in war. Their clothes are des.
Cribed as ragged and town. Some of them are
capless, others are shoeless; but their horse
are good, and their rifles are carefully kept.
1 heir discipline is perfect, and their organisa-
tion altogether superior to that of their oppo-
nents.

General Stonewall Jackson stormed Harper's
Ferry, and the garrison, consisting of 8,000
Federals, surrendered. At a place in Kentucky
another garrison of 4,000 Federals had surren-
dered. The loss of general officers from the
Federal armies in the last battles is remark-
able. In ordinary circumstances it would infer
g higher loss of soldiers than is reported.
Some of the leaders slain were men of' mark.
Genera's Mansfield and Reno were distin-
guished on the Northern side, and their places
will not be easily supplied. We have yet to
hear the Southern statements of these fights,
but the Confederate invasion of Maryland has
turned out to be a mistake. The purpose of
war is not to kill or to be killed, but to I
achieve great results. The Confederates in
marching into and out of Maryland have
achieved no apparenfresult of importance. They
may have gained some stores, they have cap-
tured some excellent artillery; but these gains
are.not worth the men, prestige, and strength
lost. Maryland is not ready to join the
South. It had an opportunity and neglected
the time and tide. Its people may know the
fate of Virginia, and may not desire to share
the honours and losses of warfare. Cotton
has advanced in Liverpool since these Federal
successes were known—the most convincing
evidence of the opinions entertained by our
speculators on the war.
Hostilities in the South and West proceed
in the o,ld relentless spirits, destroying many
lives and much property, without advancing
any decisive triumph.

articles.title: COLONIAL.
articles.text:
COLONIAL.

The South African mail brings intelligence
of many failures in the colonies, consequent
on speculations in wool, and yet that material
has recently brought good prices here.
A West Indian mail brings no particular
intelligence, but a large quantity of bullion,
drawn probably from South America. The
islanders were moving on prosperously, feeling
the dearth or scarcity of labour in some quar-
ters to be their most decided want.

A meeting of delegates from the North
American colonies had been held in Quebec,
and an agreement made respecting the pro-
posed Inter-Colonial Railway. The cost of
the works is estimated at three millions, and
the loan necessary for their completion will be
guaranteed by the Imperial Government.

articles.title: HEROES OF LABOUR.
articles.text:
THE HEROES OF LABOUR.

MA/TY writers flatter the working classes by
ascribing to them all the virtues, and refusing
them any great share of the rewards of well-
doing. The title placed at the head of these
sentences, is in accordance with this practice.
It is one of the set phrases kept for judicious
use by these writers. In the BEE-HIVE we
address a large body of intelligent men, but
neither to deceive nor flatter them. Theprodue-
tive clafises would have occupied a noble position
in this empire, and through its extent and power
in the world, if they had husbanded their often
squandered resources. The opportunity is not
lost, although it has been postponed; for even
yet industrious men, by the odds and ends of
industry's returns, may help to make a nobler
condition of society than has ever been seen
before our day in the world.

We do not ascribe to the working classes
the exclusive possession of good qualities, and
conceal the self-denial, and the devotion of life
itself, to humanity or a good object, that have
characterized many-men in the higher ranks
of society, whose path through life might have
always been over the soft grass of indolence,
and always hedged round by the flowers of
luxury. The deaths at Scarborough in one of
the storms of last winter, when a peer and a
gentleman of fortune freely gave away their
lives in efforts to save those of some sea-
men, were proofs of exalted heroism. The
journals of last week recorded the death of the
Earl of ELLESMERE, whose last public act was
an appeal against the treatment of the cotton
operatives of Lancashire as paupers, because,
by no fault on their part, but from a cruel
foreign war, they were deprived of work. A
brief life of personal weakness deprived this
nobleman of the means of working for the
public good with the energy that in better
health he might have exhibited; but he was
one of many men endowed alike with riches
and the purpose to use them well.
Mr. FORBES MACKENZIE, a landowner of
Peebleshire, was found dead in his bed, at a
house where he was on a visit, one morning of
last week. He had calmly slept into eternity.
His name was associated with blame by many,
with praise by a multitude, on account of his
measure to reduce the hours of attendance to
public houses within Scotland. Many old
opponents of the bill are now its supporters,
for they find that it emancipated them from
tedious hours of toil that were useless, and
has been beneficial in many respects.
Mr. MACKENZIE might have avoided all these
reproaches by doing nothing on the subject;
but a moral heroism was exhibited in encoun-
tering them.
The daily papers of this week record the
death of Sir J. INTaisi A few years ago that
name was in every journal, almost on every
tongue. When Sir HARRY LAWRENCE was
killed in the Residency of Lucknow, Colonel
I-Nous succeeded him in the command of the
place. How with a handful of men he defended
the women and children, sheltered there from
angry thousands, daily and nightly surging
against its weak works, through an almost
hopeless time, closed out from intercourse with
his old comrades, but strong in the conviction
that they would not desert him and the mul-
titude enclosed in that fierce siege; how he
endured and fought; how he laboured and .

watched with his wife beside him, until their
.relief was achieved, is a narrative that enriches
our annals . with one more imperishable tale
of the brave, but now of the dead. The
nation is entitled to be
:proud of men who thus
honour our race by . good deeds or great lives.
We grudge not. to them fame that should not
die ; a memory that should be ever cherished
as a rich heritage. -
Labour has its heroes, and they too merit the
reward of admiration, some meed of praise, and
a substantial recompence, never perhaps to avail
them, but to• save theirs, not out, of sorrow,
only out of a workhouse. Last week an at-
tempt was made to sink a well at a country
place, and one man had reached a considerable.
depth when he met foul air and became
insensible. His comrade, with a brave defiance
of the danger, descended after him and he
also' became insensible. Some females observed
the, calamity and raised an alarm, although!
they could not render help. A mason working
in the neighbourhood came first to the mouth
of the well. The females there Oged him to
patience until they could procure ropes, so that
they might bring him up again if he also suf-
fered from, the foul air at the bottom;' but he
went down and was not recovered. Some
time elapsed before the bodies were brought to
the surface. All were dead.. . The man who
was attacked first was a widower, whose
family have arrived at man and Womanhood.
The second man was unmarried. The mason
leaves a Widow and seven young children, who
depended on his labour and life for their sup-
port. Going down into that danger and dark-
ness to save •life by risking life, .did any vision
cross his eyes, as the light of day faded into
night, of that group not of all Whom he held
dear, but all of whom must have been dear
to him, mourning over a loss which some of
those infants could not comprehend! A rash
act was,this, perhaps, that made his little ones
orphans, and his wife a widow ; but who
can feel the less admiration for that nobility
of heart that stopped not to count the cost, or
.to be coldly prudent when men were' perish-
ing, and still a hope existed that they might be.
saved! •

Deeds of this nature,brilliant as any achieve-
ment ever done on battle field, have no -Vic-
toria cross; farther, and more deplorable still,
no provision is made to support families who
may be left destitute by a self-sacrifice to save
others.
.We do not oi4 -Seek some. record of
their names who have bravely fallen in endea-
vouring to save: life ; but provision far those
whom they leave behindthem. A little-labour
would remove this existing reproach. Few
words from a few men in good position would
secure us against the scandal that it man may
ruin his family by exertions in the . path of
duty and humanity. The enlargement of
an existing society would attain all that is re-
quired. The :Premier encourages brave men,
whose deeds earn trophies for their land and
themselves. Might he not, by his influence,
deliver us from
.the possible shame of this
brave :mason's family being confounded with
common paupers, and educated in a work-
house

The crimes of all classes are carefully chroni-
cled; a paragraph dismisses nOble deeds. An
accident has occurred at the Llanflynydd Col-
liery, near Mold, Flintshire. Three men des-
cended the shaft to repair some brick work.
More of the bricks fell on them. They
were buried among the falling ruins, assailed
by the rising water, and perished. Great efforts
were made to save them, other men went
down the shaft, and laboured to extricate the
crushed and drowning men, with a. crumbling
mass above them:loose and falling in showers;
but their labours were vain. The men were
lost. With less personal risk these labourers
might have passed through a great battle as
soldiers; but they emerged from the shaft.
leaving the bodies of theii comrades, and their
names will be mentioned in no general orders;
they do not even appear in the newsparer
paragraph that describes the scene.
The names of the lost men even are
,not re-
corded. Each belonged to somebody. Name-
less villagers unknown in society—they are
not therefore forgotten at home. One of them,
we are inthrmed, leaves a family and a very
aged parent. Another leaves "a blind parent
whom he supported." The man did merely
his duty in supporting that blind parent, but
duty is not a cold dry thing as many persons
seem to suppose. The doing of duty would
enrich society with a flow of noble acts, ever
recurring like the mercies bestowed on earth's
children, new every moment, and ever being
renewed. The blind mourner will bear no
more that good son's voice, but ever in the
dark solitude of the parent's future days, the
memory of the playful boy and the providing
son, will be of those bright stores from the past,
out of which the passing day and the present
hour often draw support.

articles.title: CIRCITIVISTANTIAL EVIDENCE.
articles.text:
CIRCITIVISTANTIAL EVIDENCE.

A CRIME, a trial, and a sentence. have caused
great excitement in Scotland, and even the
north of England, in the past and present
week. The defeat of GA.RIBALDI, or the hos-
tilities of the
,States, have not roused an in-
terest so deep and wide as a cruel murder, and
a prisoner left to die after a long trial. Mr.
FLEMING, an., accountant, with his father and
his son, three generations; and no ladies in the
family, resided at 17, Sandy-ford Place, a West-
End Street in Glasgow. One female, JESSE
M‘PHERsoN, lived with them as general ser-
vant. She was a person in middle life, and
had been in the service of the family, With a
brief interval; for a long period. She was
frequently' visited by Mrs. NPLAucimAN; who
had also
.been a servant in the family, previous
to her marriage, four years ago. JESS E
WPRERSON and Mrs.' 11PLAUCHLAN lived. on
apparently affectionate and intimate terms.
On Friday, the 4th July, Mr. FLEMING and
his son left Glasgow for a cottage at Dunoon,
with the intention - of remaining • there until
the following Monday. The elder Mr. FLEM-
ING, who is said to be 85 to 87 years of age,
remained in the Glasgow house with the ser-
vant. Although Mr. FLEMING is an aged, yet
he is also an active, "Strong man, entrusted with
the collection of weekly rents, and the general
management of houses, consisting of many
floors, subdivided into numerous tenancies,
and requiring a keen and sharp overseer.
"Upon the morning of Saturday, Mr. FLEM-
ING found the kitchen empty, and the servant
gone, but he remained in the house until the
afternoon, all the night, all the following day,
and next night, and until Monday afternoon,
without giving information to any one, or
making inquiry, respecting the absent woman.
On Monday afternoon, on the return of his'
son and grandson, they broke open the ser-
vant's bedroom, and found her dead, killed and
sadly.mangled by some rough instrument. The
elder FLEMING admitted that he was awakened
on the morning of Saturday by a scream, fol-
lowed by two Others weaker than the first. He
slept in a room above the kitchen, and rose.
The morning was beautiful and clear, and it
was then four o'clock, with the sun shining
bright, as it shines
,through ai 11110 t smoke- ,

less sky, -even over Glasgow, in these early
hours of Morn in summer time. He heard no
more, retired again to bed, slept till six, and
then -dozed 'on till nine The servant usually
brought in his breakfast at eight, but as she
came not at nine, he rose, dressed, looked for
her, found her bedroom door fastened, with no
key, knocked, and had no reply; prepared his
own breakfast in the kitchen that morning, and
his fbod on that day, on the Sabbath, and part.
of Monday; but saw no blo6d stains there, or
in the passag,es, although others found them
afterwards proceeded with his-business in the
city, was twice at church on the first day of the
week; busy with his collection of rent on the
second, replied to inquiries on domestic matters
at his door, but never mentioned to any one
the disappearance-of the servant.
Monday afternoon came, and his son and
grandson returned, heard his narrative,
opened the servant's bedroom- with one of-the
keys in the house, and found her body, cold,
lifeless, and long murdered. The old man was
finally
.arrested and examined, but after some
time he was released; for -it was found that
some silver plate had been stolen from the
house, and the articles of apparel belonging- to
the deceased serKant, on the night of Friday
or-the, morning of Saturday. As the inquiry'
proceeded, the plate was discovered in a pawn-
broker's; pledged by Mrs. M‘LAIrmiLLN, in an
assumed name and address; while the clothing
had been .sent by her to different towns, Ayr,
Greenock, and Hamilton, "to be called for."
and the box containing part of it had been
called for at Hamilton by Mrs.:M‘laucif LAN,
who had obtained it,- and had left parts of the
clothing it contained in fields and under
hedges, and a few articles had been sent by her
to the dyer. She paid her rent on Saturday
from the money received on the plate pledged,
and- on the Friday evening she left her house
and child with the expressed intention of visit-
ing JE,Nsti: M‘PuEnsoN; and did not return
until late on Saturday.inorning.
In her cLelaration She asserted that she had
not been at Jessie 111‘PitERsom on the night
of the murder, but hal received the plate Emil
old FLEMING 011 the following Saturday; that
he gave her four pounds of the proceeds with
which she paid her rent, and the clothes were
previously sent to her by the servant who
wished an alteration of part and others of them
were given to her as JESSIE _WITHER:SON inten-
ded to emigrate. Three solicitors in Glasgow
undertook her defence. A plea of not guilty
was put in for her: the trial lasted two or three
days; the FLEMINGS were all examined, the
jury.returnecl a :verdict of guilty—the judge
sentenced her to- die. The trial closed two
weeks ago on this day.
Between the verdict of the jury and the sen-
tence of the judge a remarkable sceneinter-
-vernes. The senior counsel for the prisoner
expresed her desire to make a statement. The
request was conceded. The prisoner merely
said that. she wished the statement to be read,
which was dme by Mr. CLARKE, her counsel.
It contained a circumstantial narrative of the
murder, perpetrated, according to the prisoner,
by the old man ...Her story extends over a
close and long column of consistent 'and yet
minute details.. She went to the house on
Friday evening, expecCng that FLEMING' would
have been in bed, bat found him at supper
with: the servant. Some. time after eleven,
FLEMING sent her out for whiskey, .but the
shop WAS closed and he returned without it.
Then she found 'JESSE .M.THERSON cut on the
head, and lying in the laundry insensible. The
old man said nothing of the cause of quarrel,
but she bathed the servant's face and head, and
ultimately, with his assistance, got the woman
conveyed to her bedroom. Then the prisoner
wished to call in a doctor, but the old man
opposed her proposal, and as the wounded
womar revived "she Urged the prisoner not
to leave. her. Hours wore away until day-
light came, before three o'clock. JESSIE
M.PITERSON Was able. to speak and tell her
story, which she did as the old man cleaned
the blood from . the -laundry and made tea for
himself in the kitchen. The prisoner alleges
that she was told by jEsstE M‘PuERsoN that
Old FLEMING had taken liberties with her on
some occasions, and that they quarrelled while
Mrs. M'LluculaN was out, and he struck her.
Both of them had been drinking. At three
o'clock, or thereby, JESSIE 1-I.‘PahnsoN was
helped to the kitchen, for she was cold, and a
fire was lighted there. The prisoner insisted
then on going for a doctor, which the old man
opposed, because he said it would bring him
into trouble. The prisoner persisted, however,
and ran for her bonnet, but ere she ha 4 re-
turned FLEMING had again struck MTIIERSON
that blow with a meat cleaver which must have
been fatal. The prisoner has been notoriously
subject to palpitation of the heart for a lcng
time, and says she was paralysed. and unable
to take any step. In course of some time
FLEMING persuaded her to help him to carry
the body
.to the bed from the kitchen,
having first given her an assurance of
personal safety; and made her swear on the
open Bible that she would not reveal the
secrets of that night. He then induced her to
carry away the clothes a-nd pledge the plate,
that an appearance of truth might be given
to the idea that the house had been broken
into, and the servant murdered.
We have condensed the declaration, omitting
the details, but the most important part of the
story is that the declaration was in the hands
of the agents for the prisoner a month before
the trial, yet the counsel and these gentlemen
preferred to rest her case on the difficulty of
proving that she had been in the house on that
night. The prisoner insisted on its being
read.

- The probabilities of Mr. FLEMING being con-
nected with the murder are many and not
easily met, for although he is said to be 85 or 87
years old by himself, others say that he is 10
years younger, and in his intellectual and physi-
cal condition he is equal to the average of man-
kind at 65 to 67 years old. The acquaintance
and friends of the murdered woman depose
that she spoke of him in language implying
more than being merely troublesome. She
called him "au old devil, and an old wretch"
to one: to another she intimated that she
could not describe her trouble in the house
because her friend's husband was present.
Then this man, awakened and disturbed
through the night by shrieks,, forgot them
when his servant was absent in the morning;
and allowed three days and nights to elapse
without opening her. room, informing her
neighbours or the police of her disappearance,
or making any inquiry whatever after a person
who might have been in bed seriously ill, un-
able to move or speak, and left to starve. No
innocent, sensible, sharp man, would have acted
in that manner; if he was capable of conduct-
ing the business that, FLE&IING transacted.
lie- swore that.
.one servant called to borrow
a spade at eleven, who says that she did
not call until two; but a business man, with
nothing particular to do at home, would not
have remained there on a Saturday until two.
The servant who sought to borrow his spade
was, he said, his first visitor on Saturday, but
the milk man and hi 8 boy called at twenty

minutes to eight in the mornince, and the boy
says that FLEMING took the chain from the
front door and opened it, being then drgssed
in black, and declined to take any milk. At
that hour FLEMING deposed that he was in
bed, although he afterwards said that he might
have been up, and did refuse the milk.
The motives,that might have actuated either
of the two parties to this crime are apparent.
l'he man was jealous, irritable, and had been
drinking with the servant, according to the
woman's statement. He could easily have
killed the weaker of the two women, but did
he adopt a more subtle course, and by commit-
ting her to the possession of the clothes and
the plate, provide himself with a substitute?
It is a terrible thought, but one of two persons
are guilty, and all sides of the question require
re-examination.

The • improbabi/ites of Mrs. I\PLAITCHLAN'S
guilt are nurnerous.. She is a stupid woman,
or she would not havuledged the plate in the
neighbourhood, and attempted to scatter the
clothes through the county. Still it is impro-
bable that she would have left. her home to
murder an .intimate friend,: in this rude man-
ner, leaving information with a neighbour
that she was
~going to that particular house.
She is a weak person, labouring under a phy-
sical .disease that would caution her against
seeking excitement or a death struggle, but the
servant was a healthy, strong, " wiry " woman.
Lord DEAS, the judge, hinted that Mrs.
M‘LAUGILLAN had slept with JESSE M‘PriER-
SDN, and struck her while she slept ;: but would
she also have conveyed the body from the bed-
room to the kitchen, in order. to drag it back
from the kitchen to the bedroom? • It is very
doubtful, we think, whether she could have
lifted the body on to the bed. The medical
men were astornshed to find some of the
wounds carefully washed; but would one
woman who had killed another ever have
thought of washing the wounds? The idea is
preoosterous. The passage had been roughly
washed, but in Glasgow at that season there is
scarcely a dark hour—there are not more than
two dark hours; and if a murderess had ac-
complished her. guilty object, can any sane
person suppose that she would have Stopped in
the house to wash the passages.? She would
have naturally atternpted to get away soon,
and avoided any process calculated to disturb
the old gentleman in the room above, for old
people do not sleep soundly. Some medical
men allege that an ignorant woman could not
have described the effect of the blows on the
living patient, as it is narrated in the declara-
tion,.unless she had seen "the operation," and
would a woman guilty of savage murder have
bathed the cut face, and smoothed the bloody
hair, and watched for a length of time the
sinking Shuddering victim before concluding
her work? That idea also is unnatural.

Among thcpnumerous details
.given in this
declaration, not one is found to
,be inconsistent
with any evidence colleted after it was given
and written.
Mrs. 111.`LACIILAN is sentenced to die on
Saturday next, but the excitement in all the
Scotch towns on the subject is so great that
the sentence. Could not be carried oat with
propriety: even if the authorities entirely dis-
believe her tale, It was only told when she
considered herself relieved from the Bible oath
by FLEMING not "clearing her," and a super-
stitious feeling respecting such a " forced "
oath haunts many minds.
The case is the most celebrated among all
the modern difficulties of circumstantial evi-
dence, and the feeling against the execution of
the prisoner without new inquiries, and if
possible, a new trial, shows the necessity for a
criminai court of appeal.

articles.title: WHEN WILL REFORM COME OF
articles.text:
WHEN WILL REFORM COME OF

AGE?

WE can scarcely put the question. Now that
we have got to the period when the suspended
agitation was to be revived, the movement
seems dead. The condition of the States is
quoted against an extension of the suffrage.
The argument is worth little against those who
adduced the examples Of the States as an ar-
gument in favour of reform ; and nothing
against others who never considered their con-
dition any great argument on the subject.
The circumstances of Lancashire and other
manufacturing counties, are adduced as a rea-
son for saying nothing at present calculated
to disturb good feeling and distract men's
minds from the labours Of humanity and love,
in which everybody should be engaged,
We should not say a word at any time calcu-
lated to produce this bad result, but a question
' concerning reform has no consequence of
that character or nature. The distress in
Lancashire is the reason most urgent at pre-
sent for escaping from exclusively mercantile
andy middle class legislation into a healthy
representation of all classes. Even the distress
of the present season might have been greatly
modified by active measures; taken in time,
during the year. 'lhese measures were opposed
because the holders of cotton sought to obtain
high prices and great profits, and now the
holders of cotton goods and yarns want a share
of the gain from the sufferings of the year.
The horrible calamities in Lancashire sharpen
the demand for a complete suffrage. Other
systems have produced a Legislature who heard
.of the danger in a listless mood, stood by, and '
didnothing. We want a practical Legislature,
by whom our own- colonial and home resources
will be drawn out,. for our security against
starvation.

• An argument of this nature cannot go on for
for ever. There is indeed no argument against re
form. It is on]y met by delays, postponements,
and procrastinations. It is only stifled by
popular apathy. It will come of age whenever
the people desire its majority; with themselves
their franchisement rests. It will not produce
a miracle, but it may produce a fair adminis-
tration of our resources, and not leave the in—
dustrial classes to 'know that they live ever on
the brink of ruin, with the means within their
own empire of providing all the food, all the
material, and all the customers that are needed
for national peace and prosperity. The Prince
of Wales will come of age in a few weeks, and
he may live to be king of all the land. A tho-
rough Reform Bill cannot attain its majority
at the same time, but his reign will be the
more prospero-u..5, and his position firmer and
more secure, if this Reform be not long kept
in its minority. •

-New

TO °Mt REA.DERS AND SUB-

SCRIBERS.

LIST week we promised that this paper
should be improved. This week we redeem
our promise; and we trust that the form to
which it is now permanently enlarged, with
the many other improvements effected, will
give general satisfaction. All that is now
wanting is the active, zealous, and continuous
support of our present numerous subscribers,
and the adhesion of those who, from various
causes have held aloof from the enterprize,
and the BEE-HIVE will at once take its place
amongst the first-class journals of the day.

New York, Sept. 20 (Mming).
The Governors of Pennsylvania and Ohio' have
issued a call to the Governors of all the Union States
to meet on the 24th, at Altoona, Pennsylvania. The
New York press strongly condemn the Federal officers
for surrendering Harper's Ferry, and urge a nsitittry

articles.title: GAI?IB ALM MEETINGS.
articles.text:
GAI?IB ALM MEETINGS.

The Right Hon. the Lord Mayor has kindly con—
sented to grant the use of the Guildhall, in compliance
with a requisition signed by upwards of 1,000 citizens
of great respectability and influence, for a public
meeting in behalf of the illustrious captive of Spezzia.
Notice of the meeting will be duly given.

A meeting, convened by the Garibaldian Working
Men's Committee, was held last night in the Temper-
ance Hall, Goldsmith-row, Hackney-road. There was
a crowded and enthusiastic attendance.

The Working Man's Garibaldi Committee, which
called the meeting in Hyde Park,. last Sunday, have
issued a circular on the subject, which shows that they
took every reasonable precaution against disorder, and
did nothing to provoke interruption. They announce
that they shall not hold a meeting next Sunday.
