articles.text:
CORONER'S INQUESTS.7.YESTERDAY.

By Dr. Lankester, yesterday, at the Elephant and
Castle, Camden Town, on the body of a foreign gentle-
man, name unknown. The deceased had lodged for
some days at a coffee-house in the Blackfi iars-road,
and last Friday removed to the Iron Duke Hotel,
King's-cross. He dined and went to bed, requesting
to be called at six the next morning. He was called
but did not answer; on his room being entered, the
deceased was found dying.. The bed was destroyed,
and there were evidences of a severe struggle having
taken place. No explanation of these facts could be
given, and on the evidence of the surgeon who had.
made a post mortem examination the jury returned a
verdict that the deceased had died with disease of
the lungs, but that no exaet cause of death was proved.
By Mr. Humphreys, in the London Hospital,
on the body of a newly-born female child, found in a
parcel in Glasshouse-street, St. George's-in-the-East.
The jury returned a verdict of 'Wilful murder against
some person or persons unknown.'
By Mr. Humphreys, at the Sash and Cocoanut Tree
public-house, Wilson-street, Finsbury, respecting the
death of Elizabeth Ann Abdalla, aged fourteen years,
who died from the effects of poison imbibed by sucking
the composition off some imitation grapes. The in-
quiry was adjourned.
By Mr. Walthew, at the Gossett Arms, Gossett-
street, Hackney-road, on the body of Mrs. Castle, of
30, Wellington-road, the wife of a butcher in Leaden-
hall Market. It appeared the deceased had been car-
rying on an intrigue with a man named Holdane,
which having come to the knowledge of her husband,
and Holdane having also slighted her, she destroyed
her life by hanging herself in her bedroom. The de-
ceased had several children. lair:dry adjourned for
Mr. Holdane's attendance. •

By Mr. Humphreys, in the London Hospital, touch-
ing the death of William Stockman. aged 26, a
firework maker, who lately resided at No. 8, Shackle-
well-street, Bethnal-green, and who met his death
from severe burns and injuries received in an explosion
which took place on his premises. A verdict of death
from accidental causes.

By Mr. Payne, at the White Hart, Bishopsgate-
street, on the body of Eliza Keefe, aged 40, the wife
of a blind musician, who came by her death from
being struck and kicked by her husband, while in a
quarrel. Verdict of Manslaughter against John
Keefe, the husband, who was committed to Newgate
for trial.

By Mr. Humphreys, at the Marquis Cornwallis,
Curtain-road, on the body of Mrs. Jane Burr, the wife
of an upholsterer in the Curtain-road, whose death
was occasioned from an accident resulting from the
furious driving of her husband. The jury returned a
verdict of 'Accidental Death.

By Dr. Lankester, at the Pine Apple, Church-street,
Lisson-grove, on the bodies of a boy and girl, twins,
children of a Mr. Faston, who died from the effects of
a dose of syrup of poppies, administered to produce
sleep. The children were one month 014. Verdict,
death from narcotic poison accidentally given,' the
jury severely condemning the practice of giving such
drugs to children.
By Mr. Humphreys, at the Lamb, Dorset-street,
Ratcliff, on the body -cif a female child, found -lying
under one of the arches of the Londen and Blackwell
Railway. Verdict of wilful murder against some per-
son or persons unknown.
By Mr. Bedford, at St. Clement's Vestry-hall,
Strand, on the body of a child, aged fifteen months,
named M'Carthy, who died from diarrhoea, brought on
by the unhealthy nature of the place where the
parents were living, in Robin Hood-court, Piokett
place, Strand.—Verdict accordingly.
By Dr. Lankester, at the Elephant and Castle.
Camden-town, on the body of a newly-born child, the
offspring of Rosa Clifford,.a.honsemaid, Jiving at 2,
Gordon-square, St. Pancras. The mother was in the
custody of the police, who refused to produce her at the
inquest. The coroner therefore adjourned the inquiry,
for the purpose of communicating with the Home
Secretary.

DEATH OF SIR JOHN INGLIB.---WO regret to announce
the death of Sir John Inglis, Colonel of the 32nd Re-
giment, and commander of the troops in the lonian
Islands. Sir John Inglis died on Saturday, the 27th
ult., at Homburg. He was in his 50th year. He was
the defender of Lucknow in its memorable siege during
the late Indian mutiny.

THE GLASGOW MURDER. - Messrs. Dixon and
Strachan, the agents for Mrs. M'Lachlan, left Glasgow
for London on Wednesday night, with the petitions
praying for a respite for the convicted woman. It is
stated that the signatures attached to the petitions
number nearly 100,000. The official investigation was
continued most vigorously on Wednesday by the Pro-
curators• Fiscal, who were engaged all day ' pre-
cognoscing' persona who it is thought may be able to
throw some light on the matter. The milk boys,
Paton, the old clothes man, several of the prison
officials, and others, were examined.

Suicmn .A.Nn llunnEh.—Yesterday morning infor-
mation was circulated in the City .police stations, that,
about nine o'ciock the previous night, a young woman
mounted the parapet of Blackfriars.bridge, with an
infant in her arms, and jumped into the river, and that
both had been carried away by the tide. Yesterday
afternoon a waterman, in passing along the river,
discovered near the piers of Blackfriars-bridge the
body of a female, apparently about 26 years of age,
dressed in a light cotton gown, White petticoat, brown
stockings, and side laced-up boots. isto infant was
however found; but whether the deceased was the
female who threw herself into the river on Wednesday
night is unknown.

FRIGHTFUL ACCIDENT FROld FlRM—Yesterday
morning a fearful case of burning took place at 36,
Great Windmill-street, Haymarket. Mrs. Mary
Green was waiting up to let in her son, who had been
to the theatre, and she had just opened the street door
when the flame of the candle communicated with her
dress, and she was almost instantaneously enveloped
in fire. The son was fearfully burnt endeavouring to
tear off his mother's burning Clothing, and before the
flames were smothered the whole of the upper part of
Mrs. Green's person was completely charred.

Lindsay, a widow, and landlady of the establishment,
who lost her life through her molin dress
by crinoline, catching fire. Verdict, accidentalexpanded
death
from burning.

TRADES' INTELLIGENCE.

THE JOURNEYMEN BAKERS.

TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
Sin,-1 am right glad to see that you have opened
your valuable columns to the "Poor Bakers' Cause."
I have not the slightest doubt but we shall now see a
fair and impartial discussion of -our grievances, which
will edify my brethren of the bakehouse as to their
position in society, and give the public an idea of wlat
we have to go through to supply them with their daily
bread. We do feel it very hard, with all our toils and
lack of comforts that other working men enjoy, that
we should be spoken of as we have been lately, and '
certainly by those that know nothing about us. I ,
allude to some portions of the press that have most
wantonly vilified our calling by the most ignorant
attacks. Ido not Pretend to say that we are all per-
fection, more than any other class, but we are not what
we have been represented. As to some of these scan-
dalous letters that have appeared in the papers, I'will
just take the one that appeared in the Morning Star
from Mr. Charles F. Quintin, of Cheltenham. This
gentleman states that bakers are more filthy than
chimney sweeps, and that the process of breaking
sponge would sicken the most robust constitution, and
talks of the bakers' itch as a common thing.. The
motives;for this gentleman's attack are very transparent.
It appears that he is the inventor of a bread-making
machine which does not appear to have any merit of
its own to recommend it, and the bakers are not quite
so green as to buy a thing that is no use to them, so
he would gull the public that it is impossible to have
clean wholesome bread without it is made by his ma-
chine. This is the English of his letter. We should
be only too glad if we could get any machine that
would lighten our labour. I know several that have
bought machines and tried them well, and cast them
on one side as so much lumber. Would this Ire the
case if they answered their purpose? Whatever
bakers are, they are not so blind as that. As
to their work in the bakehouse, Mr. Quintin can-
not know much, or he could not say they were dirty
there, for the very process of bread-making compels
them to wash frequently during the operation. I have
seen some hundreds of bakehouses in my time, and I
never saw anything like filth in one. True, some of
them are built in the kitchens of old fashioned houses,
therefore are not so well ventilated as we would wish,
but everything is done that can be, in most of them,
to improve it. Those that are built in modern houses
are all that could be desired. I dare say that there
may be a few exceptions to this rule. Yet are there
not exceptions to every rule? Then again, as to the
bakers' itch.' I declare I never even heard or saw
such a thing in my life. This seems to me the most
monstrous of all. Now supposing we hai one of Mr.
'Quintin's machines, and it would' do all he says, how
is the dough to be moulded into loaves, if we are not
to use our. hands? Perhaps that gentleman would
like to contract with bakers to supply them with kid
gloves to work in..
Trusting you will pardon me for dwelling on your
valuable space,
I am, Sir, your obedient servant,
T. S. R.
London, Oct. 2, 1862.

THE EDINBURGH BUILDING OPERATIVES.
(FROM A CORRESPONDENT.)
By some persons Trades' Unions are denounced as
the bane of the working-classes. Their Committees
are considered as so many secret tribunals from which
they launch their decrees, and which an unquestion-
ing body of followers are bound through inexplicable
terror to follow and obey. Others again look on these
Unions as the very sheet anchor of the working classes,
and that the real question at issue is, how they should
be managed? That Trades' Unions have effected
immense good amongst the workmen who have banded
themselves together, cannot be denied by any impar-
tial investigator. We have only to compare the rate
-of wages paid to trades that have unions, and to those
that have none, to be satisfied that combination is
not unmixed evil. The Masons' strike in Edin-
burgh, for example, must be fresh in the recollec-
tion of our readers. In spite of abuse and invec-
tive, the demand of the workmen proved to be so
reasonable that the employers granted it. The
success of the claim was, it must be admitted, in this
ease due to the combination of the men; and their
general determination not to work beyond a certain
number of hours per day, leaving the remuneration
for their labour to be determined by the inexorable
law of supply and demand, had in it so much of
fairness that a protracted strike had, while it lasted,
the approbation of some of the masters themselves,
and in the end was crowned with success. But it
must not be hastily concluded, from the success of
the masons, that no improvement either in wages or
otherwise can be attained in a trade save through
the agency of a strike.
Owing to this reduction in the hours of their labour
there is not a mason idle from necessity either in Edin-
burgh or Leith. The Edinburgh joiners had a struggle
for the nine hours and lost it. But why? Solely be-
cause they were disunited. There was no union
worthy of the name existing amongst them. If they
had the nine hours, there would not be an idle joiner in
Edinburgh at present. It is themselves thatareto blame
for the want of union. The employers will not offer them
the nine hours without asking it; and not then unless
there is a determined effort on part of the operatives to
demand it as a right. The winter is drawing near,
when the time will be reduced to seven and-a-half or
eight hours. If the work can be done in that time in
winter, why ten hours in summer? and the way to
obtain it is to come forward and be united together.
Look at the union that exists in every grade of society.
Look at the advocates, W.S.'s, S.S.C.'s, and the clergy.
No one dare join their union without going through
all the curriculum of whatever branch they are to join,
and a heavy entrance fee to pay to the bargain. The
master builders of Edinburgh have formed themselves
into a union, and to make sure that all was right, em-
ployed an S.S.C. as agent. And what is good for the
lawyers, for the clergy, for the medical profession, for
the employing class generally, cannot be far wrong for
the sons of toil.

THE LONDON ROPEMAKIRS.—The society desires to

Silver Cup Carpenters' Society, £2; Birmingham

No. 164, 3d. In last week's list, the Thorley Rope-

THE DRAWING CAPACITY OF WORICAIEN.—The draw.
mg capacity evinced by students and workmen who
have had no instruction in drawing, is to the full as
curious as the power to carve without the power
of previously drawing an outline of the form to be
afterwards carved. We have known those who with
very considerable skill could outline almost any kind
of animal form in heraldry, but who could not draw
the shield which the said animal was to fill; and a
gem engraver, who could not express on paper the
rudest idea of the shield of arms or crest which he
had before hiin to cut in hard agate; and instances
might be multiplied showing how strangely men are
constituted for the doing of certain work in certain
special materials and ways, and in no other. The
late Mr. J. Thomas could tell of many instances of
the strange and unexpected powers of common work-
men, gathered during his long experience and work
at the Palace of Westminster. May not some of our
short-comings come of our neglect to help to bring out
this power and individuality, and propensity to mere
machinery and drill ?--Building ./STeWS:
MEETING OF OPERATIVES AT SHA.WFORTH, NEAR
ROCHDALE.---011 Tuesday about one thousand operatives
assembled upon a mountainous part of the country,
above Shawforth, called Land End, to deliberate on
what measures should be adopted to meet the deplorable
state of distress now raging in Shawfortb. There are
about two thousand perlons out of employment in con.
:sequence of' four mills having ceased to run, and the
only relief that has been received by these poor people
has been a pittance from the guardians. An operative
named Wm. Southwell, was called to the chair, and in
his opening remarks said he stood before them as a
starving man, and saw no prospect of getting relief.
They were only allowed is. 6d. a week by the guardians
to live upon, and he found it was impossible to keep
body and soul together with such a sum. Au old woman
named Pickles next mounted the cart, and in a melan-
choly voice said—' Sisters and brothers, I thought I
would say a few words, as in reality we are clamming,
and very near starved to death. There's five of us in
a family, and we are only getting Is. 6d. a-head, and
we have to
,bey coal, pay the rent, and pay for our
bagging, and 1 don't think it is right to think a body
can do it. I think those great men for whom we've
worked ought now to try to keep their warkpeople froral
starving, as they'll want us again. As to the gentle-
men in the country giving, they'll weary of giving if
they don't see our masters giving "summat.” Another
old woman named Jane Dearden next addressed the
meeting in the same strain, and was followed by two
operatives, who related some heartrending cases of-dis-
tress. No resolutions were passed.
INFANTICIDE IN ISLINGTON.—OR Monday, Dr. Lan-
kester, the coroner, held an inquest, at the William

the Fourth Tavern, Ball'

articles.title: ! CO-OPERATIVE INTELLIGENCE.
articles.text:
! CO-OPERATIVE INTELLI-
GENCE.

The distress in the manufacturing districts has seri-
ously affected the receipts of the trade and, friendly
societies, but the co-operative societies have suffered
most. The members are unable to meet their monthly
calls, and the general poverty prevents any sale of
shares, and the scrip is at present almost worthless.
The manufacturing and shop-keeping class, who form
the majority of the relief committees, are now taking
advantage of the distress to 'serve out those operatives
who dared to set up as manufacturers and shopkeepers
for themselves.' They affect to consider the owners of
these at present worthless co-operative shares as owners
of property, and not coming under the class of persons
who ought to be relieved. At Bacup, near Manchester,
this principle is strictly acted upon. Working men
are thus being punished for their attempts in more
prosperous times to better their condition. If this is
not holding out a premium to vice and putting virtue
at a par, I don't know what is. In many places relief
is also being refused to those of the operatives who at
any time have made themselves conspicuous in trades
union matters. In Ashton-under-Lyne and other
places, they are actually striking all operatives off the
parliamentary register who receive the temporary relief
from the poor-rates! These petty and paltry proceed-
ings are creating much excitement and indignation
amongst the operatives, and it will not be the fault of
these middle-class relief committees if they do not
destroy that dignified and patient conduct with which
the working classes have borne their present priva-
tions. Woe be to them if this be so. Let the work-
ing classes send their subscriptions, not to swell the
funds of these relief committees who thus abuse them
by punishing members of trades and co-operative com-
mittees, but to such committees composed of working
men as those established at Pad:iham and Chorley, and
for whom subscriptions are received at the office of the
BEEHIVE. SCOURGE.

BRITISFI CO- OPERATIVE IND USTRIAL SOCIETY.—The
quarterly meeting of the above society was held in the
large schooiroom of the Battle-bridge Congregational
Chapel on Thursday evening, Sept. 11th, Mr. J. Tantz
in the chair. The secretary, Mr. J. Ireland, read the
report, which showed that a large increase in the
society's business had taken place during the quarter
amounting in the whole to £2,104 I 9s. sd. The brush
trade has just been added to the society's business.
Its transactions were not confined to retail, but whole-
sale trade was beginning to bA a considerable item in
the returns. A dividend was declared of is. in the
pound on members' purchases, 6d. on non-members
purchases, £5 per cent. on capital. It is pleasing to
state that it was decided that the storekeepers at each
of the five branches should have a weekly half-holiday,
thus showing that the members are not unmindful of
the welfare of those in their employ, by thus giving
their servants an opportunity of rest and recreation.
It was stated in the course of the evening that the so-
ciety is to be enrolled forthwith under the Limited
Liability Act. After a vote of thanks to the chairman
the meeting separated.
THE NORTH.—Another co-operative society has
commenced operations in a small way in the Blyth
district, under the title of The Newsham and New
Delaval Co-operative Provident Society.' The business
of the association will be conducted in one of the mem-
ber's houses until a more suitable place turns up. The
Blyth Society is in a very flourishing condition; the
'stores' at Bedlington and Choppington are also doing
well, eonsidering the great depression which has cha-
racterised the coal trade. The members of the West
Cramlington Stores are about to enlarge their pre-
mises, the present place being found to be too small.
As far as it has gone, co-.operation in the North has
been most successful.

articles.title: GLASGOW MURDER.
articles.text:
THE GLASGOW MURDER.

A great meeting was held in the City Hall, Glas-
gow, on Monday evening, to petition the Home Secre-
tary for a respite of Jessie M'Lachlan. An hour before
the time announced for the commencement of the
business, the hall was crowded in every part, and
hundreds had to go away unable to gain admittance.
Councillor Clark was called to the chair, and told the
meeting it was intended to forward the petition which
might be adopted by train that night to London, in
order that it might be presented to Sir G. Grey. The
following memorial to Sir G. Grey was unanimously
adopted
'That in in the case of Jessie M'lutosh or M'Lachlan,
who is at present confined in the prison of Glasgow
under sentence of death, your memorialists respectfully
submit,
'lst. That the evidence adduced at the trial was en-
tirely circumstantial, and was not such as to clear up
many doubtful and obscure points that deeply affect the
solution of this important case.
2nd. That an extraordinary and exceptional cha-
racter had been given to the case by a declaration read
by the prisoner's counsel after the verdict was returned,
which declaration purports to be a true statement of
the prisoner's connection with the crime, and is
affirmed to have been made by her to her agents on.
the 13th day of August last, before she had any infor-
mation as to the evidence to be adduced against her,—
which declaration was not made use of in the prisoner's
defence. Ilk
3rd. That from the circumstances in which the de-
claration was made the nature of the declaration
itself, and the painful excitement created on the sub-
ject, it appears to you memorialists to be imperatively
necessary for the interests of justice and the satisfac-
tion cf the public mind, that there be a special inves-
tigation into the whole matter.
4th. That, in tho meantime, a respite of the sen-
tence be granted, and upon the above inquiry being
made, that the Crown be graciously pleased to inter-
pose further in the case, as the ends of justice may
appear to demand.
'And your memoralists, as in duty bound, shall
ever pray.'
The North British Daily Mail says :—' The Crown
officials in Edinburgh, having taken into considera-
tion what has transpired since the return of the
verdict in the case of Mrs. M'Lachlan, have issued a
warrant to the Sheriff here, directing that a strict offi-
cial investigation be made into all the circumstances
which have since come to light. This warrant has
just been received, and already the Slaerift's officials
are bestirring themselves to give it due effect.' The
truth of this statement, which was published in a late
edition on Monday was disputed, and the Mail there-
fore gives the following particulars
On Tuesday the Lord Advocate arrived in Glasgow a
little before mid-day, and had a consultation with the
Sheriff's officials, including the Procurators-Fiscal,
Messrs. Hart and Gemmel. The upshot of this con-
sultation was, that a warrant or order was given for a
private official precognition to be made by the Sheriff
and his Fiscal, of all who can throw any light on the
case' and who were not examined as witnesses at the
late trial. Accordingly, on Tuesday afternoon sum-
monses were issued to about a dozen witnesses, in-
cluding ilary Black, Miss Dykes, the three young
women (the Misses Brown), Mr. Stewart, Sandyford-
place, and others, calling upon them to appear this
morning, before the Sheriff, at the county buildings.
The following are the terms of the summons
Room No. To —. You are hereby summoned
to compear before the Sheriff of Lanarkshire, within
the Procurator- Fiscals' office, County-buildings,
Brunswick-street, Ulasgow, one stair up, on Tuesday,
the 30th day of September current, at nine o'clock fore-
noon, to be examined as a witness in the case of Jessie
Ill'lntosh or M'Lachlan, and that under the penalty of
one hundred merks Scots.'

It may not be out of place here to correct a popular
error. According to the constitution of this country,
no person who has been examined as a Crown witness
can be afterwards charged with the crime regarding
which he has given evidence. At the same time, if it
be found that a person has given testimony incon•
sistent with truth on the trial, he may be indicted for
perjury.
The condemned criminal continues much in her
former state of mind. Some imprudent person, how-
ever, we understand, has informed her of the efforts
being made to get for her a respite, and it seems she is
sanguine of their success. Her husband brought her
child into the prison on Saturday, when it may well
be imagined a most harrowing scene took place.
The Calsdonian 11Lercury says It is currently
and believed to be true, that
rLuomrdou Dreedas ihnasthree city, and
a missive from Sir Sir George
Grey, requesting his attendance in London in reference
to the Glasgow murder trial, and that his lordship has
left to consult with the Home Secretary.'

articles.title: CORRESPONDENCE.
articles.text:
CORRESPONDENCE.

WORKING MEN AND THE FRANCHISE.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEE HIVE.

SlR,—May I venture to suggest to your correspon-
dent, One of the Hive,' that all the inhabitants of
the hive are not producers; there are drones in the
hive as well as out of it, and it strikes me, Sir, under due
correction, that judging from his language, and form-
ing an opinion of the spirit which animated your cot-
respondent, he is no working man, nor a friend to the
working man. One of the Hive indeed ' What hive?
The producers?
I suppose your correspondent must admit, that the
working bees in the great hive of our country receive
but a very small part of the honey produced by their
labours. He must know this, I presume; yet is he an
advocate for the continuance of the present system, by
which the working bees starve and the drones live in
splendour, at the expense of those who toil. The
premises granted, the conclusion is evident, that One
of the Hive' is a drone and not a working bee.
Yes, I repeat after him, we are ignorant and un-
worthy and as unfit to enjoy the privileges of that
Charter as the negroes of America are unfitted for im-
mediate emancipation.'
I should like to ask this gentleman Of the Hive,'
why the negroes of America are unfit for immediate
emancipation? It appears from his statement, that he
was in the United States for nine years; then he must
have seen hundreds, if not thousands, of negroes who
were free. I know somewhat of America; I ask

him whether the far greater part of these negroes were
not among the most valuable members of the States?
Will he answer this question in the negative? Will
he say that there are not thousands of white men, par-
ticularly in the large cities, whose characters are
greatly inferior to those of the coloured people? What
has his knowledge of America taught him on this
subject? 'We are ignorant and unworthy,' says your
correspondent. True, I believe the character is fairly
drawn 80 far as the writer is concerned • for, taking this
letter as a specimen of his abilities and disposition, it
does contain as much ignorance as could well be com-
prised in so small a compass. LA me endeavour to
prove this assertion.
The writer is a logician. He should like a defi-
nition of the term manhood suffrage. There is no diffi-
culty in describing the words manhood suffrage. They
mean that every man above twenty-one years of age,
who has resided in a certain place, for a certain time,
should vote for a member of Parliament. The writer
talks 'of the privileges of that Charter.' I should like
to read his definition of the word privilege. To vote
for a member of Parliament is a right, not a privilege;
it is not a something conferred by one man on another,
but a right inherent in every -male member of a com-
munity above 'a certain age who performs the duties
devolving on the members of that community.
If this writer had read any of our jurists, and if he
had noticed the principles enunciated by them, he
would better have understood the difference between a
right and a privilege. Blackstone, who copies from
Fortescue, who was Chancellor in the reign of Henry
VI., makes use of this language, 'Those rights which
God and nature have established, and which are there-
fore called natural rights, such as life and liberty,
need not the aid of human laws to be more effectually
vested in every man than they are, neither do they
receive any additional strength when declared by the
municipal law to be inviolable; on the contrary, no
human legislation has power to abridge or destroy
them, unless the owner himself has committed an act
that amounts to a forfeiture.'

The principal aim of society,' says Blackstone, 'is
to protect individuals in the enjoyment of those abso-
lute rights which were vested in them by the immu-
table laws of nature, bat which could not be preserved
in peace without that mutual assistance and intercourse
which is gained by the institution of friendly and
social communities. Hence it appears that the first
and primary end of human limit is to maintain and
regulate those absolute rights of individuals.'
Again, Blackstone says, and let me call the atten-
tion of your correspondent to this point, 'The law-
fulness of punishing criminals is founded on this prin-
ciple —that the law by which they suffer was made by
their own consent.' One more quotation: The
earliest writs of Edward Ist show that all the people
had a constitutional right to the elective franchise.'
"What answer will One of the Hive' give to these
quotations? They show clearly, too, that the power
of voting for a member of Parliament is not a privi-
lege conferred by one man on another, but a right
which belongs to men as members of a community,
and to deprive men of these rights is an usurpation, is
an abuse of the power of the law giver. Your corre-
spondent must admit or deny this ; which,side will he
take?

In reading over attentively this letter, I perceive
that there are contained in it so many important
topics, many of which ought to be understood by the
working men who read your paper, that it will be im-
possible for me in this letter to do justice to them. It
is my intention to address a series of letters to the in-
dustrious classes, which letters shall embrace the
following subjects. ,
First. The character given to the working men by
Ona of the Hive,' and the assigned cause of the
failure of the Chartist movement.

Second. The objections made by 'One of the Hive'
to the principles of the Charter (with one exception),
and the consequences which, in his opinion, would
have followed had the Charter become the law of the
land.

Third. The observations in the last paragraph of his

letter, in which he accuses those persons of ignorance
of their country and its history who contend that the
bill of '32 was of no benefit to the country.
The writer .say, While we ask a just and equit-
able reform, let us at the same time remember that a
false step may prove our ruin, and the Constitution of
our country, which is the result of centuries of labour
and deliberate consideration, may crumble in the dust
by the base passions of an hour, and thus the glorious
fabric which has ever been an asylum for suffering
humanity, and the only hope for the weak and perse-
cuted, may be numbered in one day with the things
that have been.'

From this peroration I perceive that One of the
Hive' is a rhetorician as well as a logician. Figures
of speech are very beautiful when properly used; but,
as a celebrated grammarian told his readers, they are
edged tools, and two-edged tools, too.
I have no wish Mr. Editor, to go beyond the fair

latitude allowed in controversy ; but really my ire is
raised when I read such falsehoods and misrepresenta-
tions of a class who, take them as a whole, contain mere
public spirit than any other of the classes into which
our country is divided.
Yours, &e.,
September 22, 1862.

BRISTOLTAN.

EMIGRATION.
TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.

Sm,—Your paper deserves the support of all work-
ing men, and may be the means of greatly improving
their position. I send you the rough outline of a plan
that I think if carried out will be the means of doing
a great deal of good.
There is a wide field for the employment of skilled
labour in our colonial possessions, and there are too
many out of employment in this country. Then how
to bring them together? This is my plan. You write
an article in your paper, stating that you are willing
to receive applications from
_employers in the colonies
in want of workmen, stating the wages thoy will give,
the amount they will give or advance towards paying
for the outfit and the passage, and the time they will
guarantee to find employment for the man. When
you receive'an application you will write to the trades
union of the trade that you require, and I am quite
sure they will find the man and the funds to send him
out; it being evidently ;for the advantage of all that
those willing to emigrate should be assisted to go. By
giving this plan your attention you will increase the
claims you already have on the working classes, and
oblige yours,
S. AL, A SUBSCRIBER FROM THE COMMENCEMENT.

GARIBALDI AND LOUIS NAPOLEON.
1
:TO THE EDITOR OF THE BEEHIVE.
No doubt we are more civilised than our ancestors, ],
and than the mass of mankind at the present day. But
I hope and trust, that our posterity five centuries hence
will look on tis as semi-barbarians.'—WHATELY.
SIR—I took the liberty of addressing you a few
weeks since on this question, and now hasten to re-
deem the promise I made of supplying another paper.
I have taken a lively interest in this subject, and was
present at the meeting called in Hyde Park for the
purpose of sympathising with Garibaldi, and to pro-
test against the French occupation of Rome.- I was
also a witness to the disgraceful scenes enacted in the
Park.
An object of vast importance to all those who love
Civil and Religious Liberty was included in the pro-
gramme—namely, the right of France to occupy Rome
with her army.
The Imperial master of France and Italy, Louis
Napoleon, is looking on with bated breath at every
movement England is making,—at every demonstra-
tion she is giving to the wounded patriot. It irritates
his temper; but let him not lay the flattering unction
to his soul that England's sons of toil will ever cease
to do honour to him who is greater than a Napoleon.
He was terrified at the spirit evinced at the Newcastle
meeting, and well he might he • it makes him uneAsy,
that he should be thus cpoken a in a country ho talted
of visiting this summer!
England is grateful to GarijAidi fOr what hq bps
done for Italy, and is an),Oeusly anticipating what he
may yet 40 !,..°! ioiq ;not by his ogyni himg, by thou

who shall raise his standard and echo his name, which
falls as sweet music on the ears of tens of thousands to
cheer them on in the determination, 'Rome or death!'
to the terrible dismay of Napoleon, who
'Swept through slaughter to a throne,
And shut the gates of mercy on mankind.'
The solution of the Roman question must be soon
settled; an onerous task and duty lays before our
statesmen, but I believe the present Ministry is com-
petent, if willing, to grapple with the question, and
bring it to a safe termination. • Italy, to be free, must
have Rome for its capital—no other. Italy cannot, nor
should long exist without it. It was supposed (but in
which I had no faith) that it was but a matter of time,
and France would withdraw from Rome. But now
Garibaldi is a prisoner, has she done so? and what
pretence has she for remaining there new? Napoleon
must still have his iron grasp on Rome, that he may
the more easily carry out his ambitious designs, and
use Victor Emmanuel as best suits his purposes.
But the question now is 'Does the Emperor Napo-
leon intend to evacuate Rome?' Hear his own words
through his minister, M. Thc,uvenel. He says, The
words of the Emperor have never held out a hope to
the cabinet of Turin that. Rome could become the capi-
tal of the kingdom of Italy with the consent of
France;' and further on he adds, 'ltaly would have to
renounce her pretensions to Rome, &c.' This is lan-
guage not easily misunderstood. We have here the
word ' never'—a word unknown to Englishmen—they
take as their motto, 'We'll try? We have struggled
long, and suffered much, to obtain our social and politi-
cal rights, but we were told we never should obtain
them but we did; we were told the Factory Bill
should never pass, but it did; and last, not Last, we
are told that the short time movement will never suc-
ceed, but it will.
Let the Emperor Napoleon understand that English-
men' when thoroughly aroused to a sense of danger
are determined, and this feeling, combined with
earnestness on the part of the English Government,
will make Rome the capital of Italy.' Lord Pal-
merston has already hinted the desirability of Rome
being no longer under French domination. Let then
oar government speak plainly, unmistakeably, but
firmly, on this question, and the Napoleon's chaff
shall fly before the breath of ussell, and then, and
not till then, Italy will be free.
Victor Emmanuel is the most unenviable of human
beings. He has, by his actions, made monarchy more
detestable, and has caused the heart of his bravest
general to bleed. Well may Garibaldi exclaim with
the poet--:_ . . .

Mail'S inhumanity to man
Makes countless thousands mourn.'

I hope the-d-a-Jalii-C-O-mmittee will decide on hold-
ing another open-air demonstration in Hyde Park. I
was present at the last, and pitied rather than blamed
the misguided creatures who created the disturbance.
The conduct of the committee was beyond all praise.
I have had the pleasure of working, socially and poli-
tically, with many of the countrymen of the disturbers,
who are greatly pained at their disgraceful conduct,
and will use every endeavour that free speetth shall
have its legitimate action. The park is large; let the
Pope's partisans raise a standard of their own, and
they will not be disturbed; but I advise them not to
interfere again with others.—l remain sir, yours, &c.,
W. PETHERBRIDGE.
Caledonian-road, Oct. 1, 1862.

articles.title: HYDE PARK RIOTERS.
articles.text:
THE HYDE PARK RIOTERS.

At Marlborough-street Police Court, on Monday,
Timothy M'Carthy, a labourer, was charged before
Mr. Tyrwhitt with creating a disturbance in Hyde •
park on Sunday; John Deely, a labourer, was charged
with throwing stones to the common danger of pas-
sengers in the same place; Cornelius Casey, Timothy
Toomey, and Michael Collins were also charged with
creating a disturbance in Hyde-park, and Toomey was
further charged with assaulting Edward Moyses, a
cabinet-mater, of Great Wild-street.
Mr. Edward Lewis, of Great Marlborough-street,
appeared for Collins and Toomey. The other prisoners
were undefended.
Aberdein 515 A, said: I was on duty in Hyde-park
yesterday between three and four, and I saw a large
crowd collected near the magazine barracks. Two or
three gentlemen got on the mound of earth, and began
speaking, saying they had come to sympathize with
Garibaldi. As soon as they began to speak Collins
said, Down with Garibaldi! Hurrah for the Pope.'
He then rushed down from the mound, putting his
closed fists to his head and pushed and struck everyone
before him. Some gentlemen cried out, That is the
man who meant to stab the speaker.' I did not hear
the prisoner make any remark in reply. When I got
him to the station I found £2l in money on him, but
no knife.
By Mr. Lewis: It was while I was dragging Collins
along that the remark was made about the knife. The
Garibaldi party had possession of the mound first, and
then the Irishmen took possession and kept it, never
being all driven down. Collins pushed every one be-
fore him. I was at the bottom of the mound. There
were some thousands present. The Garibaldi party
tried to regain the mound, and the prisoner's party
pushed them down.
Fair, 97 X, said: There was a large crowd, and there
was a discussion about Catholicism and Garibaldi.
The crowd were pushing one another about. I saw
M'Carthy strike a person who was for Garibaldi a blow
on the breast. This he continued to do, with other
persons, for some minutes. M'Carthy then threw up
his hat, and said he would fight any in the park,
being at the time in a state of great excitement, and
calling out to his fellow countrymen, Let's give it to
the —.' I took him, with the assistance of three
other constables, to the station; but had the greatest
difficulty in doing so owing to his resistance. He was
quite sober at the time.
Another constable said: I was on duty near the Ser-
pentine, and saw a large crowd assembled. The people
were pushing one another about. I saw M'Carthy
knocking people about. I assisted in taking two of the
prisoners. M'Carthy tried his utmost to get away, and
offered great resistance.
Edward Moyses, a cabinet-maker, of Great Wild-
street, said: I was in Hyde Park yesterday afternoon
about half-past three. A meeting had been called, and
there was a large assemblage and great confusion. I
saw Toomey and Collins there with their hats off. Col-
lins called out, 'Down with Garibaldi! hurrah for the
Pope.' Toomey then kicked out violently—leaning his
hands on the shoulders of another man, and kicked me
severely on the ribs. He (Toomey) said at the time he
did it, take that for the Pope.' Shortly after the
police came up and apprehended Collins. Toomey then
ran after the police and Collins, and said, 'Down with
the police ! I was then about to give Toomey
in charge, when he came up to me and knocked me
down with a blow in the eye.
By Mr. Lewis: Toomey was on the mound, partly
up, and I was on the ground in front of him. I don't
know whether he had a little boy with him. I had not
called out Down with the Pope I had not spoken a
word, and had only been there a minute or two.
Charles Covington, Park Constable 28, said: I saw
Toomey strike the last witness and several other per-
sons also. I made my way, through the crowd as well
as I could, but was knocked down twice myself by
some persons. I assisted in taking Toomey.
By Mr. Lewis: Toomey fought at every one right
and left. I saw no one strike at Toomey.
Frederick Vile, another park constable said: Yester-
day I saw Deely on the mound in Hyde-park. I saw
two gentlemen with their beads cut open by some
stones having been-thrown. I then saw Deely with a
stone in his hand. He then threw the stone amongst
the crowd, and I then took him into custody and to
the police-station.
Davis, 576 A, said: In Hyde-park yesterday after-
noon I saw Toomey striking at everyone he came near.
I saw him strike Moyses in the face.
Sedgwick, 546 A, said: Yesterday afternoon I saw
Casey striking right and left and knock four persons
down with his fist. I went up to take him into custody,
and I was knocked over by one of his party, but got
the prisoner, and, with the assistance of others, took
him to the station. A large mob while taking the
prisoner to the station pressed on him, but the prisoner
did not resist.
Mr. Lewis said it was to be regretted that the law
was not strong enough to repress these open air party
meetings, for where there were large assemblages fac-
tions were sure to meet and disturbmces take place.
There was a general fight between both parties—those
for Garibaldi and those for the Pope—but the police
had not by their own showing been assauited. If per-
sons wished to express their opinions let them meet in
a proper place and do so, but he (Mr. Lewia) must
again say that it was to be regretted that such meetings
were permitted, and that on no part of the Continent
would they be suffered.
Mr. Tyrwhitt said it was to be regretted that the
Park, which was intended for the recreation of persons,
should be made use of for such a purpose, but the public
peace must be kept at all hazards. The cases of th,e
prisoners were different. He (Mr. Tyrwhitt) regretted
these meetings, but no OXIQ 001ild say that the u,tmoat
liberty was not given. It was impossible to. ace that
Toomey had not viclently kicked the witness Moyses.
He should fine Toomy £5, or two months ; Casey, 405.,
or two inoritl;ls ; Deely, 40s„ or month, for throwin
stones; M'Carthy, or fqvirtm days; and Conj.%
205., or fouTtee4 days,

articles.title: TIIE MYSTERIOUS _DEATE OF A G.ENTLEMAY.
articles.text:
TIIE MYSTERIOUS _DEATE OF A
G.ENTLEMAY.

NEW USE FOR PHOTOGRAPHY.

On Wednesday morning Mr. H. Raffles Walthew
resumed at the Black Horse Tavern, Kingsland-road,
the inqury into the death of a person unknown, who
dropped dead on Wednesday last under very singular
circumstances. It will be remembered that the
deceased, a well-dressed respectable-looking person,
was seen in East-road, New North-road, talking to a
female, and that he said to a police constable that the
woman had robbed him of a sovereign, a half-crown,
and a railway ticket. Whilein the-act of speaking he
fell dead, and the woman ran away. The woman was
subsequently arrested, but nothing was found on her.
Deceased's purse was empty, and nothing was found
on him to indicate where he came from, but the name
Stourbridge ' in his hat and a Crystal Palace Guide-
book in his pocket. Photographs of the deceased were
taken by a juryman, Mr. Pearce, and sent to Stour-
bridge with a view to his identification.
At the resumption of the inquiry,
Harriett Roberts, residing at Rye, near Stourbridge,
said that having read the account of the deceased in
the newspapers, she saw the photographs sent down to
Stourbridge, and recognised it as a portrait of her
brother, Charles Roberts. He had left Rye a week
previously to go to the Great Exhibition, and was to
have returned on the day he so unaccountably died.
He was a healthy man, forty-seven years of age.
The coroner said that the result of Mr. Pearce's ex-
ertions were very satisfactory, but he thought that the
police ought to have circulated an account of the cir-
cumstances in the country as well as over the me-
tropolis. He had received letters from parties in the
country suggesting that in such cases photographs
should always be taken and circulated, so that the
relatives might have it in their power to identify
deceased friends.

Inspector Webster said that he had reported the
fact of deceased's death within five hours of its occur-
rence to the commissioners. The matter was then out
of his hands. and ho could not circulate the information
in the country. He would, however, report to Scot-
land-yard the desire of the Coroner and jury with
regard to such cases.
The jury then returned a verdict in the case of the
immediate object of inquiry, that deceased died in the
street from apoplexy.

THE ALLEGED XANSLAUGITTER Dl
CLERICAN WELL.

On Monday evening' Dr. Lank-ester resumed the
inquiry at the Royal Free Hospital respecting the
death of George Smith, a carpenter, aged 24, who was
alleged to be killed in a quarrel originating in a concert.
hall in John-street, Clerkenwell. Mr. F. Lewis, of
Ely-place, appeared on behalf of Hobert Hanks a
carman in the employ of Mr. Jay, who is in custody
on a charge of manslaughter, and Mr. Wakeling ap-
peared for the relatives of the deceased. Mr. J.
Pitney, 31; Clerkenwell-green, said that on Saturday
night week he heard a disturbance, and upon
looking out he saw seven persons. Two of
them took off their coats to fight, and after
sparring and striking at each other the deceased
ran down the hill, the other pursuing him. De-
ceased slipped and fell, when a female came
to the other man and induced him to go away. De-
ceased then got up, and was putting on his coat, when
a short.man came up to him and said, You coward!
you say you can fight, and you ran away. I can fight
such a• fellow as you myself.' Deceased said something
which witness could not hear, and the short man struck
him a tremendous blow on the side of the head. De
ceased fell fiat at once, and the short man ran away.
As he was going past the group which he had left before
he went up to strike deceased, a female said, 'Oh,
what a shame to serve the man like that! How
would you like it yourself?' Witness believed the
blow killed the deceased. Mrs. Elizabeth Nash, 33, Cler-
kenwell-green, also described the manner in which the
deceased was struck by a short man, who then ran
away. George Whitehead, a glass-cutter, said that on
the night in question he was at the concert-hall of the
Red Lion and Punch Bowl in St. John-street, Clerk-
enwell, and there he saw deceased, Robert Hanks, two
other young men, and two young women. On their
way home witness remonstrated with the deceased for
being quarrelsome, upon which he took off his coat
and told witness to take it out of him; Some sparr-
ing ensued, but no blows were struck. John Hahn,
35, Clerkenwell-green, gave the same account as
the previous witness of deceased being struck down
with fearful force by a man whom he believed
to be Robert Hanks. Deceased's head struck the
pavement with a noise as if a gun were let off.
Elizabeth Chantrey, crinoline .maker, said that she left
the concert-hall with her brother and deceased and
others, at twelve o'clock on the night in question.
Deceased was drunk. Witness did not see Hanks strike
' him. By Mr. Wakeling : Witness knew Hanks two
or three years, and had been with him to various
places. She had been in deceased's company that
night for an hour or two before Hanks came to the
concert. Mr. Brooks, builder, said he paid deceased
his wages on the evening in question. He was then
perfectly sober. He was a steady man. It was shown
that deceased's money was missing, as was also his
waistcoat, when he was taken lifeless to the hospital.
The coroner then summed up, and the jury returned a
verdict of manslaughter against Robert Hanks. The
coroner then made out his warrant for the committal
of Hanks for trial at the ensuing sessions of the
Central Criminal Court.

articles.text:
EXTRAO.RDIA T eIRY SUICID_E OF A
Y 0 VIRi- LADE

An inquiry was held on Tuesday at the George and
Vulture Tavern, Pitfield-street, New North-road, by
Mr. H. Raffles Walthew, respecting the death of Miss
Mary Martin, aged 21, who committed suicide in a
most determined manner on Saturday, under very
melancholy circumstances. Mrs. M. Martin, 20,
Ascot-place, said the deceased was her daughter, and
resided with her uncle at 9, Haberdasher's-place,
where she had euarge of his house, his mother being
an invalid. In consequence of this last fact she was
without company, and complained much of the dulness
of the place. Witness, however, had not anticipated
that deceased would have committed suicide. She had
every comfort that she could wish for.
Miss Ann Cole said that being requested by deceased's
grandmother, on Saturday morning last, to look for
deceased, who was missing, she did so, and found her
hanging by a rope to the rail of her uncle's bedstead.
Her throat was cut, and the blood was issuing from
the wound. A bloody razor lay on the mantel-shelf.
-Witness's mother entered the room, and with the ,
razor cut down deceased, who was still warm, but was
quite dead. She had evidently endeavoured to destroy
her life first with the razor, but failing to inflict a
mortal cut, she made a slip-knot on a rope, and
accomplished her purpose by hanging. Deceased was
debarred from society owing to her relative's illness,
and had frequently lamented her position to witness,
and said, It is not strange I should never have a
young man.'
The jury returned a verdict of 'Suicide while of
unsound mind.'

FEARFUL ACCIDENT AT STAMFORD-BRIDGE.—On
Wednesday evening, about half-past eight o'clock, a
very serious accident occurred to Mr. Macdonald, jun.,
son of the station-master at that place, who fell from
the viaduct crossing the Derwent river and valley,
near the above-named place. When we state that his
fall was to a depth of 40 feet, among the debris of the
protecting wall, our readers will judge of the nature
of the accident. The parapet wall gave may eighteen
months ago, and for some reason had not been renewed.
The unfortunate young man had occasion to speak
with the driver of a luggage train, to inquire whether
annother engine should be telegraphed for, as part of
the carriages had to be left, the engine not having
power to take the whole train from Stamford-bridge to
York. The night was dark, and the conversation
having been continued until after the engine was in
motion on Mr. Macdonald alighting from it he fell
over the unprotected bridge and received very severe
internal injuries. He was removed the same evening
to the York County Hospital and on inquiry
1 we learned that he was in a very feeble state, but hopes
I are entertained of his ultimate recovery.— Po-kslare

articles.title: ALLEGED FATAL MISTAKE AT THE _ROYAL GENERAL DISP_ENSAR Y.
articles.text:
ALLEGED FATAL MISTAKE AT THE
_ROYAL GENERAL DISP_ENSAR Y.

Dr. Lankester, held an inquest at the Prince of
Wales Tavern, Sudely-street, City-road, on Monday,
on the body of a child, the daughter of a solicitor's
clerk, named Frances Selina Winter, residing at 12,
Graham-street, City Gardens, whose death was sup-
posed to have been occasioned or accelerated by the
mistake of an official at the 'Royal General Dispensary,
Bartholomew-close, in not giving proper directions-for
the administration of medicine prescribed. According
to the evidence of the mother of deceased and other
witnesses it appeared that the child was rather un-
healty and scrofulous, and that on Monday last it did.
not seem as well as usual. In consequence on Tues-
day she went to the Dispensary with a letter containing.
a prescription for the child, given to her by a doctor of
the institution some three months before, and no doctor
-
being there to see the deceased one of two- young men
in attendance made up the prescription which Mrs.
Winter produced; and as no verbal instructions were-
given her she went away with the impression that the
medicines, which consisted of a phial containing a
cough mixture and another phial containing a mixture
of steel wine, were properly labelled. The instruc-
tions on the labels were, that a tablespoonful of the
cough mixture, and a half tablespoonful of the steel
wine mixture, were the quantities to be administered as
doses. On Wednesday afternoon, after four doses of
the former and three doses of.the latter had been given,
the deceased fell into a kind of stupor, such as would
be supposed to be caused by an over dose of laudanum,
and died the same afternoon. Mr. Winter then went
to the dispensary, and was told that the doses should
have been a teaspoonful of one, and a teaspoonful of
the other, instead of a tablespoonful and half ditto.
Subsequently he requested that the officer who served
the medicine should attend the inquest to explain
his conduct in the matter, and was told he was
not there. Doctor Morris, who attended the de-
ceased, deposed that, being unable to account for the
death, he performed a post Riortem- examination of
the body, and ascertained that it was produced from
congestion of the brain from a convulsive fit, in all
probability from natural causes. He was inclined to
the opinion that the overdose of the medicines referred
to did not accelerate death, as they seemed to be of too
harmless a nature. The coroner said, on examining
the labels of the phials, that in one case an instruction
of I-, written very small and carelessly in pencil, could.
be discerned, which probably meant (as it appeared to
have been stated at the Dispensary) that a teaspoon-
ful, and not a tablespoonful, should be administered.
He agreed with the medical testimony that the mis-
take had nothing to do with the cause of death, but
he could not refrain from remarking that it appeared
to be a most careless proceeding, and should be pub-
_ _

holy noticed to avoid serious -Consequences for the
future. The jury deliberated, and finally returned a
verdict of death from natural causes, with an addition
that the coroner should write to the authorities of the
Royal General Dispensary representing the unanimous
feeling of the jurors that sufficient care had not
been taken in labelling the medicine sent to the de-
ceased plitid.

articles.title: IifiEROUS ASSAULT BY AN • OFFICER.
articles.text:
IifiEROUS ASSAULT BY AN
• OFFICER.

On Tuesday Lieutenant William M'ltae, a lieu-
tenant in the 46th Regiment of Foot, was brought be-
fore Mr. Woolrych, at the Thames Police-court,
charged with attempting to murder George Pavey,
cook and steward of the *hip Northumberland, now
lying in the St. Katharine's Dock. The prosecutor,
who exhibited a scar on his forehead and a bruised
hand, is still suffering from the dreadful attack made
upon him by the prisoner.
The prosecutor stated that the prisoner was a paa-
senger in the ship Northumberland, from Madras. On
Friday, the 19th ult., at half-past nine in the momng,
the prisoner followed him from the cabin to the galley or
cook-house on deck, and as he was leaving the galley
the prisoner struck at him with great force with a.
heavy iron instrument called a maul. He broke the
force of the blow with his hand, which he raised, and.
closed on the prisoner, who let fall the hammer. They
fell on the deck, and the prisoner was on the top of
him. He called for assistance, and the prisoner was
seized and secured. The captain and mate dressed the
wound on his head and bound up his hand. The
blood spirted from his head all over the deck.
Mr. Woolrych : What led to this strange and mur-
derous attack upon you ?—Witness: On the same
morning, when the breakfast was ready, I called out
to Lieut. M‘Rae in his cabin, Breakfast ready, sir.'
He said, All right,' but did not come to breakfast.
called out again, and he said, don't want any.' I
cleared away the breakfast things. I took some down
into the chief cabin, and he followed me down and
said, 'You must do something for me, I shall cut my-
self in the side.' I said, I can do nothing for you.'
He kept following me about the ship, and I could not
get on with my work. I went on the poop and made
a complaint to the captain, and said, 'He is following
me about the decks.' Then the lieutenant came down,
and the captain said Mr. M‘Rae, you are very wrong
in interfering with the steward;' and he then delibe-
rately followed me to the galley, and aimed a tremen-
dous blow at me with the maul. - -

Mr. Woolrych : Did you observe anything singular
in his conduct before this? - _

Before this question was answered, Rowcroft, the
constable, produced several daggers, scimitars, and
other weapons of offence and defence, belonging to the
prisoner and taken from his cabin. He also put in the
ship's log-book, in which there were entries of strange
and violent conduct on the part of Lieutenant 11‘11ae.
Rowcroft, in answer to a question by the magistrate,
said the Northumberland only arrived yesterday.
There was no one present from the ship.
Mr. Woolrych repeated the question he had before
asked, and added, 'Had Lieut. M‘Rae been drinking?'
Pavey : He had not tasted strong drinks for a
month before.

---- • ----- •
Mr. Woolrych : "Was he considered eccentric on
board? _ _

Witness: No, Sir. We sailed from Madras. The
prisoner was then in a weakly condition, and in bad
health. He wanted me to receive money, and com-
plained that I had talked about him. He made out
two papers, or cheques, on a bank for £5OO sterling,
not to bring an action against him for defamation of
character. I did not have the papers. I was never
offensive or insolent towards him.
Mr. Woolrych remanded the prisoner for the attend-
ance of the captain and chief mate.

articles.title: ALLEGED MURDER OF A .310THER
articles.text:
ALLEGED MURDER OF A .310THER

NE-4R 11A LIFA X.

On Friday forenoon a man, named William Halle-
well, a weaver and farmer, of Soyland, near Halifax,
was apprehended on a charge of murdering his aged
mother, with whom he lived. The prisoner is forty-
one years of age, and unmarried. The deceased, his
mother, is about sixty-six years, the widow of John
Hallowell, farmer. The deceased was found dead at
the bottom of a precipice, near!her farm-house, on Fri-
day morning. It is suspected that she was thrown
into the excavation by the prisoner, who it is well-
known has frequently treated her with violence.
During the last few weeks he has been very un-
kind to her, and quarrels have been of frequent
occurrence between them. She accused him of
neglecting to assist her in maintaining the
farm, of getting money from her and not
paying her back, and of keeping company with
a young woman of whom she disapproved. There
were two sons living with the mother—William the
prisoner, and David. The latter left the house on
Thursday night, at half-past ten o'clock. The mother
was then in bed and the prisoner had gone upstairs.
The fire was out. There had been a quarrel, and.
David was afraid to remain in the house. He left and,
rambled about on the hill tops and in the valleys of the.
vicinity until tho morning. At six o'clock he went
back to the house, and was surprised to find no one in.
There was apan on the fire containing some hot water,
and the fire had burnt out. The prisoner was soon
after seen in the farmyard, but he denied all know-
ledge of his mother, and appeared very moody. The
body of the poor woman was found abaut two hours
after by some stone delvers. There were several deep
cuts on her head and a bruise on her arm.. The cuts
appear as though they might have been made by fall-
ing over the cliff, which is about thirty-four feet high,
but the injury on the arm seems to have been caused
by a blow. In the course of the forenoon the son
William was apprehended on suspicion of murd,ering,.
his mother, and taken to Halifax.

TEE HYST_ERIOUS DEATH IN XIIE
CITY.

On the 29th Mr. Payne resumed: the adjourned in-
(lnky at the Saracen's Head Tavern, Northumberland-
alley, Fenchurch-street, as .to the circumstances con-
nected with the murder of Elizabeth Gardiner, on the
morning of the 15th inst.
It will be remembered that at the close of the pro-
ceedings on Wednesday last, the coroner ordered the
husband Gardiner, and the woman Humbler, to be taken
into custody, since which time they were taken before
the Lord Mayor, at the Mansion-house, but merely a
repetition of the evidence taken by the coroner was
_given, and they were remanded to await the result of
the coroner's inquiry.
George Gouldburn, 25, Cold Harbour-street, Hack-
ney-road, lamplighter, said.: I have known Samuel Gar-
diner for some years. I recollect last Monday week,
when this happened. I saw Gardiner that morning at
twentyminutes before 5 in Leadenhall-street, going to-
wards Comhill. He had his chimney-sweeping machine
with him. I said Good morning,' and he returned the
compliment. He was then near to Sussex-hall. lam
sure Gardiner was the man I spoke to. I saw him again
a 8 o'clock the same morning.
Thomas Reffeild, of Belvedere -place, Southwark-
bridge-road, carpenter, said: I have known Samuel
Gardiner for four or five years. I recollect last Monday
Week. I saw
.Gardiner at the top of the alley in Fen-
church- street at two minutes to seven, as I was waiting
to get into the shop.
John M .guire, 4, Aldgate, photographic artist;said :
I know Samuel Gardiner, and have done so for two
years. I recollect Monday week, the morning this
happened. I saw Gardiner at five minutes to seven,
near Moses and Son's, in Aldgate, between the Minories
and Jewry- street.
,The Coroner said the object of calling these witnesses
was to show that the statement of Gardiner was incorrect
if their statement was true.

Mary Bywater, 14, Swan-street, Minories, said: I am
married, and my husband works on the railway at
Haydon-street. I knew Mrs. Gardiner, who was a
customer at my shop. She came to my house on the
Saturday before this happened. She said she fell down
stairs and hurt herself. She said she supposed she
should have to go to the Bow Union. She said the
was very bad, and said she saw no other resource but to
go to the Union. She always appeared very deep in
trouble. I saw her twice on the Saturday. I told her
I was very sorry for her, and I heard no more of her
until I was told that she had been found with her throat
cut.

This being the whole of the evidence,
The Coroner said it was highly gratifying to him to
find:that the jury had given so much attention to this
,case, for it would satisfy the public that the matter had
not been slurred over; but that the whole Of the subject
had been gone into. Having given the subject a calm
and patient hearing, there would be two principal ques-
tions for their consideration, and whether they
determined one or the other, out of that question then
another would arise. It was shown by the evidence
that the deceased was found with her throat cut, and the
first question they would have to consider, would be,
was that her own act? If they should be satisfied of
that, then they would have to consider the state of mind
she was in when she did it. If, on the other hand, they
were of opinion that it was not her own act, then
they would have to be satisfied who was the party
responsible for her death? It appeared from the evidence
of several witnesses that the deceased had been for some
time in a low, and desponding state, which might be
aceounted for by the fact that the man to whom she was
married had brought home another woman to live in the
house. That seemed to worry her a good deal; it led
to frequent bickerings, and on more than one occasion
he had given her black eyes. On the Sunday before her
death the deceased complained of the treatment she had '
received from his paramour, Humbler. He said that
next morning he would put a stop to it, but that Gar-
diner explained by saying that what he meant was,
that Humbler should go away that morning. It also
appeared that' several valentines were found, Which
seemed to have worried her a good deal. As to
the idea of this being a suicide, they had the evidence
of the medical men that one finger was cut en-
tirely through, and that it was not possible for the
deceased to have grasped any sharp instrument tight
enough while in the agonies of death, and so have
caused these wounds in her hands herself. Dr. Sequira
and Dr. Comely, who assisted in the examination,
both positively declared that this was not the act of the
woman herself; and although a knife was found in the
deceased's right hand, yet curiously enough the laA ck of
it, and not the edge, was placed towards the throat.
This was one of those important facts which sometimes,
came out, and it would lead in this case to the conclu-
sion that the knife had been afterwards placed in her
hand, but that the person putting it there had acci-
dentally put it with the back instead of the edge to-
wards the throat. The question appeared to him to be
narrowed' to those two points, and he would remark that
the jury would not have to try any one, but to ascertain
whether there was such a prima facie case of suspicion
against any one as to. justify them in putting him on
his trial at the Old Bailey on a charge of murder. It
must be a charge of murder, for it would be quite im-
possible to reduce the offence to one of manslaughter.-
He then proceeded to read over the evidence of the dif-
ferent witnesses, commenting briefly upon parts of it as
he proceeded. He said as regarded Gardiner there was
not an absence of a motive, which was to live uncon-
trolled with Humbler, and there was aigreat discrepancy
between the statement of Gardiner as to the time he left
the house on the Monday and the evidence of the wit-
nesses who had been examined that day. After some
further remarks he left the case in the hands of the jury,
and it would be for them to say whether this was or was
not a subject that required further investigation before
another tribunal.

The room was then cleared, and after a quarter of an
hour's 'exclusion the public were admitted, when
The Foreman said that their verdict was Wilful
Murder against Samuel Gardiner and Elizabeth Hum-
bler.'

The inquisition having been signed, the coroner
made out his warrant of committal of the prisoners to
Newgate. -

articles.title: FOTERAL OF THE LATE EARL OF
articles.text:
FOTERAL OF THE LATE EARL OF

ELLESHERE.

On the 27th the remains of the late Earl of Ellesmere
were conveyed to the tomb, amid the fervent grief of his
family and friends, and the silent and respectful homage
of a numerous body of tenantry and dependents, who
felt that they had lost a considerate landlord and a
benevolent patron. The obsequies were conducted as
privately and unostentationsly as possible; but many
thousands of persons residing in the locality assembled
in and around the church at Worsley, where the cere-
mony was appointed to take place. The interior of the
sacred edifice was hung with black cloth. The ladies of
the congregation ordinarily attending the church were
admitted in the morning, and occutiied the aisles. They
were attired in deep mourning. Shortly after eleven
o'clock, the tolling of the muffled bell announced the
preparation for the ceremony; about noon the funeral
procession left the hall. As it entered the church, the
organ pealed forth Dr. Callcott' s beautiful trio—'.Forgive,
blest shade, the tributary tear.' The solemn and impres-
sive service was read by the Rev. St. Vincent Beechey,
and the scene was a very affecting one, the whole con-
gregation being moved to tears. As the body was con-
veyed from the church, the Dead March' in Saul was
Asyed by Mr. Whittington, who officiated as organist.
'Me churchyard throughout the whole of the ceremony
witalcawried, but a most decorous silence was maintained.
The cball, oicate I.Q.d of which was placed the earl's
coronet, was deposited 0/9. a marble slab, immediately
adjoining that on which the body of his illuatrious father
nate. After the ceremony the family retired to the hall,
accompanied by the tenantry and servants. The widow
of the deceased and the dowager countess were at the'
hall. The present earl, who is sixteen years of age, was
at Eton when he received the intelligence of his father's
death. It was stated that he would return again to his
studies, and it is expected that during his minority the
establishment at Worsley Hall will be broken up. The
younger brother is only eight years of age. A muffled
peal was rung on the bells of the Manchester Cathedral
the occasion of the funeral.

Jacob Saffia a Jerusalem Rabbi, is in Australia, col-
lecting funds for erecting Jewish buildings on Mount
Zion. The rabbi speaks English, and converses fluently
in Hebrew, German, Spanish, Italian, and Arabic.
There are now nearly 8,000 Jews at Jerusalem. An
opinion prevails amongst them that scripture warrants a
belief that the Holy City is to be re-established on
Mount Zion.

THE NEW POACILING Acr.—ln opposition to several
decisions which have .been given under the new Poach-
ing Act, the magistrates of Leicester, acting upon the
advice of their clerk, have aecisled that a person found on
the highway in possession of game, suspected to have
been unlawfully obtained, is not bound to show how he
became possessed of it. It rests-with the proceputor, in
their opinion to prove the charge of unlawful possession
by distinct affirmative evidence.

At GainSborough, the other day, at -a
dinner of the
Rifle Corps, Major Hutton said he had had the pleasure
some little time ago of visiting Garibaldi at Caprera.
The first thing spoken, of on reaching his house was the
volunteer movement. I consider. it,' Garibaldi said,
to be the finest thing England ever did.' For a full
hour he continued to put questions about the movement,
and in bringing the, conversation to a close he said, So
long as this movement lasts, England never need fear
an enemy'

articles.title: ZATER FROM AMERICA.
articles.text:
ZATER FROM AMERICA.

Igsw Ironic, Sept 20 (Morning).—Later accounts
horn General M'Clellan's head quarters state that Tues-
day last was chiefly passed in deploying the forces and
gaining position, but on Wednesday a seveye battleAvas
fought, lasting from, dawn till dusk. The resultof the
battle was indecisive, but the superiority of position
remained with the Federals. Their loss is -estimated at
fr0m.6,000 to 10,000 men. Federal General Mansfield
was killed, and Generals Hooker, -Dureya Sumner,
Meagher, Max, Weber, Dana, Hartsuff, Richardson,
Sedgwick, French, Ricketts, and Rodman were
wounded,. The loss of Federal generals and
field-officers is said to be so large as to be unaccount-
able. Little beyond skirmishing occurred on Thursday.
General Dl'Clellan officially reports on Friday morning
that the enemy abandonecl his position on Thursday
night, leaving dead and wounded on the field, and
says.:----` I do not know if the enemy is falling hack to
an interior ,position, or crossing the river. We may
safely claim the victory for ours. In a later dispatch
he reports that General Pleasanton is driving.the enemy
across the river' and says:—.' Our victory was complete.
The enemy is driven back into Virginia. Maryland
and Pennsylvania are now safe.' The -newspaper
accounts state that the Confederates commenced
crossing the Potomac at Shepherdstown Bridge
and two fords above and below, it early on .Thursday
night. During the night General M`Clellan advanced a
battery, and shelled the Confederates from the sur.
rounding heights. Early on Friday morning General
Pleasanton pursued Ahem with two batteries and two
regiments of infantry, and captured some of their am-
munition and supplies, and a small portion of ~a South
Carolina Brigade. General Stonewall Jackson con-
ducted the Confederate retreat into Virginia, and the
Confederate army appears to have crossed the Poto-
mac with but slight loss of men, waggons and artil-
lery. The Confederates retreated in the -direction of
Winchester. A considerable Federal forcp under Generals
Siegel and Heintzelmann is on the Virginia side of the
Potomac, and speculation is rife whether this force will
interfere with the Confederate retreat. It .is not de-
cidedly known whether the Federals or the Confederatcs
occupy Harper's Ferry, but it is rumoured that General
Burnside yesterday crossed into Virginia via Harper's
Ferry, and was moving against the Confederates. Gen.
M'Clellan's army crossed Antistem Creek, and is massed
between that position and the Potomac, opposite Shepherds-
town. It was supposed M'Clellan would cross the Potomac.
The capture of the Confederate Gen. Lon rtreet is not con-
firmed. The Federal garrison at Mumfordsville, Kentucky,
numbering 4,000 to 5,000, with 10 pieces of artillery,
surrendered -on the 17th to Confederate General Bragg,
• whose forces numbered 30,000. The reported invest-
ment of Charleston is officially denied. The Federal
gunboats have destroyed Prentice' Mississippi. The
Confederates are concentrating at Goldsborough, with
the intention of attacking Newburn, North Carolina.
Large bodies of Federal recruits continue leaving for
Washington. A large steamer, supposed to be the Oreto,
ran the blockade at Mobile.

NEW YORK, Sept. 20.—The Confederates all sscceeded
in crossing the Potomac on Friday morning, saving
their transports and all their wounded, except no.
The Confederates are still visible in force on the Potomac
shore, opposite 11`Clellan's position, and have posted ar-
tillery to prevent the Feklerals from crossing. The Fe-
derals estimate the Confederate loss at 18,000 to 20,000
men.

NEW Yonx, Sept. 22 (Evening).—The Confederates
have retired from the bank of the Potomac, opposite
M'Clellan' and have retreated in, the direction of Win-
chester. The Federals are crossibg the Potomac at
Shepherdstown and William's Point. The Confederates
evacuated Harper's Ferry on.. Friday last, after destroy-
ing all the Government stores and the pontoon bridge,
and partly destroying the bridge of the Baltimore and
Ohio railroad. The Federals , now occupy -Harper's
Ferry and Maryland. heights. Generals Siegel and
Hemtzlemann remain for the defence of Washington.
Commander Preble has been dismiSsed the U.S. service
for permitting the steamer Ovieto to enter Mobile.
