arrlN4 AN.D JAPAIV:

The following is from the summary of the overland
China .3fail of August 11:
The only item of news from Japan was to the effect
that all the ministers had left Yedo, the American
minister included. There is considerably more signifi-
cance in this fact than may at first appear. Such an
*vent has never happened since foreign relations were
opened with the country; but that this is precisely the
consummation that a party in Yedo have been sedulously
scheming for during the last few years is now pretty
well understood andadmitted by many political observers.
In our last summary of news we recorded the con-
tinued residence of all the ministers, who seemed
to vie with each other in remaining at their re-
spective posts. Of this course, however, they
have. simulta.n.eously become weary, and now, for
the first time, the . Japanese authorities behold
Yedo without a foreign official. We have often pointed
out the present state of affairs as being wrought ibr with
great patience and not a little
.skili by Ile Japanese
government; and if the reports can be relied upon, a
move has been' made by the combined foreign am-
bassadors, which, while quite voluntary on their part, is
yet entirely satisfactory to the native dignitaries.
Another report to the effect that the great princes of Japan,
grudging to the Tycoon the'exclusive revenue he derived
from the foreign trade, were about to demand the open-
tog of additional ports in their own territories, is not at
all likely to prove true although pleasing and rather
plausible. The result of the alleged gathering of
Daimios at Yedo has not transpired; it may simply have
been an auxiliary move towards inducing _Colonel Neale
and others to retire from Yedo. Matters in Japan are
therefore, with one imfortant exception; pretty much as
when we last wrote.

With regard to China,, the last fortnight has passed
without any incident 'of importance. Cholara has been
raging frightfully among the native population of Tien-
tsin, and is said to be moving in the direction of Peking.
Farther accounts say that -the statesman Kweiliang has
succumbed to it. Only one foreigner has fallen a
victim in Tien-tsin. At Chefoo, also, the pestilence has
committed dreadful havoc, 26,000 'people it is reported,
having died of it. The Rev. S. Hall arid other four of
the foreign residents expired within a few days.
At Shanghae everything is quiet. The dimensions
and importance of that settlement are increasing with
the growing trade on the Yang-tsze river, already very
large. A movement is at present on foot to have a
regular municipal corporation, or sothething equivalent,
with power or authority over the community to the
extent of levying taxes for public purposes.
Canton and Macao have both suffered most seriously
from the effects of 'a typhoon which swept over that
district about a fortnight ago; it is said to -have been
of a more severe nature than any that has been expe-
rienced for upwards of thirty years. The destruction of
life and property at Canton is immense, the loss of life
in the city and neighbourhood being estimated at forty
thousand; that is the highest estimate, but continued
inquiries show it to be probably the most correct.
The following notice of a pirate fleet in this neigh-.
bourhood is from our Shanghae contemporary:—
By the steamer Sir Charles Forbes wee learn that
I these pests of humanity are again becoming troublesome
on the coast between Shanghae and Ningpo. The cap-
tain of the above-named steamer informs -us that he
spoke the Heather Tell, -which had been fired on by
pirates off Chin-hae, on her voyage down from this port ;
also, that another small craft in compiny with her at
the time is missing. These pirates are said to be very
daring, and belong to Apak's fleet of buccaneers, the
greater portion of whom are now in the Imperial service,
keeping the Taepings in check at a place some thirty
miles inland from Ningpo.
In Hong Bong, everything goes on smoothly. The
late typhoon was felt here in smart gusts of wind,
which did just sufficient damage to show what we have
to fear should any other part except the extreme edge
of a cyclone approach us. About a week ago, the
Snake picked up a beat's crew who had left their vessel,
the Lord of the Isles, after she had caught fire. The
ship, being full of gunpowder in cargo, was abandoned
soon after the efforts to extinguish the fire were seen to
be unavailing. The crew reported the captain (Davis)
and eight passengers (including six French priests) as
at sea in another boat. These have since, we are glad
to say, turned up safely after considerable hardships.
The weather here is pleasant, but the barometer is very
low, and it is feared that the last has not yet been heard
of typhoons, but that one is, either imminent or raging
somewhere in our neighbourhood.

A DEFAULTING AGENT.—The English public has re-
cently been startled by several extraordinary instances
of defalcation ; but, unless general rumour is untrue, a
case has occurred on this side the water that equals some
of the worst of them. Names, for obvious reasons' - an-
not be given at present. It is -sufficient to state how-
ever, that an agent to several extensive properties has
decamped in default somewhere about £30,000. Two
writs, it is stated, have been taken out against him for
29,000—0ne for nearly half the sum by a noble lord,
well known in scientific and fashionable circles, thG other
by a wealthy 'landowner. The cause of the fug;tive's
misfortune ' is said to be speculations on the Stock Ex-
change.—Lettey from Dublin.

RAPID PONMONING.—An interesting experiment was
made on Thursday last on the Seine, opposite to the
Palace of Si. Cloud. A bridge was thrown across the
river in the r.iclest part within the short space of 20
minutes. This operation, which was formerly considered
to be one of the most difficult in the presence of an
enemy, is now accomplished with comparative facility.
The bridge thrown over the Seine within
.so Short a:time
on Thursday was suffieien. solid infantry,
csFalry, and artillery to crc tho.

The month of May was, without exception, meet&
finest that we have had for many years; the fortnight i
which ended with May 10th was n its mean tempera-
ture five degrees above the average of those fourteen
days; tho rain measured amounted to an inch and a
half, some falling on every day of the second week.; the
mean temperature of the following week did not differ
from the average, and nine-tenths of an inch of rain
were recorded, which amount fell in three days,; the
mean direction of the wind, which had previously been
S.W., was this week from the N.E , a circumstance
that fully accounts for the decrease in the tempera-
ture. The two following weeks, ending the month of
May, were very similar to each other in character,
both ,being in excess of their respective averages by
about two degrees only three-tenths of an inch of rain
fell, a little falling on five days out of the fourteen.
The warm rains of this month had a wonderful effect
upon vegetation everywhere, and were highly beneficial
in the hop gardens. There was notwithstanding the
high mean temperature, a decided lack of sunshine—a
I want which was continued through the entire summer,
and but for which our wheat crop would probably have
been one of the finest we have had for many seasons.
The first week of June was nearly two degrees above
the mean average temperature for the same week; and
rain fell on two days, amounting to only a quarter of an
inch. The next week was below the average tempera-
ture y nearly three degrees; and the rain, which fell
on five days, amounted to nearly an inch; the following
was a very cold week, being 4.1- degrees below its aver-
age; rather more than half an inch of rain fell. The
following week was very similar, the mean tem-
perature being 56 degrees, or four degrees below the
,average value; there was no rain of any importance
during this wek. The week ending July 5 was still
below its mean value for the time of year; the rain
during this week amounted to 35-100ths of an inch; it
fell on three days. The following week was three or
four degrees in defect, and seven-tenths of rain was
measured, a little falling on most of the days of the
week. The next week was two degrees below its
average; rain fell to the amount of half an inch. The
following period of seven days, ending with August 2nd,
was only one degree below, the average, and there
was no rain to an appreciable amount. From thesedata
we gather that May was warmer than the average by
three or four degrees, and that the months of June and
July were below their averages .by about the same
amount. Comparing the rainfall of .the past summer
with the average fall for the seasono we have the fol-
lowing_result _

So far then from being an excessively wet summer, it
has actually been drier, by a small amount, than is
usual. The want of sun retarded the ripening a the
wheat crop, and in the northern counties it suffered
from the high winds, and by rust. Oats, barley, and
beans are throughout the country showing average
crops. The swedes promise remarkably well.. The
potatoes are somewhat diseased, as indeed they are most
years more or less, but to no very alarming .extent.
The summer just past has been exceptionable in this
respect, it undoubtedly has been a cold-one, and that in
a marked degree; but it certainly has not been what
would be termed with propriety a wet one.—Mark-lane
Express.

articles.title: T.HE ROYAL MARRIAGE IW ITALY.
articles.text:
T.HE ROYAL MARRIAGE IW ITALY.

(From the Times Correspondent.)
Timer Sept. 27.—1 t is strange and it is pleasing to see
the soothing influence exercised on public feelings by
what in reality is merely a private occurrence. The
Princess Maria Pia and her wedding have established a
week of Truce of God' in Italian politics. Grim old
warriors are resting on their swords, and the lists are
strewn with flowers as if for a festive dance. Nothing
is going on, nothing is talked about, except the wedding
and its gay doings. The Italians are eagerly seizing
the first opportunity to evince their loyalty to the
reigning dynasty by volunteering their sympathy in
the auspicious event. Bologna, Ravenna, Parma, and
the minor CEmilian towns, vie with the large cities of
Lombardy and Tuscany in sending nuptial gifts, no less
remarkable for good taste and appropriateness than for
splendour and costliness. I already told you that the
Pope, as the bride's godfather, sent the Princess Pia
a token of his affection. The Patriot Committee at
Rome, not to be behindhand, have been collecting
large sums to join their countrymen of all parts of
Italy in giving the King's daughter a proof of their
devotion. Poetical effusions, as may be easily imagined,
are not wanting. The Commendatore Prati, a native of
Trent, compliments the bride in high-strained Italian
lyrics. A Professor of Bologna sends a string of high-
sounding Latin distiches. "here are odes from Modena,
erotic songs from. Florence, inscriptions from Novara.
The Minister of the Finance, a prosaic soul, at a loss how
otherwise to testify his good will, has bethought himselfof
paying down the Princess'sdowry (200,0004) in so many
Marenyi or bran new pieces of 20f., fresh from the Mint
and bearing the new stamp of Reyno d' Italia. These
25,000 gold coins were to be delivered to the head of the
Portuguese mission together with the person of the bride.
The wedding ceremony took place this morning, at
11 o'clock, in the internal chapel of the Royal Palace—
that is, privately, and away from the gaze of tbe profane
multitude. The family party consisted of the King, the
Princes of the blood, the Duchess of Genoa, Princess
Matilde Prince Napoleon, and a few of the dignitaries
of the Slate, among whom were the Presidents of both
Houses of Parliament, the Ministers, and. our cousins,' the
Knights of the Annunciate. Four of the privileged
members of that order, one of whom was Farini, had
the honour to sign the nuptial contract on Thursday
last. We hear nothing of
_briiesmeids. The Princess
Clotilde knelt at the altar by her sister's side. The
Marquis of Louie represented the King of Portugal.
The Archbishop of Genoa, M. Charvaz, assisted by four
bishops officiated at the sacred ceremony. Charvaz is
the Liberal prelate' as you know, whose promotion to
the see of Turin the Pope lately refused to confirm.
Many of the luckless ,wights whom etiquette did, not
allow to be of the party this morning, had a good chance
of seeing the bride and the bridal party at a great Court
concert last evening. The Italian Court is terribly
democratized, and the King hardly opens his palace
doors without everybody and his wife' being invited
to walk in. There was an awful crush invading
the splendid royal apartments last evening, and
the blaze of stars and crosses which dazzled
the eye was not sufficient to satisfy the be:
holder that Italy could boast so many
guished persons' as were there assembled. It was a
bespangled mob and no mistake.; and the King, or I
should say his Prefect of the Palace, seemed anxious to
screen the Royal party from the consequences of such a
vast, promiscuous invitation by intrenching them with a
chosen few in an inner room, to which 999 out of 1,000
could gain no access. This exclusive sanetum-sanetorum,
this delubrum in delubro, gave great offence, especially to
some of the Southern members of the assemblage, Tus-
cans, Neapolitans, &c. who contrasted. the ease and affa-
bility of Bourbon and Lorraine Royalty with the stiff,
ungenial demeanour of the Savoy dynasty, not greatly
to the advantage of the latter. Democracy and Court
etiquette, certainly, do not well suit together; but
there is hardly anything more galling and mortify-
ing than. for any self-respecting man to be in-
vited on any other than perfectly equal terms.
Undoubtedly the King knows nothing of these ante-
chamber and back-stairs arrangements. The fault lies
with the Majordomo or Prefect of Ihe.Palace Marquis
de Breme a very aged nobleman who understands
nothing of? the spirit of the age and would sooner the
than give in to it. A better chance of gazing their fill
at the great Royal personage.- was afforded to the well-
dressed multitude at the great hall of the University,
where prizes were distributed to the best pupils of the
various technical schools throughout the kingdom. The
Minister Pepoli availed himself of the occasion to pay
very handsome compliments to his cousin, Prince Napo-
leon, praising him to his face as the Prince who in the
Senate of his country with admirable eloquence defended
the cause of Italian unity, and who loved Italy as a
second country.' The Minister, also spoke words in
praise of the Princess Clotilde, of the Savoy Princes, all
present, and wound up, begging those students who
belonged to other provinces of the Peninsula to bear in
mind this generous city of Turin, which at the present
day longs for nothing more than to lay on the altar of
the country her queenly crown, that the national work
may be fulfilled, —an allusion to Rome as cepital of
Italy, which, together with many, other passages in
,the
Minister's speech, was received with 'loud applause.
In the evening there was a serenade and illumination,

THE LORD-LIEUTENANT OF STAFFORDSHIRE.—Every
inhabitant of Staffordshire will lcarn with regret that
the continued ill-health of Lord Hatherton has compelled
him to resign the office of lord-lieutenant of the county;
an . office which he has filled with most remarkable
efficiency and It livereal approval for upwards of eight
years. It is anticipated that the Earl of Harrowby, who,
as vice-Lieutenant of the county, has for same months
past acted as Lord Hatherton's deputy, will succeed to
the office vacated by his noble friend. Like Lord
Hatherton the noble earl, in early life, served hie
country with distinguished ability in the House of Com-
mons; like him, too, Lord Harrowby has satin the
cabinet and has, always taken an active share in the
county business, and the general county interests. The
unblemished character and the high esteem "in -which he
is held by everyone will render his appointment pecu-
liarly. grateful to Staffordshire, and do what is possible
to alleviate .the regret Lurd Hatherton's retirement will
occasion,

articles.text:
PALIVC_ESS PIA'S 21.4.RRIAGE GIFTS.

The presents sent.by the Pope to :his goddaughter,
the Princess Pia, en the occasion of her marriage, are
much more valuablothan was at first-stated, being worth,
it is said, several hundred thousand francs :

One consists ofn double leaf of massive gold, opening
in the form of an album, and containing two precious
relics-_a piece of the veil of the :Holy Virgin, and a
thorn from the crown of our Saviour. Those two relicS
are imbedded in the gold leaves, and surrounded by a
.border of precious stones. The two outer surfaces are
ornamented- with two extremely beautiful miniatures,
,corresponding to the recesein which the relics are placed.
The miniature at the back of the veil represents an
Adilolorata, and the other an Bees Homo. There is also
a chaplet of 3.15 beads each separated by a pearl and a
diamond,; also a timepiece of exquisite workmanship,
the hours of which are each represented by a relic;
lastly, there is an heraldic album of the Popes, with
portraits and inscriptions relative to each Pontiff, the
whale ornamented with precious stones. The binding is
in gold, studded with jewels. The present of the
municipality of Naples is a splendid set of ornaments
in pink coral of the 'value, of 30,0001., consisting of
a necklace of two rows; several 'bracelets; double
pins, one in a single piece, worth 3,0001.; twelve large
buttons fora riding dress, others for cuffs, with combs,
and pins for the hair—the whole most admirably carved.
The artist took_ four years to complete this set, as the
coral fishery could not sooner supply him with the pecu-
liar kind of coral required. These ornaments are placed
in a case covered with velvet, and studded with coral-
headed nails.'

The Syndi,'Commander Colonna, has left for Turin
to- prestht this gift to the Princess.
The definitive marriage at Lisbon of the Princess Pia
with the King of Portugal will take place on the 6th
October. The Princess is expected to arrive in that
capital the preceding day.

articles.text:
IIVDIA.

The following is "from the summary of the Friend of
India, August 22: - -
Colonel Bruce, Inspector-General of Police in India,
having recently visited the Godavery during the rainy
season, has been able for the first time to give the public
and Government a clear idea of its capabilities for navi-
gation, and as -a means for the export of cotton. He
shows conclusively that the navigation is open only four
months of the year, and that it is hopeless to spend
money on the, third or highest ,barrier of rock, which
stretches for thirty miles. lie recommends that a road
be made from Chanda, the most easterly of the cotton
marts, to Mogelep, at the foot of that barrier. But as
all the cotton is ready for export by March, it is
evident that it will prefer the railway to Bombay, in-
stead of waiting four months on the banks of the river
for its rise. The local advantages to the central pro-
vinces, however, of the opening of the two lower barriers
are evident.

Government has just entered:into a contract with the
Burmah Steam Navigation Company which will do
much to develop the coasting trade of India.
Cholera has been spreading in several of the canton-
ments of the 'North-West and the Punjaub. The
cholera report by Mr. Strachey has been in typo for the
last three weeks. It is a most elaborate production, and
contains admirable suggestions of a prophylactic and
sanitary character. Meanwhile, a panic is said to have
spread among the English troops. How long does
Government mean to delay the publication of the re-
port?

- There has been printed a memorandum of observa-
tions on the administration of India, drawn up by the
Hon. Rajah Dinkur Rao for private circulation.
Under fifty heads the writer discusses the problem
of how the British should govern so as to be popular
with their subjects. He approves of no measure not
in accordance with caste prejudices, or that does
not preserve established customs and existing rights.
Ile tells us the people have now forgotten the good-
ness of the Government, and have begun to prefer
the tyranny of the native princes.' He would keep all
rights in land as Well as the practice of selling hucks
or rights'. by judicial process for personal debts, all
hereditary rights in certain offices, such as exist in large
villages, where water-carriers, watchmen, barbers,
washern2en, have all remolded in particular families
from time immemorial as entailed property of which
the life interest only Can be alienate ?' All this would
be disappointing if we did not believe that the British
Government has a higher day in India than to make
itself popular 'vyth Asiatics degraded by centuries of
idolatry. ',.'rzt,yiip •
The Morrellgunge affrai7 appeal has been deelded.
Eleven natives are found guilty ef riot attended with
mnrderand abduction and sentenced to transportation
for life. Doulut Chokedar," a principal in the dreadful
outrage, is sentenced to death., Hely now awaits his
trial on a charge of -homicide arising out of this case.
The Agra Sudder Court has confirmed the sentence of
death, for murder and rebellion, passed on Pandoo Rao,
an adopted sen: of the last i'eishwa, and cousin of the
Nana. Thus the blood of Bithoor and Cawnpore will
be avenged.

The Corriere Mercantile, of Genoa, announces that
the Italian Minister of Finance has caused the 500,000 f.
constituting the dowry of Princess Pia, to be coined
expressly for the purpose in 20f. pieces, bearing the
effigy of the King of Italy and the date 1862.
THE WITHDRAWAL OP THE FRENCH TROOPS PROM
ROME.—The following letter lies been received from
Mr. Macrae Moir, Secretary to the Garibaldi Italian
' Unity Committee :----Stn,—On behalf of this committee
I beg to suggest that the memorials in favour of the
withdrawal of the French troops from Rome now being
agreed to at various meetings throughout the country
should be simultaneously presented to Earl Russell by
deputies from each of the towns and places memoralising:
To effect this a day must be named when the various
deputations shall assemble and together wait upon
the Foreign Secretary. IVe, therefore, invite those in
whose hands memorials have already been, or may here-
after be placed for presentation to communicate with us
without delay. -' • ' •
Two women condemned to death at one time for
separate eases, each equally, atrocious and horrible!
Such is the case at present, and we are glad that it is
but seldom so. The 'doubts which have arisen since the
conviction of the Glasgow-murderess as to the truth or
falsehood of her statement make it probable that she
will eScape the last dread penalty, but we cannot express
the same for the virretch who awaits her doom at
Newgate. She-seems to have-been a wholesale criminal
who made a trade of inurder,-and who, for the most
trivial sums, -put to, death persons who, far from
suspecting her, had treated and trusted her as a friend.
For such a miscreant we may well keep in existence the
horrid gallows and looking back a quarter of a century
on the host of wretches who were executed for the
smallest crimes, and for offences which we should deem
but petty larceny,-we cannot express much pity for her
who waits her fate.., It is some years since we had this
horror of a woman's execution in the metropolis, and
long will be the interval, we hope, before the like occurs
again—London Gossip.
A TURKISH SUPERSTITION AS TO BUILDING OPERA-
noNs.—There exists in Turkey an ancient superstition
(carefully fostered and encouraged by the wise architects
of the East), to the effect that men never die while in
the act of building a house to live in. The consequence
is, that in countries where the superstition prevails, rich
old gentlemen are often seized with a passion for building
at a period of life when it might be thought that they
would very much prefer the dolce far niente, so precious
in the East, to the-long string of anxieties and vexations
well known to be inseparable from dabbling in bricks
and mortar. Among others seized with this kind of
building mania was the indolent and sickly prince, the
late Abdul Mejid. As he got more and more sickly, he
at last roused himself from the half lethargic state which
generally accompanies a life of Oriental luxury, and set
about building a new palace on the Bosphorus. It is a
rather singular coincidence 'that the sickly Sultan lived
en, in his half lethargy, during the whole period of the
building pf the palace, which lasted for several years,
and died soon after its completion • thus confirming the
truth of the old Turkish proirerl; by the very highest
authority in the State, to the great profit and stimu-
lation of the architectural profession in the East.—
Builder.

LORD RUSSELL AT GOTHA .-Mr. E. Yates, in the
Northern Whig, writes :—And, by the way, a perusal of
that delightful column, the Court Circular, is calculated
4 the present time to make you and me and other every-
day hum-drum readers grateful in the highest degree
that we were not born -as- some other men are' states-
men diplomates, Ministers, persons of the highest official
rank! For, herein recorded we find that Earl Russell
is staying at Gotha, and that he comes over nearly every
other day to have iaterviews--business interviews—
with secluded English Majesty at Reinhardtsbrunn.
Here is an old gentleman_ going on for seventy years .4
age not veil strong in bodily health, but marvellously
resolute, •proud and self-sufficient—a man much more
O British than the majority of his class, and with any-
thing but continental affectations—a man who, report
says, specially enjoys his domesticity and the society
of his family, ana here he is, at his age and with his in-
clinationi, compelled to trot off to the wretchedest little
German Stadt, to do kotoos and advisings, to grind away
at business when he ought to be at rest, to swallow,
literally and metaphorically, all sorts of things that he
dose not Like, and to undergo a thousand unpleasantries,
and all because he is Foreign .Secretary. . Happy you
and I, Blogg, my boy, we can go to Margate with our
carpet-bag, and take our dip in the, sea and our chalice
in the raffle in Tullrs Bazaar, and be freed from all
thoughts.cedouble-entry Or bills of parcels in the ledger
at the office in the City!

articles.title: CAPE •OF GO OD HOP.k
articles.text:
THE CAPE •OF GO OD HOP.k

Emigration from the Cape to New Zealand is at
present all the rage here. The Government of New
Zealand has appointed agents in Cape Town and Port
Elizabeth, who are empowered to grant passages to
Auckland at £l2 10s. per statute adult, with the promise
of a grant of 40 acres of land each on arrival at their
destination. in Cape Town there has been a 1: rge
number of applicants, who would be glad to escape from
the distress that exists amongst our city population.
Many of them, however, have not the means of paying
for their passage, but there are hundreds who, if con-
veyed free, would gladly embrace the opportunity. The
distress amongst our industrious population is at present
very severe; not a few cases of utter destitution have
been brought to light.
At the Cape during the past month there have been a
number of severe gales, involving some dreadful ship-
ping disasters. _ _

lii passing, I may mention that Dr. Biekersteth, bro-
ther of the Bishop of Ripon, died suddenly in Cape
Town, on the 6th inst. Ile had only a short time re-
turned from a visit to England, vhich he had Sunder-
taken for the benefit of his health.

Native affairs are at present quiet. Apprehensions
are entertained of disturbances amongst themselves.
British Kaffraria is prosperous. In extent its capital
is rapidly progressing, and the value of land has been
much enhanced.

There is sad news again from the Zambesi. Follow-
ing closely on the deaths of Bishop Mackenzie, Rev.
Mr. Burrup, and others, is that of Mrs. Livingstone (the
wife of the celebrated traveller), who died from fever,
on the 28th April, at Shupanga. This intelligence was
brought by her Majesty's ship Ariel, Commander Old-
field, which arrived at Natal August 3. Dr. Living-
stone, with the Pioneer, was, at the last date, about to
proceed to Mozambique and Johanna, with the inten-
tion, it is said, of exploring the river Rovooma. Sink-
ness had prevailed largely amongst Dr. Livingstone's
party. Lieut. Burton, R.N.,-has returned in the Arid,
having suffered severely from the climate.
The news from Natal is not of importance. From
some returns that have been published, it appears that
the revenue is in a highly prosperous state.
In commercial and monetary matters there is not
much to report this month. A new steamship company
has been projected, with the view of connecting the
Cape of Good Hope, Natal, and Mauritius. The pro-
posed capital is £120,000, in 12,000 shares of 1;10 each,
with power to increase to £200,000. 4,000 shares are
to be reserved for the colonies of the Cape, Natal, and
Mauritius, and 8,000 to be disposed of in England.
There have been very few arrivals of shipping in Table
Bay, and business is duller than it has been for a long
time back. Transactions have been on the most limited
scale, but prices notwithstandtng, have been main..
tamed. The dullness is largely attributable to the
stoppage of the country trade by the recent heavy rains.

articles.title: COTTON. FRO3I EGYPT.
articles.text:
COTTON. FRO3I EGYPT.

We are now on the eve of the new *cotton season, and
the attention of the whole country; from the wealthiest
landholder down to the pooreat fellah, seems absorbed in
the contemplation of the dazzling prospects with which
the new campaign is opening. A few occasional lots as
yet, it is true very trifling in quantity, are already ap-
pearing in the Alexandria market, and, although more
than doubtingly accepted as new cotton, they are realis-
ing enormous prices. Ismail Pasha and Mustafa Pasha,
the two largest producers in the country, have com-
menced cautiously selling comparatively small lots for
forward delivery, and their prices have rapidly risen to
50 dollars the cantar. Cotton is, in short, at this me"-
ment fully three, perhaps nearer four-fold, what at any
other time would have been considered its natural value.
Immense wealth seems, therefore, destined•to pdur into
the country within six months. According to moderate
computations, the incoming crop will amount to consider-
ably more than 1,000,000 of cantars, and unless an
abrupt and seemingly unlikely change takes place in
American affairs, little, if at all :less than £8,000,000
sterling will be required to pay for it. It is gratifying
to be able to add that in the midst of these brilliant
prospects, it does not seem likely to be overlooked that
the same causes that are operating so mush to the
advantage of the Egyptian planters are inflicting great
and undeserved distress in the manufacturing localities,
whence these vast amounts are to be derived. Hahn
Pasha, I am informed, has already sent a sum of £2OO
to aid in the relief of the English operatives, and that
without waiting absolutely to secure any portion of the
benefits of which the prospects are before him. This
example will, without doubt, be followed by others,
and the act, honourable as it is to the Prince's good feel-
ings as well as to his intelligence, will, I feel assured,
not pass without due.appreciation from all condition's of
Englishmen.
The forthcoming visit of Prince Napoleon to Egypt
has, it is said, been officially announced to the Govern-
ment, and although contradictory rumours are at this
moment afloat, extensive preparations have been
arra.nged for receiving the Prince with special honours.

CHINESE HONOURS TO ENGLISH AND FRENCH OFFI-
CERS.—A Russian journal publishcs two decrees of the
Emperor of China which it had copied from a Chinese
print. One expresses the sorrow of the son of Heaven
at the news of the death of Admiral Protet, and ordeis
100 Zibeline skins and four !ieces of Thibet velVet to be
sent as a present to the fat. y.of that brave officer. The
other decree relates to the funeral honours to be paid to
a French colonel and an English officer, who were killed
at the capture of Ning-po.
AN AFFRAY AT ROME.—A letter from Rome in the
Nord says:---' A serious occurrence, though unfortu-
nately by no means surprising, has just taken place in
the Roman territory, on an estate belonging, to Mgr.
Bedini. Two French soldiers, yielding to h, very excus-
able temptation ventured to pick a few bunches of grapes
from the Cardinars vines. They were seen by the
farmers, who furiously attacked them, killing one of
them and wounding the other. The guilty parties then
fled in Mgr. Bedini's own carriage, but they were over-
taken, and at the instance of M. de Montebello, have
been removed to Rome for trial.
THE POST OFFICE ROBBERIES IN AUSTRIA—PubIic
attention is at this moment occupied with the details of
the Kalab trial, which has just commenced before the
Criminal Court. Kalab is the postman who stole more
than 80,0'00 letters. The aecused, on his examination,
declared that he had only committed those frauds ía
order to force the Post Office authorities to reorganise
the administration. With the product of these robberies
Kalab had purchased two handsome country houses at
Hitzing, near Vienna. The authorities have sequestered
the houses, in order to compensate the sufferers 'with
the money arising from the sale of them.—Letter from
Vienna.

WHAT IS AN An°',momsT P—' An abolitionist is any
man who does not love slavery for its own sake as a
divine institution; who-does not worship it as a corner-
stone of civil liberty; who does not adore it as the only
possible social condition on which a permanent republi-
can Government can be created; and who does not, in
his inmost soul, desire to see it extended and perpetuated
over the whole earth na means of human reformation,
secondonly in dignity, importance, and sacredness to the
Christian religion. He who 'does not love African
slavery with this love is an abolitionist.'—The Literary
Messenger,C.S.A.
AN M.P.'s. BREACH OF THE COLLIERY ACT.—At the
Abdare Police-court, last week, Mr. Crawslaay Bailey,
M.P., was summoned at the instance of the Inspector of
Mines, Mr. Evans, for not complying with the tenth
general rule of the Aet of Parliament 29 and 24 Viet.,
cap. 151, which enacts that no single-linked chain shall
be used for lowering or raising persons in any working'
pit or shaft. The offence was admitted on behalf of Mr.
Bailey, and in mitigation Mr. James said everything was
now being done to carry out the provisions of the law.
The magistrates fined defendant £lO and costs.—Bristel
Mercury.
A NOVEL EMPLOYMENT FOR NAVVIES.—The Bylin
Courant states that many of the masons, navvies, and
others connected with the Strathspey Railway works
have been sized with a mania for pearl fishing. Tuck-
ing up their shirt sleeves and trousers, they wade in the
Spey, but do not dive, pick up the shells with their
hands, and throw them ashore. -Generally they pick
them up with a cane split at one end, and when they
have collected some they open them with a stout' knife,
finding the pearl in the softer part of the animal, but not
in every shell. The pearls are of different sizes and
colours, from the size of small shot to that of a good-
sized pea. The smaller and coloured ones are of little
value; the larger ones are pearls of great price.
THE ECCLESIASTICAL Commrssiox.—The Select Com-
mittee appointed by the House of Commons to inquire
into the present state of the Ecclesiastical Commission,
and report whether the ecclesiastical revenues Could not
be more advantageously administered for the interests of
the Church, have now reported to the House. They
have held numerous meetings, and taken evidence Upon
various branches of the inquiry submitted to them.
They have not,' however, acquired sufficient informa-
tion to enable them to pronounce a decisive opinion upon
all the questions bromght under their notice. There are
also some other questions which may require investiga-
tion.' They therefore content themselves with reporting
the evidence to the House, and recommend 'the re-ap-
pointment of the committee at the commencement of the
ensuing session.
A GREAT FRI7IT SEASON IN AMERICA. - There has
never been known in the Union such a fruit season as
this. On every side-walk are stands; in every
,corner
grocery you will find pyramids of Bartlett-pears, luscious
peaches, purple plums, niountains of water lemons and
cantelopes. Apples are ebuntlessj and grapes are given
away! They are all cheap. A Jersey man, who came
to the city expecting' to get a good price for a load of
pears, finding that he could- not get one-twentieth of the
prig) of last year, gave them all away.—Letter from
;Yew York.

articles.title: RIOT IN BIDE PARE:
articles.text:
RIOT IN BIDE PARE:

Three o'clock on the 28th having been the time fixed'
by the Working Men's Garibaldian Fund Committee for
holding an open air demonstration in Hyde Park to
express sympathy with Garibaldi, and to-adopt a protest
against the French occupation of Rome,' at that hour it
was estimated 5,000 people had assembled. A mound of
earth capable of accommodating about 200 persons,.
situate midway between Grosvenor Gate and the Marble
Arch, had been fixed upon as the platform from whence
the speeches were to be made. A few minutes after
three the committee made their appearance on the
ground, but just before their arrival the mound had been.
taken possession of by a mob of Irishmen and'roughs,'
evidently bent on mischief. Immediately surrounding.
the mound was a mob of about at least 500 Irish
labourers, who protested vehemently they would not
allow the meeting to be addressed from the spot, ac-
companied by three cheers for the Pope.' The com-
mittee, determined not to be thwarted, and,backed up by
a large portion of
,the crowd succeeded, after a severe
struggle, in obtaining a footing on the mound amidst
great cheering and considerable confusion. Mr.
Charles Murray was called on to preside, and, amidst
the greatest uproar, asked Mr. Bradlaugh to move the
first *resolution. On Mr. Bradlaugh coming foward a
desperate rush was made forward by the Irish party,
many, of whom were armed with bludgeons, and the
speakers and several members of the committee were
thrown violently off the mound. The Garibaldians
hereupon again rushed forward, and after some hard
fighting succeeded in reinstating the chairman in
position. The Scene now became alarming, it being
evident that the partisaes of the Pope were determined
to stick at nothing to prevent the meeting being held.
Mr. Bradlaugh again essayed to speak, but the continued
struggles between' th_e contending parties to obtain pos-
session of the mound rendered it a hopeless task, and he
concluded by moving a resolution in accordance with
the •object of the meeting. Mr. Clegg came forward to
second the-resolution, but he had not uttered two words.
'before the Irishmen reinforced. by several hundreds of
the most desperate-looking ruffians, again succeeded in
clearing the mound of the Garibaldi party. A fearful
riot now ensued, each party succeeding in turn in gain-
ing possession of the mound. During the struggle
sticks, umbrellas, and stones were freely used, and several
persons were severely injured. The crowd had doubled
in numbers by this time; but although the Garibaldians
outnumbered by thousands their opponents, they were im-
plored by the committee to remain quiet, and let the onus
of these disgraceful proceedings rest upon the Irish party.
Some of the more ardent spirits, however, disregarded
this advice, and the. struggle was again renewed with
increased violence, At last the Irishmen, by the free
use of their bludgeons, obtained full possession of the
mound; but, not content with this victory, they cern-
Menced throwing stones indiscriminately amongst the
crowd, seriously injuring several persons. At this time.
there were about 50'0 of the lowest class of Irish la-
bourers on or about the mound, when a stone thrown
from"amongst them' struck a seZdier of the Guards
violently on the breast. The soldier, without a
moment's hesitation, rushed up the mound, and, dash-
ing into the midst of the Irishmen, singled out the man
who had thrown the stone, and by a well-directed blow
felled him to the ground, amidst the cheers of the-
crowd.' The soldier, in his turn, was set upon by
a dozen of the ruffians, and was being severely
handled, when several of his comrades in the crowd,_
foll Owed by about twenty civilians, charged up"
the mound, and, -after severe fight, drove the
Irish off the mound and pursued them some distance
across the park. Here they were met by a body
of police who had been sent for, and, several of the ring-
leaders having been pointed out, they were taken into
custody and conveyed to the station-house, the soldiers
being borne back in triumph on the shoulders of the
crowd to the top of the mound, which was now again in
possession of the Garibaldi party. The secretary of the
committee now stood forward and announced that,.
owing to the disgraceful riot which had been created by
the Irish party, the meeting would be adjourned until
-Sunday next, when the committee would be prepared to
meet any similar attempt. This announcement was re-
-ceived with loud cheers, amidst which the committee
declared the meeting dissolved. The excitement
amongst the crowd, occasioned by the conduct of the
Irishmen, had, however, by this time considerably
increased, and, under the leadership of the soldiers, a
large force was being organised by the Garibaldians with-
the object of inflicting summary chastisement upon the
Irishmen,. and an onslaught was upon the eve of taking
place when the rain, which had been some time
threatening, came down in a complete deluge, speedily
damping the ardour of the belligerents, and causing every
one to make a hasty retreat out of the park.

Yesterday afternoon (says the John Bull of Saturday)„
in consequence of the illness of the Lord Chamberlain,
Mr. Spencer Ponsenby received a small deputation instead
of a larger one that had been proposed, who presented a
memorial, very numerous].) and influentially signeds
praying that the ancient clause prohibiting the opening of
theatres in the Holy Week may be inserted in the licenses
about to be issued for next year. The names of one or
two bishops known to be most opposed to the innovation
will be missed; but we learn that the reason they are not
appended to the memorial, which has been got up by the
English Church Union with such zeal at this dull season,
is that they thought it was a matter for the whole episco-
pate as a body to take up. We trust their lordships may
yet adopt this course, as, although the time for granting
the licenses is close at hand, the forms have, we under-
stand, not yet been drawn up.
,
MELANCHOLY DEATH OF A LADY.-1111 Inquest was,
held at Datchet,• near Windsor, on the 27th, by Mr.
Charsley, on the body of Mrs. Watson, the wile of a.
gentleman residing near Tottenham. Colonel Sissmore
said the deceased was his sister-in-law, and they both
were on a visit to Mr. Fowler, of Southley-house,
Datchet, the father of the deceased. She had exhibited
a little' excitement, but was under no restraint. On.
Wednesday night, a little before eleven o'clock, she re—
tired to rest, and on the following morning at eight
o'clock the servant came to toll him that she could not
get into the bed-room of the deceased. Witness told the
-
gardener to enter the room by a ladder. placed against,
the window. Deceased was not there, but footsteps
were afterwards discovered below the bedroom window,
and there was a broken branch of a tree which convince&
him that deceased had escaped in that way. After ex-
amining the grounds and hrubbery, and obtaining no.
trace of her, witness sent a man in a punt to search the
water, in which she was shortly afterwards discovered.
Deceased was about fifty-eight years old. The two
windows in her bedroom were about fifteen feet from the
ground, and very small. Could assign no reason why
she should commit suicide. The jury, after a long con-
sultation, returned a verdict of 'Found drowned in thet
river Thames, without any marks on her body, but by
what means she came into the river there was no evi-
dence to show.'

STATE EQUIPAGE Pon THE SHERIPP-ELECT.—The
state carriage, which has just been completed; is an
elegant vehicle of very tasteful design. The body is in
colour bright claret, with white reliefs, and the carriage
and wheels are painted to correspond, having decora-
tions of brass mouldings and snake body loops. Upon
the panels are the City arms, &c., and the private arms
of the alderman, with motto, Per ardua stabilis.' The-
hammercloth, of white kerseymere adorned with scarlet
fringe, scarlet and white hangers, Br,e., displaying on a
field of scarlet Geona velvet the alderman's crest. The.
interior, lined with figured silk, white shot with pink,
the pattern tulips and other flowers, with foilage and
lace, cerise and white, with curtains of crimson silk in
festoons. This elegant chariot has been manufactured,
by Messrs. Wyburn and Co., of Long-acre. The state
liveries, made at the establishment of the late Mr.
Jones, of Cannon-street, comprise coats for coachmen
and footmen of superior claret cloth, bordered with broad
gold lace, pattern oak leaf, with gold scroll braiding,
and lined with white silk, having bullion buttons and
massive gold aiguillettes. The waistcoats are of white
kerseymere, and the continuations, of white doeskin,
with ornaments of gold lace and bullion tassels.
EMBEZZLEMENT AND SUICIDE.—An inquest was held
before the Warwick county coroner, on the 27th,
respecting the death of William_ Neville, the late perma-
nent secretary to the Southam Sick Fund Society, who
had been found lying in a garden with gunshot wounds
penetrating his heart and lungs. Considerable interest
was attracted to the case, as deceased, who was a barber
and newsagent, had been suspected of defrauding a num-
ber of poor persons by embezzling the subscriptions
which were intended to be forwarded to the Nottingham
Ancient Imperial Order of Odd Fellows for their benefit
in cases of sickness or death; and it appeared from the
evidence that arrangements had been made by the local
managers for his paying off the amount of the defal-
cations he had committed by instalments, but, although
the members were warned not to pay him any further
subscriptions, the charges against him had not been fully
investigated, and it would appear that he shot himself
at the very hour when he had arranged to meet the club,
and render an account of his stewardship. The general
secretary of the Odd Fellows had written to complain
of his frauds upon the members, the extent of which it
was impossible to tell, as he refused- to give up pos-
session of the funeral receipt book. The jury came to
the conclusion that .he had committed suicide while in
an unsound state of mind, and returned a verdict to that
effect.

• SUICIDE OP GENERAL GYULA.Y.—General Count
Gyulay, late Commander-in-Chief of the Austrian
i
troops n Italy, shot himself On Tuesday, at .noon, in
Vienna. This is the fifth or sixth suicide of eminent
men—among them the distinguished and genial Minister
of Finance, Baron von Bruk—which has taken place in
the capital of Austria within the last few years. Count
Gyulay was born in 1799,, entered the service in 1816,
and became Major-General in 1839. He was Minister
of War during the critical period of 1849-50.—Spec-
tator.

THE INTERNATIONAL _EXIIIBITIO1V;

Saturday was the worst day-of Oki worst week at the
Exhibition. The total number of payments was only
3.0,010, of season tickets 5,477—in,a11.15,487. As eom-
pared with the corresponding week in 1841 the decrease
in the attendance on this occasion is very great indeed,
rather more, in fact, than 10,000 a-day. The returns
for the two periods are as follows :-

TuesdaY (is.) .. 60,362 43,880
Wednesday (Is.) .. 54,540 44,844
Thursday (Is.) .. 57,161 .. 41,369

.Saturday (51.) 20,236(28.61)15,487

seme set-off to this rather discouraging statement,
it must be remembered that at this date in 1861 the
Exhibition was within a fortnight of closing, and that
this building has still nearly five weeks to run. When
the time for the closing of the present display draws
near, we have not the least doubt of seeing the returns
ap to 90,000 and even 100,000 daily. His R.yal High-
ness Prince Alfred, attended by Major Cowell, It
and ac.ompanied by Mr. Sandford, the secretary, paid a
visit to the building on Saturday. The Prince visited
Mr. Minton's beautiful porcelain court, and also spent
some time in examining the mechanism of Benson's
great clock, waiting to watch it strike. The rest of the
visit was spent almost entirely among the foreign courts,
which for a time were left comparatively disregarded by
the general visitors, who eongregated at the east end to
hear a very excellent concert which was given there
upon the instruments exhibited by Messrs. Rudall, Rose,
Carte, and Co.
The parochial antherities of South Kensington have
sent in a claim of .£ll5 for poor, lighting, and pollee
rates due to the parish, and also a similar one to Mr.
Mulish for no less than £9OO. These claims are
apparently put forward as feelers, as, if established they.
would render all exhibitors who have taken orders for
goods liable to the same charges. Considering that
the building already pays its full quota of rates and taxes,
and that the parish in which it stands has gained more
by its erection than all the other parts of the metropolis
„put together, these claims for rates upon exhibitors, who
are, after all, only the lodgers of the Commissioners,
seem a piece of sharp practice, to say the least of it As
a matter of course, the elaims are resisted by aIL parties;
We may also mention that many orders have been
.given- for articles from Cephalonia manufactured like
lace from the fibre of the American aloei. This fabric,
though pretty, has not received a prize, and our reason
for alluding to it is the attention directed to the material
during the last few days as A ptSSibie substitute for cot-
ton. Mr. Rideout, of Standish Mills, Wiginran exten-
sive cotton spinner and paper manufacturer, has ordered
a bale of the fabric to experimentalise , with in both
branches of his business. The plant grows in great
Abundance both in Italy and the lonian Islands, and, if
found available fer manufacturing purposes, might be
-obtained in large quantities.

articles.title: ALLEGED MATRICIDE.
articles.text:
ALLEGED MATRICIDE.

William Helliwell, a weaver, is in custody at Halifax,
charged with the murder of his mother, Betty Helliwell,
-aged 66, who lived in a cottage in the township of
-Soyland, about four miles from Halifax. The deceased
woman was found dead in stone quarry not very far
from her own house last Friday morning. Her head
was mu3h bruised, and there were other injuries on her
.person, showing that she had suffered great violence:
The deceased was found at a depth of. 36 feet from the
top of the quarry. Under the circumstances, it was at
once suspected that the unfortunate woman had not
eome to her death by fair means, the more so when it
was known that there had been many quarrels between
her and her son. There had been a violent quarrel on
the previous night about the payment of £2 ss. for
the keep of a stirk belonging to her by John Parsons,
of Upper Lumb, Cottenswnes, during the summer, the
term being concluded on Thursday. The quarrel was
.as to who ought to pay for the animal's maintenance,
.and she said to William that he ought to pay, as
she knew he had £25, and that she .had nothing. She
said 'You want to get me out of the way so as to have
the farm to yourself.' A brother of Williams, named
David, urged upon him the propriety of paying .for the
.stirk, but tte would not, and they also had some angry
words with each other, which had such an effect upon
David that, after going to bed, he got up at 11 that
might,and left the house, being afraid of the consequences
of his brother's Violent temper, which was roused by the
-quarrel with his mother. When David came to the
house,. at 6 on Friday morning he found that his mother
was not in bed, though William was- at the time, but
immediately after got up, dressed himself, and went out to
seek for his mother. On hearing that a dead woman had
been found at the quarry he went thither and found it
was his mother. David sent for Policeman 'Follis, and
told him that he suspected his brother William. Follis
having taken William into custody, told him that he was
'charged with the murder of his mother, to whi.ch he
replied that he had not seen his mother since 10 o'clock
the previous night, but he had heard her blowing the
fire, during which he fell asleep, and never saw her
again. Follis took him to the lock-up at the West
Riding station, Halifax, and all the way he held his
head down and kept repeating the words, Oh, mother,
you wor a stubborn woman.' When Hannah Whitley,
-one of the deceased's daughters, heard of her mother's
body being found, she said, My brother Will has killed
her. It is supposed that when the unfortunate woman
left her hoxse at half-past 10 on Thursday night the
prisoner followed and overtook- her on the way, and,
seizing his opportunity; carried her to the quarry and
threw her into it, and the lantern found near the body
was thrown after as a blind, to make it appear that she
had missed her way and fallen over, and so come by.her
death.

articles.title: MR. CADOGAN AND M. VEILL.4IO.
articles.text:
MR. CADOGAN AND M. VEILL.4IO.

The Hon. F. Cadoo•an gives the following
explana-
tion of a transaction which has recently occupied much
attention : _ _ _ -

--'My position towards M. Veillard was strictly defined
by an agreement drawn by my family solicitors, Messrs.
Fladgate and Co., which agreement was further settled
by counsel, for the double purpose of securing me
against the risks of M. Veillann engagements, as also
against any possible imputation of having made an
agreement which could offend against public,. policy in
principle or detail. The existence of this agreement
was well known, not ply to the executive, by whom
my position was fully recognised, but also by most of
those gentlemen who, I regret to say, are now the largest
creditors of the estate, and who form the committee of
inspection for winding up the affairs. The payment I
received under the above agreement was in considera-
tion of services rendered for now- more than twelve
anonths to M. Veillard, in conducting for him the nego-
tiations with capitalists and others incidental to the
undertaking, preparing his tenders, procuring a large
portion of the capital, superintending all the construc-
tions and legal arrangements, and above all, in being the
intermediary between the executive of the Exhibition
and M. Veillard in all the endless questions of detail
and management, which ft was manifestly impossible
for a foreigner to have personally conducted. Her Ma-
jesty's Commissioners and most of M. Veillard's princi-
pal creditors and supporters can bear witness to the num-
ber and importance of those arrangements, which for
nearly 'four months required, not only daily, but con-
stant attendance upon the Commissioners and their offi-
cers. I have received £2,400, which was paid to me by
the daily receipt of one-eighth of a penny per head for
each visitor to the Exhibition. On the other hand a
large portion of this amount was lent by me to. M. Veil-
lard, who still owes me a balance of £550 on this loan
account. lam further personally liable for £1,500 ad-
vanced to him upon my private security. It is not for me
to decide whether the services rendered, and the respon-
sibilities incurred. have been over-remunerated by the
balance remaining in my favour. The sole purpose of this
statement is to reply to your natural question as to my
connexion with M. Veillard's contract, and to refute the
cruel and libellous attacks of which, in my absence, I
have been made the object by some of the press and its
correspondents, by whom it as insinuated that I used
undue influence to obtain the contract for M. Veillard,
and that I put forward a man of straw in order to
victimise his creditors to my sole profit. All the
negotiations that tool/ place with her Majesty's Commis-
sioners on behalf of M. Veillard were conducted by me,
solely with those gentlemen in their official capacity. It
amounts to an insult to them that I should be
requested to assert that on- no occasion, either by
word or by implication, did I receive any preference
or advantage over thesother parties tendering for
this contract. My previous knowledge of M. Veillard,
confirmed by the result of the inquiries I made here
and in France, satisfied me that his antecedents were
those of an honourable man, fully able to conduct the
department in questiOn, with whom I could safely and
creditably enter into the arrangement already named.
Commissioners to form their I left it to her Majesty's
opinion of his credit and capabilities through their own
private channels of inquiry. The result of those in
quiries and the reason for his tender being accepted are
stated by her Majesty's Commissioners in your (The
Times) impression, of the 18th. To the unexpected de-
tention in Scotland of the gentleman who, cognisant
this business in all its details, would have repre-
sented me at the meeting of M. Veil-lard's creditors,
during my unavoidable absence on the Continerl,
is, I trust, to be attributed the unfounded and Beall-

THE BEE-HIVE, SATURDAY, OCTOBER 4, 1862.

THE ROU.fPJL FORGERIES.

Although the charge of forgery against the prisoner
William Roupell has been thus far disposed of by his
pleading guilty and his being sentenced to penal servi-
tude, there appears to be very little doubt that there
will still be a large amount of litigation before the
matter is finally disposed of, and as, in all probability,
Mr. Roupell will have to appear on many future occa-
sions as a witness, it is expected that he will remain in
Newgace for a very considerable time. Since his con-
viction he has been treated in just the same manner as
ordinary persons would be under the circumstances and
the late M.P. for Lambeth has each day his task of
oakum-picking assigned to him, and he will be so em-
ployed all the time he continues in the gaol of Newgate.
In some respects, it would seem that the fact of the
prisoner being sentenced to penal servitude for life is
rather an advantage to him than otherwise. The rule
that is acted upon in these matters appears to be that
where prisoners are sentenced to only short periods or
penal servitude, they are sent either to Portland or the
Millbank Penitentiary, or some other of the government
prisons in EnglavA where the discipline is very severe
and the confinement most irksome; but in the case of a
prisoner sentenced to penal servitude for life, he is,
unless very much advanced in years, invariably sent to
ene of the colonies, where, after the lapse of a certain
period, ranging between eight and ten years, if his
i.uct is good a ticket of leave is generally granted to
him. These tickets of leave are, however, always given
with the special condition that the prisoner shall not
return to England. If that condition is broken he is
liable to be tried for felony in being at large before the
expiration of his sentence, and he would be sent back
to complete it. The chances therefore are that in the
course of a few years Roupell will be again a free man,
and in his position it is not likely that he will consider
the condition of net returning to this country, where
he has attained such an unenviable noteriety, a very
great privation.
Now that the prisoner stands formally convicted, and
under sentence for the forgery of the will, by means of
which he was enabled to make away with the great bulk
of his father's property, there is no doubt that the pro-
ceedings that were initiated by the heir-at-law in the
trial at Guildford, to recover possession of the Kingston
estate, which was the subject of the deed of gift, will be
continued, and that an endeavour will bemade to regdin
possession of the whole of the property, or at all events
to induce some of the present holders to consent to a
compromise. It appears, however, that this is riot
likely to be effected so easily as was at first imagined.
It would seem that some portions of the property
were sold by Mr. Roupell in comparatively small
amounts, under £5,000, and the holders of these
portions may possibly be ready to agree to some terms of
compromise, rather than incur the expense of defend-
ing an action of ejectment, and possibly losing the
whole of the property they had purchased. In a! good
many instances, however, it appears that very large
sums of money have been advanced by insurance com-
panies and other large corporations of the like kinctupon
portions of this property, and it is said that they are de-
termined not to lose their money without a struggle, and
that they intend to take the opinion of a jury upon the
question whether Mr. Roupell has spoken the truth in
charging himself with forgery, or whether, after having
squandered his inheritance, he has not resorted to this
extraordinary scheme with a view to procure a restitu-
tion of the property to his family.
The will and the deed of gift that were the subjects
of the indictments against the prisoner at the Central
Criminal Court have been ordered by Mr. Jusliicoßyles
to be retained in the custody of Mr. Avery, the principal
officer of that court, in order that they may be forth-
coming on any future occasion when they may be re-
quired.

articles.title: TILE GLASGOW MURDER.
articles.text:
TILE GLASGOW MURDER.

Several meetings have already been held by the sym-
pathisers with the woman M`Lachlin, and 'the Korth
British Mail says that Sir George Grey will have a
pressure put upon him probably unequalled in his- expe-
rience as Home Secretary.'
The Inverness Courier has the following The un-
fortunate heroine of this tragedy is, as she stated, a
native of Inverness, 28 years of age. Her father,
William Mackintosh, came from Strathdearn, and
struggled hard here to bring up a numerous family.
He wrought some time as a sawyer, and afterwards
kept a small butcher's shop in Waterloo-place. 'Jessie
has been gone from this town about nine years, but
visited her relations last year. Many here recollect her
as the smart barmaid or waiter in a public-house at the
shore, kept by one of her sisters.'
The Edinburgh Courant says In connexion with
Jessie M‘Lachlan's "statement," a neglected piece of
evidence has been recurred to, which seems to be imsome
tleg,ree corroborative of an important averment in that
document. The prisoner said that old Mr. Fleming,
after inflicting the
,wounds on the deceased, took off and
burned his shirt at the kitchen fire. On Saturday, 12th
July, the day prior to Jessie 111‘Lachlan's arrest, and
while old Mr. Fleming was in custody, the authorities
proceeded to the house in Sandyford-place, and made a
minute search for all articles which might import guilt
or participation in the murder. Among the ashes under
the kitehen grate the officer found a shirt button,_ burnt
but entire. It was taken possession of and preserved;
but, appearing to have no connexion with the case one
way or other, and especially as no burnt clothing or what
appeared to be burntclothing, was found, and there being
only one button, it was thought to have no bearing on the
case, and was accordingly' thrown aside. After the
statement, however, the button was remembered, and
the article, fortunately, has been kept in safe custody.
It bears unmistakeable evidence of having passed
through the fire, and although whole when found, has
now to some extent crumbled away.
•A distinct seg-
ment, however, still remains. The disclosure of this
little incident on Friday naturally tended to increase
the excitement in the Case. It is undoubtedly a likely
enough thing that the button was thrown into the fire
previous to the fatal encounter; and the fact that dressed
shirts were actually hanging over a screen in the kitchen
that night may favour the supposition that the deceased,
in dressing them, threw a loose or broken button into
the fire. It may also be said that if Jessie 141‘Lach-
lalt's story is true, we ought to find, not one, but several
buttons.
We have just been informed that Mrs. M`Lachlan is
pregnant.

INNOVATION NOT ALWAYS IMPROVEMENT.—The Elin-
btvgh Courant remarks Nothing so conciliates the
youth of Europe to innovation as the notion that inno-
vation is the clever and generous man's natural side—
that it brings talentforward—and that only old fogies are
interested in the maintenance of the old principles.
But let those who have believed this look at America,
and they will see dolts and vulgarians dragging their
countrymen under fire, and getting them shot like birds
at a battue, with a stupidity worthy of the lower
animals. There has hardly been a good thing said, or
written, or done, since the war began, to counterbalance
its constant brutalities and habitual rudeness.'
Loss or A. LlvEnrooL COTTON SHlP.—lntelligence
has been received at Liverpool by the Cape mail of the
wreck of the ship Swithamley, of Liverpool. The tele-
gram states that the Swithamley, from Bombay for
Liverpool, had been totally lost on the Blenheim Reef,
Cape of Good Hope, but that the crew were saved. The
S withamley, Weir, sailed from Bombay for this port on
the 4th of June, with 2,975 bales of cotton. She left
Liverpool for Kurrachee on the
•31st of August last
year. The Swithamley was built in the year 1844 by "
Messrs. Moore and Co. of this town, for the trade be-
tween Liverpool and India, and was classed A 1 in red
for twelve years, since which time she has been repaired
and re-classed. She was of 620 tons regieer. This,
with the loss of the America, from Bombay, with up-
wards of 7,000 bales of cotton, -already reported, makes
a total loss of upwards of 10,000 bales.
EXCITING OTTER HUNT.—The other day a party of
gentlemen, among whom were Sir Thomas Ersliine and
Colonel M`Dougall, met at Dairsie Bridgejor the pur-
pose of engaging in an otter hunt. The party, accom-
panied by a number of trained otter dogs, proceeded
down the river to. within half a mile of Guard Bridge,
but during the whole of their progress they never had
the pleasure of having a single cry.' They then re-
traced their steps, and not long after reaching their ori-
ginal starting-place, the dogs set off at full cry, and the
chase commenced in right earnest. After pursuing the
otter up the water for some distance he disappeared, but
after a short time' reappeared, and was hotly pursued
both by the dogs and the gentlemen. A second time
the dogs at fault, but the same or another otter
appearing farK:sr up the water, they were again in-
stantly in full cry. On reaching the boat-house, near
Tailabout, the otter took refuge in a drain and a small
dog was sent in after him, which :in a little time reap-
peared with a bleeding proboscis, and otherwise show-
ing symptoms tif having been engaged in a desperate
encounter. The drain was then opened from above to
discover the precise whereabouts of the otter, and having
accomplished this, means -were taken to drown him out.
He was now completely at the mercy of his pursuers,
who agreed to allow the fugitive liberty and life for a
little longer. The chase will be resumed on an early
day.—Dundee Advertiser.

articles.title: VIEW-AR IY IfEAICO.
articles.text:
VIEW-AR IY IfEAICO.

A letter from Vera Cruz, receivedthr6ngh New YOrk,
gives the following nein relating to the state of affairs
in Mexico:—
The army of General de Lorencez has not been the
object of any fresh attack on the part of the troops of
Juarez,. and it is probable thatiheditter will not hence—
forth attempt anything hostile. It wao at one time re-
ported in the French camp that General Zamgoza in-
tended marking the Insperialfete-of the 15th of August
by an attack on the French intrenchments. But the
state of his forces rendered such a project foapossiblo; as
they scarcely eitist as a united corps,. and a letter which
we have before us affirms that he could not succeed in
assembling more than 0,000 effective troops. The
liberty allowed to the soldiers of carryin& on war-
fare in small bands—which suits- them infinitely
better than, a regular canapaign—has-eOmpleted the dis
organisation of an army which never had any great
cohesion. There may be expected, rather, on the part
of the Juarez generals, a system of tactics totally differ-
ent from that attributed to them by letters from the
Mexican capital. The intention, on the contrary, is to
effect a still greiter division of the troops, and to scatter
them as guerillas all over the country, so as to harass
the progress of the French, both between Vera Cruz
and Orizaba, and between that town and Puebla and
Mexico. An organized resist ,nce would only be opposed
just in front of the capital; the Government would per-
haps even abandon it and retire to Moreria, leaving to
time, isolation, and the difficulties of a prolonged occu-
pation the task of tiring out the patience of France. This
plan, the author of which is General La Llave, meets,
however, with an obstacle which renders it impossible,
that is, the increasing disorder manifested both in the
Government and in the country. The misunderstanding
which has so long existed tetween Juarez and Doblado
had degenerated into an open rupture. The Minister
gave in. his resignation on the 14th of August, and
retired to Guanajuato, taking with him the military
contingent of that State. Already for some time past
he had formed a sort of Proetorian guard, in the midst
of which he lived atsTacif-saya, not trusting himself at
Mexico, where he feared some ill turn of Juarez. A
pronunciamento is evidently in preparation. Already
overthree-are spoken of as made by Doblado to Almonte,
-'-to consider the means of a:Voiding the shedding of
blood.' The meaning of that is well known. At
same time, it is announced that the ports of San Bias
and Manzanilla, on the Pacific, have declared in favour
of the French intervention,; the town of Colima has
done the same, and the report of a similar movement at
Guadalajara is current.

articles.title: ANOTHER GREAT STORM. 117
articles.text:
ANOTHER GREAT STORM. 117

ALGERIA.

Setif and the valley of Boumerzoug, near Consta.ntina
(Algeria), were visited last week by one of the most
destructive btorms of hail, rain, and wind ever known in
that part of Africa. The storm passel rapidly over Con-
stantixa itself without doing much injury, but burst
with indescribable fury over the country of Kroubs and
the Oued-Tmenia. In the former place not a vestige of
cultivation remains. The hail literally cut all the grow-
ing crops to pieces, and the river of Ain-Guedjaou, swelled
to a torrent, swept everything before it, leaving a bed of
mud in some places not less than three feet deep. Sevo-
'ral houses were thrown down, and one woman drowned
At Oued-Tmenia and Setif, the hailstones were of enor-
mous size, and the flood from the mountain torrents
came down with such rapidity that a great number of
Arabs assembled-for the marketat theformer place were
soon breast-deep in the water. Some of them took
refuge on a large iron roller used for the roads, and
weighing at least six tons; but in vain, for the water
drove the roller a distance of 1,000 metres, and all of
them were drowned. Ninety-five men perished at this
place, and of 250 pigs brought • for sale only one
escaped. When the flood subsided the bank of the
-torrent were strewn with the dead bodies of men and
animals. At Setif, not less than-100,000 tiles were broken
by the hail, and nearlY all the game and ffiall domestic
animals in the environs were killed. All the-inhabitants,
40 in number, of a kabyle villiage;about four leagues
from Setif; were drowned, and their houses destroyed.
One dead bady was carried by the Bou-Selam to
Djidjelli, more than 30 leagues. During the storm the
cold was intense, and many-Arabs who had been carried
aw4by the torrent were fain& clinging ,to trees, and
frozen to death in thatposition.—Gatignani.

articles.title: LION IftLYR
articles.text:
A LION IftLYR

_ .
A letter from Bathna, in the Independant (of Constan-
tina, contains an account of a recent 6.Xploit'Of The lion-
hunter, Chassaing in that neighbourhood..
Numerous depredations had been -committed among
the flocks belongingtto-the:Arab village .nf. T'amint,
.at
the foot of a hill near the river Bouariff, and the pre-
sence of a large lion was clearly demonstrated .from the
amount of injury done. Chassaing arrived in the vil-
lage on the 12th, and- in Spite of a heavy rain imme-
diately explored the high ground, inquiring into the
resorts of the animal, and arranging his plans. Tha
spot chosen by him for his operations was a ravine, near
which the lion had a few days -before killed- a fine
sheep. There, by his directions, the Arabs fastened an
old mule to a st +kg aS a bait, and then retired, -Chassa-
ing at the,same time fixed himself in a convenient,
ambuscade.. Night came on, and .the rain increased.
Nevertheless, about , eight in the evening, a, lion ad-
vanced to the mule-and seized on it. The darkness was
such that Chassaing hesitated, and it was only when the
lion had satiated itself, and was about leaving, that he
fired. The moans which followed showed that the
animal was wounded, but from the obscurity Chassaing
did not venture to follow up the attaCk. The moaning
soon ceased, and Chassaing remained in his ambuscade
until two in the liiprning,,. when the moon appearing
through the clouds, enabled him to distinguish around
At about forty paces distance was seated a lioness gravely
watching the remains of the mule. In about fen minutes
she appreaehe the carcase, when ,on her turning her
-her hide to The place of Chassaing's concealment,
exposing her right flank, the htioter fired both barrels.
One-of the-balls fractured the thigh of the animal, while
the second, lodging in the intestines, burst, bringinr, her
dead to the ground. At daybreak Chassaing followed
for some distance the, traces of the wounded lion, but the
rain had so completely washelthe ground they were at

after quoting our declaration of February, 1861,

THE DANDY AND THE WAITER.-,-At a West-end
eating-house the other evening a young and fully mous-
tached dandy was seated at the table at rather a late
hour, when the waiter, according to custom, when the
work of the day was over, came in and took a seat
directly opposite. ' The dandy tipped back his chair,
• and, gazing at the waiter, exclaimed, 'Fellah, do the
servants mix with the gentlemen in this house No,
Sir,' was the reply.—' Are you not the waiter Yes,
Well, a waiter is as much a servant as the
scullery maid.'—' True,' replied the waiter, but I did
not enter the room until I lookdd in and saw there was
not a gentleman at the table!' Here the Conversation
ended.

The theatres selected, with the managers of which an

Railway ; the Pavilion, Wlaitechaiel - road ; and
Sadler's Wells Theatre. The first Sunday in October
has been appointed for the opening service at each
establishment.—Era.
