Letters from St. Petersburg inform us that Russia
celebrated her thousandth birthday, on the 20th inst.
There were great rejoicings at St. PetersWarg and
Moscow, but the chief festival was held at Nevogerod,
which, as our readers are aware, is regarded by native
historians as the cradle of the Russian Empire-, though
the Poles assign a more modern origin to what is now.
called 'Russia,' and look upon, it merely as anaggran-
disentent of the Grand Duchy et Moscow, whose- Tartar
traditions it continued,- and has not yet entirely de-
parted from. But if the political origin of modern
Russia is to be found in old Muscovy,' and if Mus-
covy had the misfortune to be subjected for two
centuries and more to the Tartars—to whom she
never would have been abandoned by Western Europe
had she consented to abjure- her ancient religion
and, acknowledge the supremacy of the Pope—that is
surely no reason why the Russians of the present
day should not look back to the period before the
Tartar invasion, and trace their history through various
channels to its true starting point. The founder of St.
Petersburg was of the same race as the founder of
Moscow, and the founder of Moscow was lineally
descended from Mirk, the great Russo-Norman, who,
when the Republicans of Novogorod were disgusted
with liberty, kindly went over to tr.em a thou-
sand years ago to teach them the blessings of
despotism. As, in spite of this more or less friendly
invasion, the Novegorodims retained their popular
institutions until many centuries afterwards, when they
were destroyed by the Moscow Czars, it is clear that
despotism in Russia was of a milder character in the
ninth century than it has shown itself-on several occa-
sions in the nineteenth. For this reason, and. on account
of the reflections which Novooc'orod.raust suggest, it is
well that thatsity should have been chosen for the great
conignemorative festival that has just been held. About
half a thousand years have now elapsed. since the
establishment of the Czarate of Moscow,, and, ac-
cording to many historians, it is- there,, where the-
great bell of Novogorod is preserved as a trophy
taken from the free city after the massacre of its
inhabitants, that the Russian Empireourcht to celebrate
its birthdays. Any departure, however,, from Musco-
vite traditions is desirable; and no man—not even an
Emperor—can be expected, in recalling his ancestors,
to dwell upon the merits of those who are known to
have been the least meritorious. Whatever strict his-
torians may say, it is better that Russia should regard
Novogorod and not Moscow as the cradle of the
Russian monarchy.' Besides, in plain truth, Russia
has not inherited. Tartar-Muscovite- traditions alone.
Novogorod and the other duchies in which representa-
tive institutions were maintained were not without
their effect on the central duchy whish destroyed and
absorbed them. At the beginning of the 17th century
the first of the Romanoffs was elected by the States-
General of Russia., and, in accepting the crown accepted
also a constitution, which was abolished by Peter the
Great, but which since his death has been constantly
redemanded-; in the reigns of Nichalas, Alexander 1.,1
Catherine, and her predecessors, by conspirators; in
that of Alexander IL by the, nobility of the Empire in
open assembly.
Our letters state that on the 19th inst. the Emperor, the
Empress, the heir to the throne and the Grand Dukes
Alexander, Vladimir, Alexis, Michael, and Nicholas, with
the Grand Duchesses Marie and Olga, proceeded by the
Moscow Railway to Sotnitzki, and thence by steamer to
Novogorod, where they were by the nobility of
the province, the merchants of the city, and the elders
of the village communes. The banks of the -river
Volkov were lined with. peasantry, who are said to have
exhibited the greatest enthusiasm and to have filled the
air with shouts as the Imperial steamer passed.
On Sunday, at a quarter to 1, the news was re-
ceived by telegraph at St. Petersburg that the com-
memorative monument had been uncovered at
Novogorod. This was announced to the city by a
discharge of artillery from the citadel. A Te Daum
was sung in the Cathedral of St. Isaac, where Divine
service had already been performed by the Archbishop
of Riga, in presence of the chief military and civil
authorities. The Square of St. Isaac- was filled With
troops of all branches of the service, who, after the
'To Deran; were paraded by the General-Governor
(Souvaroff.) The peasantry were in a -Very excited
state, but wherever General Souvaroff, the Emperor's
representative, appeared, he was received with acclama-
tions.
St. Petersburg was illuminated in the evening, and
gratuitous performances were given at the Grand Opera,
the Maria Theatre (Russian Opera), and two other
theatres. Outside the Kazan Church. the Novogorod
monument was reproduced in illumination lamps.
Monday (21st) was also to be kept as a holyday.
None of the Russian newspapers appeared on Sunday,
nor were expected to appear on Monday.

The will of Richard Warwick, Esq., of Wydrington-
House, Cheltenham, Gloucestershire, was proved in the
London court under £140,110U personalty. The testator,,
who died in June last, executed his will in December,
1861, and was possessed of very considerable property,
comprehending realty and personalty, the latter com-
prisin-g, a large number of shares in various public com-
panies. Thislatter property the testator has bequeathed,
in certain specified portions amongst his executors for
their sole use and benefit, and also to his sister, nephews,
nieces., and other relatives and -friends. The bequests
are liberal and numerous. There are also annuities left
to three nieces and to a son of a deceased niece, and
legacies to the testator's servants. His real estate and
the remainder of the personal property, together with
his 'residence, furniture carriages, &c., he leaves to
his nephew, William Atkinson Warwick, Esq., whom
he has noininated residuary legatee.—The will of
the Rev. George Clayton, late of Great Gaines,
ITpminster, Essex, was proved in London, on the sth
instant. The will bears date 1859,.. This well-known
Dissenting minister, who died in July last, has left
both real and personal property, which he has be-
queathed, with the exception of some legacies to friends
and others and charitable bequests, to his wife and the
members Of his family. To his wife he has beTieathed
a life interest in his real and personal estate, and, upon
her decease, he has apportioned his farms and other pro-
plrty amongst his nephews and niece. To his daughter
Mary he has bequeathed a life interest in certain funded
property, and 'upon her decease the following charities
will receive the rev. gentlanan's benevolentconsider; :-
ton, viz.: The British and Foreign Bible Society; ditto
School Society; Congregational Fund to Believe Neces-
sitous Ministers of the Gospel; Orphan Working Sehcol,
ILverstock-hill ; New Asylum for Infants and Father
less' Children; London Missionary;, Congregational
School, Lewisham' the York- street Chapel Sunday-
school, Walsworth ; ditto Girls' School; Royal Humane
Society; Religions Tract Society; British School, Tip-
minster ; and Surrey Mission Society—to each a legacy
of £lOO is bequeathed; also £4OO to/the trustees of the

Jones, Esq., took place on the 27th at- the- Guildhall.
The-Sheriffs elect had entertained the Aldermen and the
members of their companies—the Carpenters and
Spectdele-makers--at the Albion Hotel, from whence
they proceeded in procession to Guildhall, and were
received in the Aldermen's Chamber. A procefsion was
then formed, consisting of the Lord Mayor, preceded by
Mr. Sewell and Mr. Beddome, the sword and mace-
bearers, the Recorder, the Sheriffs and Sheriffs elect, the
Comptroller, the Rernembrancer, the Town clerk and
other officers of the Corporation, and they preceded to
the hustings erected at the east end of the Guildhall,
where the oaths were formally administered; after which
Sheriffs_Cockerell and Twentyman divested themselves
of their chains and brooches and suspended them on the
necks of the new Sheriffs.
AN AUSTRALIAN COMBAT.—Never did I see anything
more horrible! The two men fought like wild beasts,
and for a time Mrs. Hughes and myself looked on. For
a quarter of an hour did I watch these two men, each
endeavouring, by every means, however unfair and
contrary to the rules of Boxiana, to injure the other
mortally, when at last Hughes succeded in getting his
opponent on the ground, and, to my horror, to commence
battering the wretched man's head upon the ground.
Disgusted; I thought it time to interfere, and seizing
hold of David by his neckcloth, I tore him off his prey,
when, to my infinite disgust, Hughes's spouse rushed
at the man, who had not yet risen from the ground, and
began to batter his head with a quart pannikin. Quitting
David, I 'min went to the bully's rescue, and snatched
the tin pot frem her hand; and I believe, had not the
servants have come in I should have received awful
punishment at the hands of both host and hostess.—
Stretton' s Mmoirs of a Chequered Life.

Lucxy DAYS—The Angio-Saxons deemed it: highly
important that a.. child should be born on a lucky day,on
which the whole-tenor of his life was supposed to depend;
for, in their opinion. each day had its peculiar influence
upon the destiny of the newly-born. Thus, the first
day of the moon was preferred to all others for the
arrival of the little stranger, for they said, a child born-
on that day is sure to live and prosper.' The second day
was not so fortunate as the first, as the child born on,
that day would. grow fast, but not live long.' If he-
were born 'on the fourth thy of the moon,, he was
deStined to be &great politician • if on the 10th, a great
traveller; and, if on the 21st, a bold marauder. But of
all the days of the week on "-which to be born,, Sunday
was by far the most.lucky, and it it fell on the new moon,.
.the child's prosperity was destined to be unbounded.
Friday was an unlucky birthday, not only because it
vas the day of the crucifixion of our Lord and Saviour,
but because, according to Anglo-Saxon calculAtions,
Adam.ate the forbidden fruit on a Friday, and, was also
expelled froni paradise, and died and descended into hell
on. that day.—The Anglo-Saxon Home. By Jahn

A TALE OF FUNNY SOE, HAINES, THE COMEDIAN.
—One day Joe was arrested by two bailiffs for a debt of
twenty pounds, just as the Bishop of Ely was riding by
in his carriage. Quoth Joe to the bailiffs,'Gentlemen,
here is my cousin, the Bishop of Ely; let me but speak
a word to him and he will pay the debt and costs.' The
Bishop ordered his carriage to stop, whilst Joe close to
his ear 'Whispered—' My 'Lord, here area couple of poor
waverers, who have Buell terrible scruples of conscience
that I fear they will hang themselves !" Very well,'
replied the bishop. So, calling to the bailiffs, he said—
'You two men, 'eonee-to me to-morrow, and I will satisfy
you.' The .bailiffs.bowed, and went their way. Joe
(tickled in the midriff, and _hugging himself with his
device) went his way too. In the morning the bailiffs
repaired to the Bishops house. Well, my good men,'
said his reverence, what are your seiuples Of con-
science?" Scruples!' replied the bailiffs, awe have no'
scruples ;- we are bailiffs, my Lord, who yesterday arrested
pout consiff, Joe Haines, foetwenty pounds. Your Lord-
ship promised to satisfy us to-day, and we hope you will
be as good as your word.' The Bishop to prevent any
-further scandal to his name, inimediately paid the debt
and costs.— Chambers' s Book of Dar.
LOED 'BACON AT ELS COVNTRY SEAT.—He isi now at
home, in his own manor, a house of his owndesign,
and among his own books.' He can 'walk under the
shadarrof his own oaks, and gain health anew, in. his
-own broad acres. Suitors in Chancery may murmur at
delays—his thoughts are not now in law, or-of law.
Here he will receive Ben .Tonsen on his foot pilgrimage
towards Scotland, and, in parting, tell Ben pleasantly
(Jacobuses not forgotten), that he did- not care to see
poetry go on any other feet than dactyls and Spondees.
Here he can walk and talk with Master Thoreas Hobbs
of Malmesbury, who then, young as he was, was most
skilled in catching the thoughts that breathe and words
that burn—falling at every second step from a head so
wise and lips so ready. Here, playing with .the strings
of his bared all the while (as was his wont), he can
fathom the- instability of human greatness, and think
little, and care less for what posterity may say about
him.—Once a Wee; .
TAPEW,OHM IN THE ET.—The son of a shopkeeper,
residing in Berlin; having complained that he could not
see so well as. usual with. one of his eyes, was conducted
to the establishment of Dr. Graefe. On examining the
patient, the doctor said it was lucky the child had been
promptly brought to him for he declared that immedi-
ately behind the iris of the affected eye there was a tape-
Worm ! This parasite he added, would undoubtedly
have soon completely destroyed the organ of 'vision, in
which it had taken up its quarters. The doctor said it
was a wonder thatittch cages were not more frequent.
They arose, he observed, from eating underdone or un-
cooked meat, and most generally pork.—Letter from
Berlin. .
TURKISH SOLDIERS.—The infantry presented- anion
creditable appearance than any I had yet seen, and the
encampment generally looked clean and orderly. Camp
life is under no cireumstanses a very agreeable phase of
existence, and least- of all in Eastern countries, when
divested of the excitement resulting from the probability
of an
.attack. L. other lands there is sure to be some
thing to attract the mind. Staff officers in gay uniforms
pass and repass in all the iinportance of official haste,
comets of cavalry bent on .performing the onerous
duties of galloper, and the pompsous swagger of infantry
drum-majori, all combine to vary the scene and amuse
the eye. .Bat in Turkey this is not so. All are equally
dirty and unkempt, while the hideous attempts at music
have very far *Alm a soothing effect. An attentive
listener may hear a single,voice four times in the day
calling to prayer; a custom which, wader no circum-
stances, is ever omitted: 'Of the internal response to -
this appeal I am of course unable to judge, but from
outward appearance I should
_imagine it to be small.
The Pachas, it is true, indulge in the soineWhat unin-
tellectal amusement of twiddling a chain of beads,
talking on indifferent subjects the while ; but I never
observed even this 'Sinai] tribute of respect amongst the
inferior. officers. And thus the day wears on in dull
monotony; until at sunsets - crash of many voices may
be heerd from the, centre of the camp, rising up to
heaven, and calling down a blessing on the Sultan's head.,
---Herzgeovino.

Good luck is to get up at six o'clock in the morning;
good, if you have only a _shilling a week, is to live
upon eleveripence and say.e . penny; good tack is to
trouble your head with your OWH business, and let your
neighbours 'alone; good luck is to fulfil the &minuend-

unto us. They must not only work, but waif. They
must plod and persevere. Pence must be taken care of,
because they are the seeds of guineas. To get on in the
world, they must take care of home, sweep their own
door Ways clean; try and help other people, avoid temp-
tations, and have faith in truth and God.—De Fiala s
Delores.

cester and Hereford Railway, through the Malvern-hills,
the tunnel has been made Sufficiently- secure for the
passage of trains, and the regular-traffic through the
tunnel has been resumed. The work of-shoring up the
shaft and making it 'secure in its altered position.was
conipleted oh the 25th, and tharst Train passed' throngh

half-past 8 o'clock. The work .has been completed in so
substantial a manner wider the direction of Mr. Wilson,
the engineer of the. West Micllana- Railway; that no
further mischief is apprehended. It seems the air shaft
sunk bodily a distance of 15 feet,- penetrating the arch
of the tunnel, and pressing into the earth beneath

ROPEMAKERS' Appeal to the Metropolitan
Trades, and Trades of the United Kingdom.
BROTHER ‘,l ORKIN° MEN: It is With ft feeling of reluc-
tance that we, the London 0, erative Ropemakers, ven-
ture to draw your attention to our present position,
knowing as we do the great depression of trade in almost
every department of manufacture, and yet we Gel
encouraged to lay our case before you, soliciting, your
sympathy and aid, by the conviction that we are well
known by the London trades, and to many trades in the
country, for our willingness to assist tltters in times of
difficulty. We will therefore simply state our case to
you, hoping that you will deem it worthy of your kind
eor: sideration.
On the 11th of last June one of our employers offered
a reduction of sevenpence per day, or three and six-
pence per week, from our wages, and we, having a: well
organised trade society, could nor, submit to :any reduc-
tion of wages,' recognising as fair work:nen should do
that a iair days work is entitled to a fair day's pay, and
having enjoyed the present rate :of wages for the last
seven years, and there being no reasonable plea given
why such reduction sheuld take place.
Having sent deputations to the employers to reason
the matter with them, and used every effort to pre-
vent a strike, but finding that: the employers were
determined if possible to effect a general reduction of
wages throughout the trade, there was no other course
ieft us but to withdraw the whole of the journeymen
from the firm, viz.—Messrs. J. and H. Baker, Bermond-
sey, This is the eighth week. of the strike, and our
men are firm and in good spirits, being convinced of the
,iustness of their, claims and ultimate success, for al-
though the firm has resorted to all kinds of .misrepre-
qentation to obtain men their shop is still•empty, for as
fast as the men come up from the country through their
egents and advertisements in the country. local papers,
they (the men) after having the question of dispute
explained to them, leave their work, and by our assis-
tance leave London again, which creates alarge expense
over the actual cost of keeping our own members on
strike. We have expended over £l5O, a large sum for
only one firm, but then we are fighting for the whole
trade, for some of the other employers have already
given notice to their men, that as soon as Messr. Baker
and Brothers get supplied with men at ths reduction
that they will give no more for their work than the
Messrs Baker's, and- if we are compelled to submit to
this reduction we shall lose £1,500 per year in wages
• (then leaving a large surplus of men oat of work), a sum
yon will admit worth struggling for. .
- Having thus briefly stated our present position we
earnestly appeal to the sympathy of our fellow workmen
in other trades, soliciting their assistance to enable us to
defend successfully our right of wages and tt ade against
these grasping employers. In appealing to our fellow
working men, we may soy that we have had always a
willing heart and ready hand to assist other trades
placed in similar circumstances; indeed, since 1853 there
has not been a question affecting the interest of the
working classes, or a dispute in any other trade, but
what we have supported and sustained to our utmost
ability. We therefoib make this appeal ' with some
.;.egree of confidene, that you will nastily respond to us
Ito our present difficulties, and show to the employing
classes that there is a spirit of union and brotherhood
amongst the working men of Englalid, that will enable
them to rally round their fellow but oppressed brother
workmen. -
We beg to remain yours very respectfully, on behalf of
the trade. Thomas Hay, Charles Howe, William Matthews,
Charles Terdre, Robert Still, committee; Richard Bur-
ridge, treasurer; Daniel Smith, secretary.

to any society to give the information that may be re-
quired, or forward any information on. the question of
dispute, by applying to
